articles.title: Jordan: Karak church shooting leaves 7 dead, dozens injured
articles.summary: A shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan happened during a funeral, according to local authorities. Two unidentified men opened fire on the procession.

image.caption: Jordanian state media published surveillance video of the attack in the village of Hammoud in Karak Governorate Image: Al Mamlaka TV/AFP

blocks.text: A shooting at a church in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak left seven people dead and another 34 wounded on Friday, Jordan's public security director Obaidallah Maaytah said.
What do we know so far?
The shooting occurred at the Hammoud Church. The shooting reportedly occurred during a funeral.
The attackers' identities and motives remain unclear. Two men opened fire on the funeral procession.

A witness told Jordanian state media there were 150 to 200 people present at the church at the time of the shooting. Videos circulating online showed wounded people on the floor of the church covered in blood, but this footage cannot be verified by DW.

Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said a group of "extremists" carried out the massacre. According to Jordanian outlet Roya News, Al-Faraya said authorities already possess the names of suspects behind the attacks but they will not publicly disclose the identities as of now.
Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said security forces have launched a probe into the attack.
Jordan King Abdullah II: 'We will strike with an iron fist'
Jordan King Abdullah II said "the terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation."

"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," Abdullah II said, adding, "We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation."
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, a Christian, also condemned the "heinous terrorist attack" in Jordan and expressed condolences to the victims.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the news regarding the attack is "devastating."

"Praying for the victims, their families and all those affected by this depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship," Waltz said. "Attacks on Christians continue to escalate worldwide and must be stopped."
Gun attacks like the one on the church in Karak are rare in Jordan.

Although Jordan is largely a Muslim-majority country of around 11.5 million people, there is a small Christian minority of a couple hundred thousand. The Karak region, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of Amman, has a significant Christian population.

articles.title: Home distillers rejoice as US Supreme Court considers whether to finally legalise moonshine
articles.summary: The Supreme Court will consider in the new year whether the 1868 legislation forbidding home distilling should be overturned.

blocks.text: Wyoming mechanic and amateur moonshiner Geno Stecks proudly details the modifications he's made at his two-bedroom home to facilitate his hobby of distilling liquor in his own home.
"I turned my dining room into my shining room," boasted the bearded 66-year-old, who uses a power drill fixed to a bowl to mix some of his recipe.

Two years ago, he began tinkering with recipes for home-producing spirits. The pastime has taught him new skills and given him a signature product to share with friends and neighbors - "coffee-flavoured shine". It also happens to be illegal under US law.
"You know, keep quiet - don't make commercials or nothing," Stecks said.

But some home distillers hope they won't have to keep their hobby a secret for longer. The Supreme Court announced this week that it would reconsider the 1868 legislation forbidding the practice, and hobby distillers hope that their spirits will soon be treated like beer and wine, which are both legal to brew at home across the country.
Plaintiffs who brought the cases say Congress overstepped its powers in restricting distilling for tax purposes during the Reconstruction era. They want the highest judges in the country to agree.
But lawyers for the government argue that Congress's measure was lawful, and necessary to stop producers from avoiding taxes.

One lower court found the almost 160-year-old ban unconstitutional, but in a separate and similar case, another lower court came to the opposite conclusion. The Supreme Court will hear the case early next year and could make a ruling in the summer of 2027.
Currently, distilling alcohol in a private home carries a penalty of up to five years in prison, a $10,000 (£7,460) fine or both.

"The particular law in question here is both absurd and unconstitutional," said lawyer Robert Alt, representing the plaintiffs. "It's interesting to note that this is a hobby which is as American as apple pie - and certainly a lot older."

Alt, Stecks and many proponents of the change point out that George Washington himself distilled spirits at home. Historian Daniel Pierce told the BBC that home distilling was first criminalised for revenue purposes, requiring anyone making spirits to pay a tax.
When federal agents began enforcing the law, small farmers who were distilling on the side as a way to make some extra money or to barter were left with few options.
"If you're a large distiller or something, you could afford to [pay the tax], but for most people, it was out of the question," Pierce said.

When the US implemented Prohibition - the nationwide ban on the production and sale of alcohol between 1930 and 1933 - it created a whole new market for illegal distillers, particularly moonshiner, Pierce said.
NASCAR, the racing sport, was born out of the high-speed, modified cars that bootleggers once used to transport illicit liquor and outrun the law.
Many continued their illegal distilling after Prohibition's end, often passing on family recipes in secret (or, at least, in tightly-knit circles) for generations.
Then moonshine and home distilling enjoyed a new renaissance in the early 2000s, he said, thanks to reality TV shows like Moonshiners, the internet and popular culture.
"You start to get this pretty dramatic revival…. in terms of home distilling," Pierce said.

Rick Morris, the founder and president of the Hobby Distillers Association, was one of the challengers who sued in Texas to change the law. He first entered the drinks industry working with soda machines and bottled water, then became a hobbyist home brewer of beer and wine with his wife.
They made a frustrating discovery when they tried to take the "next step" into distilling.

"It didn't make sense," he said. "I could make beer, I could make wine, both perfectly legally … and it was frustrating that I couldn't take what I had already legally made and do one more step to it, to start to try to make a bourbon or a brandy."
The allure for Morris and many other hobbyists, they say, is the mechanics and innovation behind the process.

"There is a lot of science and details to get straightened out, but there is still a big vein of creativity in the art that goes into it - blending flavours and aromas and all that," said Ohio challenger John Bream, an aerospace engineer by trade.
He first took up the hobby when his wife gave him a home-brewing kit around 17 years ago. He set up his operations in their kitchen but "made too many messes and got kicked out into the garage".
"Through homebrewing, I became aware that going to the next level of distilling was illegal … so I stayed away from it," he said.
But he realised he could be "part of the force for good" by joining legal challenges to the archaic law.

Not everyone is on board with the move, Courtney Armour, chief legal officer at The Distilled Spirits Council of the US, told the BBC. She worries about the challenges and dangers that come with home producing.

"The distillation process can be quite dangerous, including risk of explosion, burns, fires, and more," Armour said. "The spirits industry has a clear focus on safety and process management to mitigate these risks, but even in that careful environment there are still accidents, injuries and even fatalities."
And then there are health concerns that can arise when alcohol has not been produced properly.
"In a home-distilling setting, these dangers would not just be limited to the individuals engaging in the production but also their neighbors in the surrounding area," Armour said.
While home distilling remains federally banned, states like Missouri and New Hampshire have passed legislation allowing the production of certain amounts at home for personal consumption.
Attorney Alt pointed out that "alcohol, traditionally, has been an area of state regulation … so this question of state versus federal authority is really at the very heart of this case".
Alt also said the legal challenge addresses what oversight federal authorities have on home activities.
"This circuit court said, look, if the federal government is right on this, there's almost no limits to what they could ban at home in the name of taxation," he said.

Distillery owner and former Missouri state representative Don Gosen said he helped shape the state's 1995 law allowing residents to distill 100 gallons of spirits at home per year per person - or 200 gallons per household.

"I've never seen the federal government come and fine anybody for doing it, because it's kind of small potatoes … and so a lot of people, I believe, still do it, kind of behind the scenes like in the old days," Gosen said.
Many people have come to him for advice over the years, not knowing about the federal law. Some bring him their homemade bottles and ask his opinion, he said.
"I'll taste it, and it'll be terrible," Gosen laughed. "And I'll throw on a happy face and say, 'Oh, it's wonderful' - because they made it. They love it."
Gosen, Morris and others within the industry believe legally allowing home distilling will only help it grow.

"Home interest generally turns into a better consumer, a more educated consumer, a more sophisticated consumer, just a consumer that spends more," Gosen said. "You're going to have people like myself that are going to start opening our doors to home distillers and have classes for them and help them out."
Back in Wyoming, moonshiner mechanic Stecks agrees that more people will start home distilling if they don't risk penalties and prison - and sees only growth and good things coming from legalisation.
"That'd just make it better," he said.

articles.title: Undas 2026: Bus terminals see early passenger surge for holiday exodus
articles.summary: Several passengers have started traveling to the provinces more than a week ahead of Undas, filling bus terminals early either to beat the holiday rush or to secure their tickets before the surge of…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 11:20pm

Several passengers have started traveling to the provinces more than a week ahead of Undas, filling bus terminals early either to beat the holiday rush or to secure their tickets before the surge of crowds.

In a “24 Oras” report by Marisol Abdurahman on Friday, security at the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) was noticeably tighter, with baggage required to undergo inspection and scanning, while K-9 units were also deployed to check some bags.

The PITX expects passenger volume to reach up to 1.8 million from October 25 to November 4, but noted that some commuters might schedule their trips with the long weekend for the ASEAN Summit from November 16 to 18.

Several passengers queued at ticketing booths—some were buying tickets on-site, others who booked online were retrieving their boarding passes, while some found that tickets to their destinations had already sold out.
Precila Macatangay, a passenger, went to PITX early hoping to travel to Bicol immediately. However, she was only able to secure a 9 p.m. trip.
“Wala nang available. Mas maganda sana earlier para kunyari dating namin dun para umaga safe kami sa pag-uwi sa kaniya-kaniyang baloy,” Macatangay said.
(No earlier trips were available. It would have been better to leave earlier so we could arrive in the morning and safely head to our respective homes.)
Some passengers also went directly to the terminal to purchase tickets after seeing that the next available trips online were already scheduled for Sunday.
According to PITX, certain routes really fill up quickly, but they are assured that there will be enough trips for the Undas exodus.
“Makakasakay at makakasakay pa rin sila dito sa PITX dahil marami naman tayong nakaabang na additional units,” PITX spokesperson Jason Salvador said.
(They will definitely be able to get a ride here at PITX because we have plenty of additional bus units standing by.)
At the Araneta Bus Port in Cubao, Quezon City, the situation remains quiet, although some travelers have also opted to head to the provinces early for Undas.
A passenger shared that while they usually travel to their province in their private vehicle, they chose to commute this year due to high fuel prices.
“Sayang naman ‘yung gas, mas mahal sobrang mahal… Para makatipid, sakto lalo't may inaasahan na namang tataas ang presyo ng diesel sa susunod na linggo,” said Merlee Mendoza, a passenger.
(Gasoline is too expensive now... To save money, commuting makes sense, especially with another diesel price hike expected next week.)
The Araneta City Bus Port management stated that they are also expecting an influx of province-bound passengers in the coming days.
“We will be expecting ng karagdagan ding ruta. May ini-expect kaming isang operator papasok to Bicol,” Araneta City Bus Port Manager Ramon Legazpi said.
(We are expecting additional routes. We expect one operator to open trips heading to Bicol.) —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: A novel mRNA cancer vaccine helps cut the chances of melanoma tumor recurrence in major study
articles.summary: A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients' tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and…

image.caption: After the results of a major study of Moderna and Merck's new mRNA cancer vaccine were leaked on Thursday, the companies released the full data ahead of the planned Saturday reveal. (LookerStudio/Shutterstock.)

blocks.text: Health·New

A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients' tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and Merck.
Combined with an existing treatment, the vaccine helped reduce risk of melanoma returning by 42 per cent
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 23, 2026 11:10 AM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago

The vaccine was custom-brewed for each patient to match their tumor. Adding it to a standard post-surgery treatment reduced by 42 per cent the risk of melanoma returning two years after surgery, according to the most advanced study to date of this new strategy for fighting cancer.
"The field has been looking for a win, and I think this one is a big one," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi of MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, one of the researchers in the international study.

The vaccine, called intismeran, is made with the same Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology that was behind COVID-19 vaccines. Experimental personalized cancer vaccines made with mRNA and some other approaches are also being tested against other types of cancer, including lung, kidney and pancreatic.
Experts not involved with the new study say its success bolsters the field.
"This is a new frontier," said Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute, which helps fund cancer immunotherapy research.

"It's a big step forward for science, for oncology, because this vaccine will apply to many different cancers," said Dr. Michael Atkins, deputy director of Georgetown University's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.

When combined with an immunotherapy treatment, the vaccine reduced recurrence by 42 per cent, the study states. Experts say this new vaccine advances the field of cancer prevention. (Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters)
Moderna and Merck had announced in August that the late-stage trial of intismeran was successful.

The detailed results were set to be released this Saturday at a meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology in Madrid, but after some of the data was leaked publicly late Thursday, the companies provided a full release ahead of the weekend's scientific presentation.
Inside the personalized vaccine

Most people think of vaccines as preventing an infection, like measles or whooping cough. There are already two cancer-preventing vaccines, the HPV and hepatitis B shots that block infection from those tumor-causing viruses. And research is underway to prevent some types of inherited cancer such as Lynch syndrome-caused colorectal cancer.

But a personalized vaccine designed to block surgically-removed cancer from returning is very different. For the intismeran study, scientists hunted gene mutations unique to each patient's tumor — mutations that create proteins that shouldn't be in the body unless those cancer cells start to grow again. The custom vaccine — nine doses given three weeks apart — teaches the patient's immune system to watch out for and attack those so-called neoantigens.
mRNA skin cancer treatment shows promise: drug makers

How did it work? The study included more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma that was surgically removed. Everyone was given the standard follow-up therapy: Merck's immunotherapy named Keytruda. The participants were randomly assigned to also receive custom-brewed vaccine doses or a placebo.
Two years later, 82 per cent of the people in the vaccine group were still living without a recurrence of their cancer compared to 70 per cent who had gotten standard Keytruda alone.
"This is highly statistically significant. It is not by chance," Tawbi, the MD Anderson Cancer Center melanoma expert, told Reuters of the results.

items: Merck and Moderna say mRNA melanoma vaccine hits goals in late-stage trial
U.S. FDA approves first mRNA flu shot from Moderna

blocks.text: The trial is continuing to track participants' longer-term outcomes.

In 2024, Tony Hout joined the vaccine trial at MD Anderson after seeking care for a spot on his ear that had been bleeding intermittently and wouldn't fully heal. Doctors recognized melanoma and during surgery discovered it had started to spread.

"I want to make sure I'm doing everything I can to be here for my family," said Hout, 62, who has since moved to Cayuga, Ind., and travels back to Houston every few months for a study check-up. Scans this week showed he's still cancer-free.
Tony Hout, left, talks with Dr. Hussein Tawbi at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, on Monday, in this video still. (Lekan Oyekanmi/The Associated Press)
The vaccine's side effects were mainly the sore arm, fatigue and other reactions typical of mRNA coronavirus vaccination, MD Anderson's Tawbi said.
Moderna and Merck are talking with regulatory authorities about next steps for seeking approval of the vaccine.
Shares drop after leak
Customized medicines generally are very expensive. The drugmakers aren't discussing what such a cancer vaccine might cost.

items: Ontario cancer patients speak out over disappointment with drug funding decision
Can you ever truly cure cancer? Canadian researchers are using blood biopsies to find out

blocks.text: But Moderna president Stephen Hoge said the company's special cancer vaccine manufacturing facility in Massachusetts is providing doses for thousands of people enrolled in multiple studies underway internationally.

Hoge said it takes a few days to brew the vaccine, but the whole process, starting with analyzing the tumor genetics to come up with what is essentially a recipe for each patient, can take roughly six weeks, sometimes more. Meanwhile, the melanoma patients had already started their standard Keytruda, a different kind of immunotherapy.
Moderna, Merck stocks surge after promising mRNA melanoma vaccine testing
Moderna shares have soared since the companies in August announced the trial's success without the actual data, nearly quadrupling through Wednesday's close.

After the study’s full results were leaked Thursday on an oncology website, Moderna shares dropped 18 per cent, but remained more than 200 per cent higher than they were before investors were first told in August of the initial results. Merck shares closed down about 1.8 per cent.
Several Wall Street analysts said before the meeting that investors were looking for the combination of the vaccine and Keytruda to cut the risk of recurrence more, Reuters reported.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: US justice department investigating Corey Lewandowski over DHS role
articles.summary: Trump's former campaign manager is reportedly being investigated for allegedly using his role at the Department of Homeland for financial gain.

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice (DOJ) is investigating whether Corey Lewandowski, who was a top aide to former Department ⁠of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem, personally profited from his role, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

Lewandowski worked closely with Noem as a special government employee until March, when the two were both ousted after a series of controversies, including the fatal shootings of US citizens by immigration officers.
The probe is related to contracts the agency signed under Noem's leadership, a source told CBS.
The BBC has contacted Lewandowski's attorney, who told CBS his client denies any wrongdoing.
"Mr Lewandowski has not been contacted by the justice department regarding any investigation," his attorney, Adam Trigg, said.
Asked about the investigation on Thursday, President Donald Trump told reporters he had heard about it but did not know the details, adding, "I want my people to be honest".
"And if they're not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted," he said.
Lewandowski served as a campaign manager to Trump during his first presidential run in 2016 and helped advise his 2024 campaign.
DHS officials told Reuters that Lewandowski had approved some DHS contracts despite not having the legal authority to do so as a special government employee.
He also allegedly put certain grants and contracts on hold, including some involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the officials told Reuters.
Special government employees serve as temporary advisers to federal agencies and are given strict limits on how much they can work and what they can do.

The justice department took on the investigation after receiving a referral from the DHS inspector general's office, which is made up of lawyers charged with monitoring the agency's conduct and operations.
At DHS, Lewandowski served as Noem's de facto chief of staff.

Noem also faced a contract controversy. Shortly before she left office, lawmakers pressed her about the process she had used to award a $220m (£164m) advertising contract to two companies with ties to her and people in her inner circle.

The Wall Street Journal has reported, external that Lewandowski also allegedly tried to use his role at DHS for financial gain by asking Middle Eastern countries to hire him on the side to help with visa and other DHS issues.

articles.title: Afghan women could lose one of their last paths to a higher education
articles.summary: The US has defunded the last university giving Afghan women the opportunity to receive an education after the Taliban takeover in 2021. DW spoke with a student who says she's lost hope of ever…

image.caption: After the Taliban banned women from attending university, students turned to online classes Image: ALI KHARA/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Laila" awoke in the middle of the night for a glass of water, checked her phone almost by accident, and saw an email that made her stomach drop. The US would stop funding the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF), one of the last places women can still study in the country.
Laila said she sat on her bed, staring, her thoughts racing through the past five years and everything she had endured just to get an education.
It had not been easy to find a way to study in Afghanistan after the Taliban outlawed women's education.

The American University campus was already taken over by the Taliban, but she could study secretly through the university's online program. But now that the university is losing its financing, she told DW she and her classmates fear it will shut down entirely. Her name has been changed for safety reasons.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban
A hidden education for women in Afghanistan
Laila is in her mid-twenties. She studies political science and international studies and is one of around 1,000 enrolled students at the university, three-quarters of them women.

When the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Laila was studying at another university in Kabul, with just two final exams remaining to finish her semester. Then, in December 2022, the Taliban announced the ban. Laila's degree was left unfinished.
Laila secured a scholarship to AUAF and started over. "Not every girl got that opportunity," she said.

Laila has told few people outside of her family about her online studies. On most days, she stays home for remote lectures, alongside classmates who use aliases and keep their cameras off for security. "I just know their voices," she said.

Laila speaks English with an American accent. She learned it as a child, watching cartoons. In her early twenties, she was learning even more about the world outside Afghanistan and studying foreign governments.

Then on August 14, 2021, Laila's life changed. She and a friend sat in a restaurant in Kabul. They had just finished an exam and wanted to celebrate passing the test by ordering coffee and cake. Suddenly, a man came in, stopped at the entrance, and shouted "Allahu Akbar." He yelled that the mujahideen would always be victorious.
That was the day the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan, they soon forced women out of public life, banning them from many jobs and from attending school and university.
Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights

Laila said she recalls losing feeling in her hands or feet. She pulled money from her purse and slammed it on the table without checking the amount. "We all thought maybe this would be the last day that we are alive," she said.
Since then, some of Laila's peers have received threatening calls and messages. Now, whenever she leaves home, she worries that Taliban authorities might search her phone.
"What if they see my emails from my work, from my university?" she said. "It's always in the back of my head that maybe tomorrow it's my turn. Maybe they will detain me."
Even her home isn't safe. Laila said Taliban authorities have entered on several occasions to search their belongings.
Yet, she has continued studying. For all its limitations and risks, the online program offered a chance to graduate.
A place for Afghanistan's 'future leaders'
With the US pulling out as the university's primary funder, Laila said she doubts whether she has the strength to start over.

The American University of Afghanistan was always intended, largely, for women. Before the campus opened in 2006, former US first lady Laura Bush announced that the US had committed millions to support it.
Appearing in Kabul, Bush said the new university would teach "future leaders," particularly women. Women like Laila, who was four years old at the time.
"These are more than just development projects," Bush said at the time. "They also signify the bond between the American and Afghan people. They are symbols of our shared hopes and dreams."

Patrick Fine was Afghanistan mission director at USAID, the now-defunct American development agency. Fine told DW that many at USAID considered the university idea risky. Critics thought training elites was a waste of money.
But the Bush administration saw an opportunity to stabilize a budding democracy, Fine said.

By 2003, the Taliban had been driven from power. US President George W. Bush wanted to foster goodwill for the US-backed interim government that had replaced the Taliban. The university served that goal, and also offered other "facets of advantage" in educating women, training future politicians, and supporting the Afghan economy.
"It really impacted the lives of thousands of Afghan youth," Fine said, referencing alumni. "The organization has managed to achieve that against incredible odds."
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan
Washington pulls the plug
The university continued with US support. But in Washington, that support started to come under question.

The US government suspected the university of mishandling money. In 2016, US inspectors opened an investigation into its finances. By 2018, investigators said they could not tell exactly how it was spending US aid money, because its accounting was so poor.
John Sopko, a former US federal inspector, oversaw that investigation. When DW contacted him for this story, he replied, "I was surprised they were still funding AUAF."

This year, after the funding was pulled, the US State Department Press Office told DW in an email that the move was made given the university's "history of repeated lack of accountability for millions of American taxpayer dollars."
Fine, the former USAID director, rejected the State Department's fraud explanation.
"Those are just smear tactics," he said. He conceded that past audits found the university struggling to keep up with USAID's extensive rules, "but they didn't find major fraud," he said.
"It is still a useful investment, a worthy investment," Fine said, "and the reason for that is that it's one of the few organizations left that is reaching Afghan women."
The US isn't the university's only funder, but it has long covered most of its costs: nearly 90% as of 2018, according to a US report.

The US State Department told DW that the university is "free to identify other funders and partners, so the end of their receipt of American taxpayer money does not necessarily equate to an end to their operations."
But without the $25 million grant the State Department recently refused, the university's future is in doubt.
What is next for women students in Afghanistan?
"I have lost all my motivation and hope," Laila said, adding that each time she prepares for a lecture, she wonders whether there will be another.

Since she learned about the funding cut, she said she's barely left her room. Her curtains are usually closed, and she's lost her appetite. "Maybe I'm so disappointed that I can't even cry about it," she said.

She said she was supposed to have graduated years ago. She was supposed to be making the world a better place. She was supposed to be in studying a master's degree abroad. Now, she's thinking, maybe she'll find a way in five or ten years.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the Shamonda virus?
articles.summary: France recently reported its first case of the Shamonda virus, with the patient reportedly dying; authorities are still determining if the virus caused the death. But what is the Shamonda virus?

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 10:52pm
France recently reported its first case of the Shamonda virus, with the patient reportedly dying; authorities are still determining if the virus caused the death.
But what is the Shamonda virus?
According to GMA News Feed, the first case of the Shamonda virus infecting a human was reported in France on October 22.

According to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control, the patient died earlier in October while being treated for a “serious illness,” which made the patient more vulnerable to the virus.
French authorities suspect that the patient was bitten by a midge that carried the virus in the eastern part of the country.

The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) said that the Shamonda virus reportedly affected cattle more often, but there have also been cases where sheep, goats, horses and alpacas were infected.
The Shamonda virus is vector-borne and is transmitted through midge bites.

While there is currently no evidence of animal-to-animal transmission of the virus, WOAH says that vertical transmission, or transmission from a parent to the embryo, fetus or newborn, has been reported.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the Simbu serogroup. Other members of the group include the Schmallenberg virus, a virus that can cause reproductive disorders in livestock.
It was first identified in Nigerian cattle in 1965, according to the WOAH. Since then, the virus has also been reported in other regions of Africa and Asia.
European cases of the virus were first identified in July 2026.

Signs of the Shamonda virus in animals include fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, reproductive disorders such as abortions and fetal malformation. Less commonly, there can be neurological disorders, which have been reported in horses.
The WOAH said that the Shamonda virus has not infected humans historically,
The World Health Organization said that the case in France is likely isolated and is unlikely to spread.

“The general public, fit, well people, have very little to worry about from Shamonda. It's primarily an animal pathogen… The disease is fairly consequential in the animals that get infected and will cause economic problems for any farmer or farms, etc., that are affected by the virus. But human populations certainly, at the moment, from everything we know, have very little to worry about,” said Senior Lecturer in Virology Ben Brennan of Glasgow University said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton show
articles.summary:
Cate Blanchett and Hannah Waddingham join William on sofa for special edition to celebrate prince’s Earthshot prize

The Prince of Wales has braved the chatshow sofa, making a surprise…

blocks.text: The Prince of Wales has braved the chatshow sofa, making a surprise appearance on The Graham Norton Show.

In the pre-recorded show, to be aired on Friday on BBC One, William made a surprise appearance in a special Earthshot prize edition to promote his environmental initiative, which has an annual awards ceremony due to be staged in Mumbai, India, next month.
The prince revealed his family’s love for The Celebrity Traitors show, saying: “I love it, the family love it. Charlotte and Louis are obsessed with it. It’s really good telly.”

blocks.caption: Prince William, Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on the Graham Norton Show. Photograph: Matt Crossick/PA

blocks.text: Speaking of the EastEnders star Ross Kemp’s fear of being murdered by touch in plain sight on the Traitors show, he joked: “I saw Ross Kemp the day after the first episode and I couldn’t help but try – in the most appropriate way – to touch him to see what reaction I got from him. Turns out he was really jumpy!”

William, the first royal to appear on the chatshow, also revealed he switches off through music and film. “I love getting immersed in deep-thinking films. I like action films too, but I like something a bit different. I’m a big fan of everything Christopher Nolan does. His films are fantastic – The Dark Knight series is psychologically dark and deep and I absolutely love that.
“He takes concepts that are completely out there and makes them incredibly entertaining.”

Joining him on the sofa were the actors Cate Blanchett and Hannah Waddingham, and the environmentalist Robert Irwin, who are all connected to the Earthshot prize which was founded by William in 2020 to recognise and reward issues and ideas to help save the planet.

William told Norton and the other guests about the origins of the prize and its role in identifying and supporting innovators around the world. He said: “For many years I was hearing stories about environment issues, and one thing that struck me was the negativity and doom, which got me down.
“I thought we could do something more powerful and more optimistic and the idea of an awards’ ceremony came about and we could talk about urgency and optimism together.
“It’s all about getting excited.”

articles.title: US supreme court sides with Republicans on rejecting student IDs in New Hampshire midterms
articles.summary: Voting rights advocates say directive would disenfranchise young and low-income voters, but Republicans say it’s needed to combat voter fraud

blocks.text: The US supreme court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to prohibit student IDs as a form of voter identification ahead of November’s midterm elections.

In a brief unsigned order, justices sided with a Republican National Committee (RNC)-backed appeal on the matter. They cited a longstanding rule that lower federal courts should not “alter election rules” too close to election day.

The challenge stemmed from a directive that New Hampshire state officials made earlier this year, which stated student IDs could not be used as a form of identification when voting at the polls, even as a backup under what is known as “safety valve” identification.

New Hampshire has required voters to present an ID to vote since 2012, but earlier this year the state’s Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, signed a law tightening the rules by removing student IDs from the list of standard forms of voter ID.

Voting rights advocates had challenged the directive, arguing it would disenfranchise young voters, who may not have access to a driver’s license or passport. But Republicans insisted the directive was needed to combat voter fraud.
A lower court judge blocked the directive, leading state officials to ask the supreme court to intervene.
The dispute involving voter ID requirements highlights a national debate triggered by Donald Trump and other top Republicans who argue that voter ID laws are necessary to prevent mass voter fraud.

Despite there being little evidence that voter fraud affects the outcome of elections, the president and his allies have seized on the narrative to convince lawmakers and conservative voters to back initiatives that require ID at the polls.

Voting rights advocates argue that voter ID laws can disenfranchise low-income voters who may not be able to afford a government-issued ID, voters who may not have access to official documents, such as a birth certificate, to obtain an ID, rural voters who may not be able to go to a location with ID services and more.
after newsletter promotion
While the supreme court justices did not disclose how they voted on the matter, Ketanji Brown Jackson, a member of the liberal wing of the court, dissented from the majority.

Jackson argued the lower court did not err when it blocked the directive because the lower court judge was asking state officials to correct guidance which “could mislead voters and local election workers”.

articles.title: Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster', White House says
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia have not confirmed the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.

blocks.text: US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October, though Ukraine and Russia have so far not commented.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added.

Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.

articles.title: Nobody Wants This creator says she disagrees with Adam Brody’s ‘free Palestine’ comments
articles.summary:
After Brody called out the ‘death and misery’ in Palestine, the Netflix hit’s Jewish creator said they don’t see eye to eye

The creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has…

blocks.text: The creator of the hit Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This has responded to star Adam Brody’s recent support of Palestine amid the Israel-Gaza war.
“Everyone is entitled to a different opinion,” Erin Foster said in an interview with the Not Skinny Not Fat podcast when asked about Brody calling for a free Palestine.

“You know, it’s complicated,” said Foster, who also has an acting role in the new season. “I think our work environment, our set is very similar to dinner tables around the world where people are having debate and discussion and disagreeing.
“While I love Adam, I also disagree with him. And that’s OK.”
Nobody Wants This, which returns for its third season this week, chronicles the unexpected love story between agnostic podcast host Joanne Williams (Kristen Bell) and rabbi Noah Roklov (Brody).
The story was inspired by Foster’s own real-life love story after she converted to Judaism after meeting her husband.

“As the creator of the show, all I can say is that I want our Jewish fans to know that I see you and I hear you and I understand how you feel,” Foster said. “The show has always been and always will be a love letter to Judaism. That is why I made this show. It’s because of how beautiful of an experience I’ve had becoming Jewish and being a Jewish person.

blocks.caption: Adam Brody and Erin Foster in Nobody Wants This. Photograph: COURTESY OF NETFLIX

blocks.text: “Sitting here right now at this time in the world where there is almost zero positive representation of Jewish people, I think it’s so important to have that.”

Last month, Brody opened up about his political views for the first time. “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” he told GQ. “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

Nobody Wants This’s third season sees Joanne and Noah move in together while their siblings continue to look for love. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Jack Seale said the new episodes will make fans of the show “fall in love with it all over again”.
Foster has often posted about the Israel-Gaza war on social media.

“Nothing that is happening in Israel/Palestine is acceptable or comfortable to look at,” she wrote in 2021. “Innocent lives lost as casualties of war, as well as the atrocious lack of human rights that exist under a Hamas run government.

“There is a chance for peace here, and it involves a two state resolution where both exist next to each other, respecting each other’s beliefs, and sharing the holy land that all three major religions call sacred. Palestinians deserve to live in peace without fear. So do Jews.”
An independent UN inquiry in June found that Israel continues to commit genocide by targeting children in Gaza.
The Guardian has reached out to representatives for Foster, Netflix and Brody for comment.

articles.title: Allegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrative
articles.summary: Duchess of Sussex’s decision to cut ties with elderly father cast in new light as he faces sexual abuse image claims

blocks.text: The depiction of the Duchess of Sussex by certain sections of the media has often been one of a fame-hungry daughter casting off an elderly father in his declining years and keeping him from his grandchildren as she embraces the international celebrity stage.

Their estrangement has been the subject of countless headlines since her marriage to Prince Harry. But her statement today, released after child sex image allegations made against Thomas Markle Sr, 82, suggests deeper, darker fears as the cause.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said.

It has been speculated that the source of the estrangement between Meghan and Markle Sr, an award-winning TV lighting director, was over his decision to collude with a photographer and be paid for setting up shots of him preparing to attend the Sussexes’ wedding at Windsor Castle where he was due to walk her down the aisle.

In the end, Markle Sr pulled out due to health issues, and it was Harry’s father, now King Charles, who lent the bride his arm on her final steps to the altar of St George’s chapel after she walked the first part of the aisle alone.

Since that day in May 2018, the relationship between daughter and father has never recovered. Now it appears the reasons why are contained in a letter from the same year, sent to the Metropolitan police and containing “troubling and disturbing allegations” against Markle Sr and shared with Meghan in the summer after her wedding.

blocks.caption: Thomas Markle Sr on ITV’s Good Morning Britain in June 2018. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The precise nature of those allegations has not been clarified, though they were enough for Meghan to want to keep her own family at a distance from him, her statement makes clear.
The fact she says that “the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine”, suggests the 2018 letter did not go as far as what has now been alleged.

Markle Sr has vigorously denied the latest allegations, which are made by his son Thomas Markle Jr, 60. First published by the Sun newspaper, they claim Markle Sr downloaded child sex images to computers and mobile phones found at his former home in the Philippines.

He has called the accusations “sick lies” from a son with whom he has a troubled relationship, and claims to have had no access to the computers and phones in question in the two years since he left Mexico, where he was previously living, for the Philippines, according to the Daily Mail.
Meghan clearly hopes to reframe the narrative of her estrangement from her father, which has often been shaped by his loquacious tendencies in many media interviews.
after newsletter promotion

When speaking to journalists, Markle Sr has frequently lamented the breakdown of his relationship with his youngest daughter (he has two other children, Samantha Markle and Thomas Jnr, from an earlier marriage). He has spoken of how he has been unable to reach Meghan, and of how he has never been allowed to meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The media depiction has often leaned towards that of an uncaring daughter, whose father paid for her education, helped sow the seeds of her acting career and found himself abandoned in his time of need.

For the most part, Meghan has not publicly acknowledged his many health woes – he has suffered a series of strokes and recently had a leg amputated due to complications with a blood clot – and she clearly believes this has been weaponised against her.

However, in 2025, Meghan’s spokesperson confirmed that the duchess had “reached out” privately to her father when he was hospitalised and very unwell. He is now understood to be in a rehabilitation centre in Florida undergoing physiotherapy after the amputation of his leg.
Whatever the outcome of this latest development, it adds a new dimension to the complicated, fractured relationship between Meghan and her family.

articles.title: Romania blames Russia for ship attack in the Black Sea
articles.summary: Russian strikes against ships attempting to export Ukrainian grain and cargo through the western Black Sea have sharply increased this month.

image.caption: Romanian president blames Russia for the ship attack in western Black Sea [FILE: May 2026]Image: Malina Norocea/Inquam Photos/REUTERS

blocks.text: Romanian President Nicusor Dan blamed Russia for an attack on a merchant vessel in the Black Sea on Friday morning.
A drone strike sank the merchant ship, with 13 Ukrainian and Azeri crew members on board, near Romanian territorial waters.
The attack killed at least 1 sailor, and three others were still missing, according to Dan.
Nine of the 13 crew members have been rescued.
Attack on merchant shipping on the rise in the Black Sea: What to know
The drone strike on the ship, called Khoryv, is believed to be the fourth merchant vessel to have been attacked off the coast of Romania this month.
Two weeks ago, two merchant vessels were also set ablaze in the western Black Sea, which is a vital shipping corridor heavily used by Ukraine.
One of those ships was inside Romanian territorial waters. Romania raised concerns about Russian provocation in waters at the edge of or controlled by NATO members.
That's because Bulgaria, also a NATO member like Romania, has raised similar concerns too.
Bulgaria has raised concerns about Russian strikes having edged too close to its exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea after merchant ships were hit by drones earlier this month too.
Both Romania and Bulgaria have blamed Russia for the attacks and have called on the alliance to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
NATO said earlier this week that it was sending more maritime patrol aircraft and radar systems to the Black Sea without having blamed any country for the attacks there.
About 23 sailors had been reported dead or missing in incidents in the Black Sea in the 10 days leading up to October 15, according to Reuters.
That tally is higher now.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, condemned the increasing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea too, earlier this month calling it "unacceptable" that "the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

articles.title: Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia
articles.summary: Repeated Ukrainian drone attacks are increasingly disrupting operations at Moscow's airports. The pounding is part of Ukraine's plan to shut down Russia's airpace.

image.caption: Passengers wait in line at Moscow's Sheremetyevo International AirportImage: Alexey Belkin/Russian Look/news.ru/press.media/picture alliance

blocks.text: For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.

In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.
The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Poland's ex-president: Putin's war in Ukraine was a miscalculation
Can Ukraine succeed?

Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.

"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."
Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.

blocks.caption: Sheremetyevo International Airport is the busiest in MoscowImage: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."

"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.
Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.
Can Russia stop Ukraine's drones?

Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.

Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.

Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.

In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.

The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.

blocks.caption: The site of the Azerbaijan Airlines plane shot down by a Russian missileImage: Meiramgul Kussainova/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."

In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.
Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.
How will international airlines react?
Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.

He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.

Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.
"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: what’s next for France? Ask our Europe columnists – live
articles.summary: Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst are taking questions from readers about the riots and protests in France. Join the discussion in the comments
articles.byline: Rokhaya Diallo, Alexander Hurst, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation

blocks.caption: The Hôtel de Ville in Limoges, central France, on fire during a weekend of unrest. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors, resulting in a debt sell-off, with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.

The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”

Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”

And the Guardian’s editorial noted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”

What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in which France finds herself?
France-based Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST today to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.
Post your questions in the comments below or email conversations@theguardian.com
Key events

items: 3m agoAre these protests the result of foreign instigation?
10m agoCan any winner solve France's financial crisis?
18m agoHow will France's EU financial contribution affect the elections?
28m agoDo the protests this month compare with May '68?
2d agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Are these protests the result of foreign instigation?

blocks.caption: ‘Foreign actors may try to exploit unrest, but that does not prove that they created it’ … Russian President Vladimir Putin. Photograph: Mikhail Metzel/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP

blocks.text: Mike asks: Are these and other similar protests partly as a result of foreign instigation? We have been warned about such things.

double quotation markRokhaya: I don’t think so. Protests have grown out of concrete, local grievances that have gone unanswered. People took to the streets because they believe in their right to speak out and challenge those in power. I attended some of the demonstrations and met many people protesting for the first time. Foreign actors may try to exploit unrest, but that does not prove that they created it. People’s agency is central to what is happening, and we need not divert attention from the demands that brought them on to the streets.

double quotation markAlexander: They’re not happening because of foreign instigation, they’re happening because there are fully legitimate reasons for them to happen. That said, I think it would be naive to imagine that state actors like Russia – which is already engaged in an ongoing campaign of physical sabotage across Europe – aren’t hard at work using videos of violence as part of ongoing social media manipulation campaigns designed to create anger and division. The Kremlin is no stranger to this, and it clearly wants to propel its preferred candidates into office across Europe and the US with the goal of weakening European unity in general and on Ukraine specifically, having some countries defect on sanctions and strike fossil fuel deals (like Trump recently did), etc. On the other side of the Atlantic, the US far right is also trying to fuel disinformation in service of its own identity culture war and anti-immigration project in order to close out the final weeks before the US midterms.
Can any winner solve France's financial crisis?

Michael1611 asks: As Jon Henley suggests in his recent column, public attitudes to Macron have toxified the entire centrist bloc. But if (as seems very likely) Marine Le Pen’s RN party wins the election what on earth can they do that is viable in economic terms, given the financial crisis the country faces? It seems to me there is a risk of a huge backlash when the promises they are making cannot be kept?

double quotation markAlexander: I’m going to repurpose a trite phrase and say that nobody’s political programme is going to survive first contact with France’s coming debt crisis. The French thinktank Terra Nova did a breakdown of the RN’s error-riddled economic plan, which seemed to have been co-created with or at least edited with AI. Interest rates on French debt are already unsustainably high, and the RN has already voted against raising taxes on the wealthy and the ECB isn’t going to run to bailout a far right government promising to go to battle with EU’s institutions, so it will be left with budget cuts and betraying everyone who thinks Le Pen will actually lower the retirement age. Unfortunately, the same probably goes for Mélenchon (even though I think the chances of him defeating Le Pen are extremely small, given the persistent polling on that matchup), who will probably face a similar situation of spiking interest rates and EU partners who will want things in return … and he’s already made ‘disobeying’ a central point of his future relationship with the EU. So, why would they offer a condition-free bailout to a country with a lower retirement age than their own citizens enjoy (even in the Nordics where many benefits, like year-long paternity leave, are more generous than they are in France), and that’s made antagonism and confrontation its starting point? The EU mismanaged the last financial crisis in ways that were more costly than it should have been, and resulted in a lot of lost time. Hopefully it won’t repeat those mistakes the next time – but that’s also predicated on having national governments in power that are able to build coalitions around what those different approaches might look like. As far as public attitudes, I think the major point is that France has very low tolerance for rising inequality, or for the suspicion that the rich are getting off easier than everyone else – and this is certainly what tanked Macron from the beginning with a huge chunk of the electorate. There’s no path forward to social calm without the wealthiest people paying more than they are today.

blocks.caption: Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of French far left opposition party La France Insoumise, delivers a speech to public sector workers. Whoever wins will have to deal with France’s looming debt crisis. Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Reuters

blocks.text: How will France's EU financial contribution affect the elections?

wyrcommunity asks: How do you envisage the financial contribution by France to the EU playing out across the various political groupings at the next elections, given France’s escalating financial problems, and that Macron has previously defended the funding of €2tn for the 2028-2034 EU budget, which will equate to a French contribution of c. €38bn-a-year?

double quotation markRokhaya: The RN is likely to use this to argue that France is financing Europe while neglecting its own population. Other parties will need to explain what European spending delivers and how it should be funded, which is legitimate. The proposed €2tn budget is still being negotiated, so I would be cautious about presenting the €38bn annual French contribution as a settled commitment. To me public finances involve political choices, including choices about raising revenue. France’s debt cannot become a permanent justification for leaving schools understaffed and buildings deteriorating. As I wrote in my Guardian column last week, the economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris, for example, propose an inheritance tax reform that could generate €11.8bn in additional education spending. It would target only the largest inheritances, the wealthiest 1% of heirs. So there are alternatives to asking that public services are cut back and ordinary households to absorb further austerity. The presidential election debate should address who contributes, who benefits and which investments serve the public interest. Defending European cooperation requires showing how it improves people’s lives concretely; it cannot remain an abstract commitment disconnected from urgent material concerns.

double quotation markAlexander: Financing the EU based on national contributions is an error that should be corrected. It immediately gives the right an argument that “we” are “sending” money to the EU. It would make so much more sense to replace contributions with an EU-level corporate tax floor to give the EU its own resources, and at the same time prevent race-to-the-bottom style tax policies that fuel tax evasion schemes. I’ve never understood the opposition to this (other than corporate capture, I guess) by states that maintain low corporate tax rates; they would be fully free to go above the tax floor or keep their tax rates as close to it as they wished. And it wouldn’t harm any single state’s competitiveness, since the common corporate tax rate would apply across the board. As far as France’s domestic spending goes, interest payments on the debt will soon become the government’s single largest expenditure, soon exceeding total spending on education. Allowing that to happen isn’t coherent with a vision of social and comic justice. Interest payment on the debt - ie. money paid out to creditors – is going to be €73bn next year, and rising quickly. That is money that cannot be spent on education, healthcare, rural areas, green transition … Raising taxes on the wealthy and on inheritances and cracking down on corporate subsidies and tax evasion is a necessary step, but in the long term, there are other models that France might learn from as well, like sovereign wealth funds that generate returns for the public, instead of leaving the market’s returns to be captured primarily by the wealthy.

blocks.caption: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Emmanuel Macron. ‘Parties will need to explain what European spending delivers and how it should be funded.’ Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPA

blocks.text: Do the protests this month compare with May '68?

blocks.caption: A placard reads “Generation ‘67’ is bringing back May ‘68”. ‘Every generation wants to have its own “Revolution” that then cements its place in the national narrative.’ Photograph: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Eamon McCrisken notes: Comparisons are being made with May 1968 but I think the following should be borne in mind from those times:

‘De Gaulle and Pompidou warned the country was threatened with a Communist coup. De Gaulle announced a snap election, calling upon the French to choose between legitimate government and revolutionary anarchy. The May Events in France were curiously peaceful by the standards of revolutionary turbulence elsewhere, or in France’s own past. The French ‘psychodrama’ (Aron) of 1968 entered popular mythology almost immediately as an object of nostalgia, it was above all a victimless revolution. (Tony Judt, Postwar)

double quotation markRokhaya: This comparison reminds me how familiar the political framing sounds: a social movement with concrete grievances is presented as a threat to the nation, and the public is asked to choose between the government and chaos. That framing allows those in power to elude questions about their own policies and responsibility for the escalation, as it is the case for the current protest. May 1968 was not really “victimless”: people died during the May–June events, including striking workers at a Peugeot factory in Sochaux. Relative restraint compared with other historical upheavals should not erase those deaths. France’s relationship with nostalgia is also something that can be underlined. We celebrate past rebellions while treating those protesting in the present as dangerous or irresponsible. We should take their demands seriously now, while they can still be answered and not wait for the future to romanticise them.

double quotation markAlexander: Part of me loves to talk about national mythologies and how they can also become our national pathologies, and part of me hates it because I know I’ll inevitably end up reducing and simplifying things because I haven’t, unlike Tony Judt, written a chef d’oeuvre like Postwar on it. But to go there anyway, if the US mythology has a large dose of “someday I can get rich, too” in it, I think the French mythology has a dose of “someday, I too can overthrow a despotic government”. I obviously wasn’t around in May 1968, and I didn’t grow up in France, but it does often seem to me like every generation wants to have its own “Revolution” that then cements its place in the national narrative. The country obviously has a high propensity for large-scale street protests and confrontations that don’t really happen in the same way as the US or UK. Lately, I’ve been wishing the US would take some inspiration from the French. But is the confrontational nature of French politics a sign of it working, or a sign that it’s not really working? I’d lean towards the latter.

articles.title: PSG v Lyon moved as Paris prepares for more protests
articles.summary: Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon at the Parc des Princes is pushed back 24 hours as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.

blocks.text: Paris St-Germain's Ligue 1 match against Lyon has been pushed back 24 hours to Monday as the French capital prepares for another weekend of protests.
The fixture at the Parc des Princes in Paris had been scheduled to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Sunday but will instead take place at 20:30 on Monday.
The Ligue de Football Professionnel (LFP) announced the postponement in a statement, external on Friday after French police prohibited the fixture from taking place on its original date.
French authorities are preparing a major security operation for demonstrations planned for Saturday.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations last Saturday to protest rising fuel prices, education standards and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.
Marches took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions and student groups, and were marred by some incidents of violence, looting and destruction.

The security challenge is further complicated by Sunday's NFL match between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints at the Stade de France, an event expected to require a significant police deployment.
The game will be played in Saint-Denis, about 10km from Place de la Bastille, where the protests are expected to begin.
The disruptions have already affected France's domestic football schedule with Toulouse's Ligue 1 home game against Troyes moved from Saturday to Sunday at the request of authorities.
Reigning French and European champions PSG are second in the standings after seven matches, while Lyon lead the table on 14 points, ahead of the holders on goal difference.
The match will also now be played on the same day as the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London.
Injured PSG pair Ousmane Dembele, the 2025 winner, and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are among the contenders for the award.

articles.title: Motorcycle taxi riders urge LTFRB not to drop riders due to over-boarding
articles.summary: Some motorcycle taxi rider groups have staged a protest in front of the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) office on Monday, urging the agency not to drop riders over issues…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 10:12pm

Some motorcycle taxi rider groups have staged a protest in front of the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) office on Monday, urging the agency not to drop riders over issues of "overboarding" and "ghost riders."
In a “24 Oras” report by Jonathan Andal, overboarding refers to a situation where the number of riders on a ride-hailing application or platform exceeds the limit set by the government.

According to Jayson Luna, co-convenor of the Motorcycle Riders Association (METRO), there is a cap of only 15,000 riders per platform, and as of now, the number of active riders on some platforms appears to have already exceeded that limit.
“Ito po ‘yung mga kasamahan namin na hindi alam na napaloob doon sa iba't ibang platform na platform provider. Hindi namin alam kung kami kasama roon sa labis na itinalaga ng gobyerno,” Luna said.
(These are our fellow riders who didn't know they were included in those different platform providers. We don't know if we are among those in excess of the limit set by the government.)
He added that they fear riders exceeding the LTFRB-set limit might be banned from operating.
Meanwhile, the riders' group KAGULONG argued that overboarding is not the riders’ fault, as it was the ride-hailing apps that accepted their applications to become MC taxi riders.

“Ang usapan with the LTFRB ay walang mawawalan ng trabaho, walang maiiwang rider… ‘Yung issue ng overboarding, hindi kasalanan ng rider ‘yan… Kaya hindi dapat ang rider ang mag-suffer dun sa nangyayaring mga kalokohan na ‘yan,” KAGULONG Secretary General Don Pangan said.

(The understanding with the LTFRB was that no one would lose their job, and no rider would be left behind... The issue of overboarding is not the riders' fault... So the riders should not suffer from the irregularities taking place.)
Following the rally, Pangan and Luna were called inside the LTFRB office, where they spoke with the agency's executive director.
In a text message, LTFRB Acting Chairman Greg Pua stated he was in Tacloban at the time.
According to Luna, the LTFRB official assured them that no MC rider would lose their job once the institutionalization process for MC taxi riders moves forward.
At present, riders are awaiting the passage of the law that will formally recognize MC taxis as public utility vehicles.
GMA News is trying to obtain a statement from the LTFRB regarding the matter and will publish it once available. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News
