articles.title: Many feared trapped under collapsed building in Nairobi
articles.summary: People are feared to be trapped after a large, unfinished building in Nairobi collapsed during construction. Rescue operations have proven complicated as police fired tear gas to disperse looters.

image.caption: Building collapses and constructions are unfortunately not uncommon in Nairobi, KenyaImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A multi-story building that was still under construction collapsed in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi on Friday, resulting in casualties and looting at the site, according to local media.
The Nairobi County governor's ​office confirmed the collapse, adding in a ​statement that people may be trapped beneath rubble.
Videos spreading online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building came down in a busy business-residential mixed-use district.
The Red Cross sent teams to the site, posting on social media: "At around 1340 hours, a multi-story building under construction collapsed on 9th Street in Eastleigh, Nairobi."

There were conflicting reports on the size of the unfinished building. Nairobi Police Chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 floors under construction, while other accounts range from 12 to 18 stories.
Governor Johnson Sakaja's ​office said only the building's ground floor ​was occupied.

"There were some businesses in the basement, and workers who were busy building," local resident Abdi Aziz, 25, told the AFP news agency. "But since it was Friday prayers, a lot of them were at the mosque."
Rescue work underway at Nairobi building collapse site
A video published by Reuters news agency showed people gathered at the scene as ⁠an excavator moved rubble.

But rescue operations were proving complicated. Police officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams but had to fire tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops.
Eastleigh is a densely packed residential and market area, known as a hub for the Somali community.

It was not ​clear what caused the building to collapse. Nairobi is undergoing an extremely rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings shooting up all over the city as Kenya's population expands.

blocks.caption: Rescue work was underway in Nairobi, with some people feared trappedImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kenya: How common are building collapses?
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi.
County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with construction standards and safety guidelines.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
Meanwhile, a separate audit of almost 15,000 buildings by the National Building Inspectorate found that 4.8% were very dangerous while 72.3% were classified as unsafe.

The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has set guidelines for delivery riders amid the effects of Super El Niño.

In a "24 Oras" report from Bernadette Reyes on Friday, DOLE met with representatives of online platforms to discuss the welfare of their riders amid the heat brought by the drought. DOLE Secretary Francis Tolentino asked the companies to support their riders.
“Napagkasunduan kung paano ang proteksyon sa mga rider… na hindi ma-pe-penalize ang mga riders at di rin mai-inconvenience ang mga customers,” Tolentino said.
(We have made an agreement on how to protect the riders… that does not penalize them and inconvenience the customers.)
Some of the guidelines set included allowing delivery time to be extended and scheduling deliveries when it is not too hot. If the heat is too intense, then deliveries could be suspended altogether.
There will also be no penalties if the delivery is cancelled because the rider is in danger.
“Lalabas sa app nila na ganito kainit, puwedeng hindi tanggapin ang delivery, at aabisuhan din yung customer na ma-late dahil sa sobrang init,” Tolentino said.
(Their app will indicate how hot it is outside. They may decline the delivery, and customers will also be notified that their orders may be delayed due to the extreme heat.)
The company representatives said that they will ensure the safety of riders.
“The safety and welfare of riders is our number one priority,” said lawyer Marien Lucenario, the Public Affairs Manager of Grab Philippines.
“We are also going to make sure our partner riders are safe and taken care of during El Niño,” InDrive Country Public Policy and Government Affairs Manager Reini Evangelista said.
DOLE is also studying including riders from ride-hailing apps in the guidelines.
However, some riders are still worried about canceling their bookings, as it may affect their standing on the app.

“‘Pag nag-cancel kami, kami mawawalan ng booking, yung account namin hihina… wala kami magagawa pag mainit kailangan pa rin namin maghanap buhay,” delivery rider Michael Remion said. (If we cancel, we will lose the booking; our account will weaken…we cannot do anything if it is too hot; we need to make a living.) —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
articles.summary: Exclusive: Angela Eagle tells utility bosses next price review ‘must focus on value for money for customers’

blocks.text: Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.

Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to lower bills and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.

There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.

Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.

The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.
The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”

The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”
The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.

blocks.caption: Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has written to water companies to demand better value for money for bill payers. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images

blocks.text: Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.

A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.

“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”

The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.

Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.

The prime minister criticised the decision, warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.

However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.

“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.
“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. ⁠Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”

articles.title: Ebola patient in Nigeria did not visit DR Congo, escalating concern over spread of virus
articles.summary:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

An Ebola patient in Nigeria is a Swiss woman who has not travelled to the…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Coast Guard drives away foreign fishing vessel off Lawak Island
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Friday said that it successfully chased off a foreign fishing vessel from the waters of Lawak Island. Friday’s operation is the sixth…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Friday said that it successfully chased off a foreign fishing vessel from the waters of Lawak Island.
Friday’s operation is the sixth time the PCG drove away a foreign vessel within the Kalayaan Island Group (KIG).
The vessel’s position was monitored 2 nautical miles (nm) northeast of Lawak Island, which is well within its 12-nm territorial sea, the PCG stressed.
Upon sighting the foreign ship, PCG personnel were deployed aboard a rubber boat to conduct maritime patrol.
They issued repeated radio challenges and warnings to direct them to leave the island’s territorial waters.
The vessel eventually steered northward away from the island, while the PCG team escorted it from a safe distance.
There were no untoward incidents throughout the operation, the PCG said.
Lawak Island is part of the municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan province.
“Under international law, the Philippines exercises full sovereignty over its territorial sea, where no foreign vessel may fish without authorization,” it stressed.
It added that the act is likewise in violation of Philippine laws, including the Philippine Fisheries Code and the Philippine Maritime Zones Act.

In less than four weeks, the PCG recorded six incidents within the KIG, including China’s fishing vessel YUETAIYU 63168 and four small boats off Lawak Island in Oct. 18 and a foreign fishing vessel off Kota Island three days later.
It also repelled five foreign fishing vessels within the territorial waters of Kota Island last Oct. 11.
Meanwhile, the PCG also reported that Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel 9622 and its sampans were also chased off after being anchored off Kota Island in Sept. 28 and Oct. 9. /gsg

articles.title: Canadian planemaker Bombardier to spend $270M US expanding in 4 states
articles.summary: The company says it will add some 800 jobs and has earmarked millions to expand in Kansas, Indiana, Texas and Connecticut. U.S. President Donald Trump indicated the expansion was coming in a social…

image.caption: Bombardier workers assemble a Global 7500 business jet at the company's Mississauga, Ont., plant on Jan. 22, 2024. The Montreal-based planemaker said Friday that it plans to expand in the U.S., investing $270 million US and creating some 800 jobs. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

The company says it will add some 800 jobs and has earmarked millions to expand in Kansas, Indiana, Texas and Connecticut. U.S. President Donald Trump indicated the expansion was coming in a social media post on Thursday — after he walked back earlier threats to prevent Bombardier from selling in the U.S.
Company says it will add 800 jobs and expand in Kansas, Indiana, Texas and Connecticut
Aerospace manufacturer Bombardier says it plans to invest millions in the U.S. to expand its business south of the border.
The Montreal-based company said Friday it plans to add 800 jobs in Kansas, Texas, Indiana and Connecticut, 500 for which it is actively recruiting.
Bombardier says it's earmarking about $270 million US to build infrastructure in the initial phase of the investment.
The company's president and CEO called the American side of the business a "key pillar" of its growth strategy.

"Based on our constructive conversations with the U.S. administration, we see a bright path forward for our highly skilled aerospace workers as well as a positive environment for Bombardier to continue pursuing direct investments to grow our American footprint," Eric Martel said in a statement.

The announcement comes after U.S. President Donald Trump said on social media post that Bombardier was investing in three of those four states, claiming it would create thousands of jobs. He also credited Sen. Roger Marshal of Kansas and Texas Attorney General Ken ​Paxton for the deal.
Trump tells Bombardier it can't sell in the U.S. unless it builds in the U.S.

Trump had threatened Bombardier in September amid the worsening U.S.-Canada trade war, saying the planemaker wouldn't be able to sell in the States unless it started manufacturing there — despite the company having a factory in Kansas and employing about 3,500 people in the U.S.

items: Trump walks back threat to ban Bombardier sales in the U.S.

blocks.text: The president walked that threat back earlier this week at a rally in Wichita, Kansas, which serves as a home base for Bombardier's defence division.
"I always viewed them as a Canadian company ... but now I find out they have a presence here, and we're not hurting them if they're in Kansas. So we'll take care of those people," Trump said.

The company also recently unveiled its North American Learning Center in Wichita, a facility meant to train newly hired aircraft technicians. A $50 million US investment in that facility is part of the $270 million US announced today, a Bombardier spokesperson confirmed to CBC News in an email.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, state media say
articles.summary: Another 10 people are injured in the southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.

blocks.text: At least seven people were killed when two gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, the country's state media report.
Another 10 people were injured in the church in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car and began shooting inside the church before fleeing the scene.
Security forces have been deployed, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said.
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said the two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.

articles.title: Netanyahu orders ‘very extensive’ operation in West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed
articles.summary:
Israel’s prime minister gives order after military says it thwarted ‘terror attack’ by two armed Palestinians

Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive”…

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint in Hebron.

Netanyahu said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the occupied West Bank for decades, after the Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” by two armed Palestinians on Friday, amid heightened tensions before next week’s election.

According to the Israel Defense Forces, the two assailants opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where the Israeli military believes they had intended to attack civilians. According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes, leaving five Israelis wounded, two of whom later succumbed to their injuries.
An AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank starting on Friday.

After the shooting, the Israeli prime minister held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He said Hamas was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.

During a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
A large-scale military operation named the “Iron Wall” launched in January 2025, forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said, according to his office.

Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. Friday’s lockdown was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads, which will remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area.
Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a military campaign in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”.
He said: “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon.”
Smotrich added: “In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”

Human rights groups warned that Netanyahu and his government could use the attack on Israeli soldiers to justify tougher measures against Palestinians and bolster their security credentials before the election.

“Every day in the West Bank is a dramatic day for the Palestinians,” Yariv Oppenheimer, the former director of Peace Now told Al Jazeera. “The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible.

“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers … making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more.”

Voters go to the polls on Tuesday in an election that will help to determine whether Netanyahu secures another term as prime minister. The vote comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, and authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers, whose violence has surged during the annual olive harvest.

On 16 October settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The next day they attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

articles.title: Who will be the Philippines' next Chief Justice?
articles.summary: The Judicial and Bar Council is in the middle of interviewing five Supreme Court associate justices, all vying to be the country's next top magistrate as Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo retired in…

blocks.text: The Judicial and Bar Council is in the middle of interviewing five Supreme Court associate justices, all vying to be the country's next top magistrate as Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo retired in November.
They are Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa, Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda, Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao, and Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez.
Who will be the next Chief Justice?
Here are brief profiles of the candidates.
Marvic Leonen
Leonen was appointed to the SC by then President Benigno Aquino III on November 21, 2012.

Prior to his appointment, he served as chairman of the Government Negotiating Panel in Talks with the the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process from 2010 to 2012.
He also served as the former dean of the University of the Philippine (UP) College of Law from 2008 to 2012.

He was the Vice President for Legal Affairs for UP Diliman from 2004 to 2008, the General Counsel of UP Diliman from 2000 to 2003, and the Director for the UP Diliman Office of Legal Aid from 1998 to 2000.
Leonen was also the former Vice Chairperson of Friends of the Earth International.
The senior associate justice was also a founding member and former executive director of the Legal Rights and Natural Resources Center and the Sentro Para sa Tunay na Repormang Agraryo.
He was also a member of the Alternative Law Group Network and the Free Legal Assistance Group.
Leonen graduated with an AB Economics degree, magna cum laude, from the School of Economics in 1983. He obtained his Bachelor of Laws degree from the College of Law in 1987.
Leonen also earned a Master of Laws degree from the Columbia Law School of Columbia University in New York.
Benjamin Caguioa
Caguioa was appointed to the SC by Aquino on January 22, 2016.
He also served as Secretary of the Department of Justice and Chief Presidential Legal counsel under the Aquino administration.

Caguioa also chaired the Inter-Agency Committee on Extra-Legal Killings, Enforced Disappearances, Torture, and Other Grave Violations of the Right to Life, Liberty and Security of Persons as well as the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking.
Prior to his government service, Caguioa was a lawyer for SyCip Salazar Hernandez & Gatmaitan (SyCip) in 1986. He served as partner of the law firm from 1994 to 2007.
Caguioa withdrew from SyCip and founded Caguioa & Gatmaytan Law Firm in February 2007.
He graduated with an AB Economics degree from the Ateneo de Manila University in 1981 and graduated with honors from its College of Law in 1985.
Caguioa was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 1986 and ranked 15th in the 1985 examinations.
Rodil Zalameda
Zalameda was appointed to the SC by then President Rodrigo Duterte on August 6, 2019.
Prior to this, he was an associate justice of the Court of Appeals for 11 years and served as the chairperson of its 17th Division.
He was also a Branch Clerk of the Makati Regional Trial Court.
Zalameda was appointed as City Prosecutor of Mandaluyong in 2002 and served as a public prosecutor in 1995.
He privately practiced law from 1990 to 1995.
Zalameda obtained his Bachelor of Laws Degree from the Ateneo de Manila University in 1987. He passed the Bar Examinations in 1988.
Japar Dimaampao
Dimaampao was appointed by Duterte to the SC on July 2, 2021.
Dimaampao served as associate justice of the CA for more than 17 years since 2004 and served as the chairperson of its 3rd Division prior to his appointment.

He also served as a Legislative Staff Officer and as a Political Affairs Assistant IV at the House of Representatives, as a court attorney of the CA, as a senior state prosecutor at the Department of Justice, and as a presiding judge and executive judge of the Mandaluyong City RTC.
Dimaampao graduated from the University of the East College of Law and is a certified public accountant.
Midas Marquez
Marquez was appointed by Duterte to the SC on November 16, 2021.
Before this, he served as a court administrator for 12 years starting in January 2010.
Marquez first joined the SC as an apprentice in 1991 and then later became a law clerk in the Office of Associate Justice Abraham Sarmiento.
He became a court attorney VI in 1995 after occupying various positions in the Offices of Senior Associate Justices Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera and Josue Bellosillo.
In 1999, he was appointed as Deputy Secretary of the Senate Electoral Tribunal.
He also served as then Chief Justice Reynato Puno’s chief of staff from 2006 to 2010.
During this time, he also held the posts of Assistant Court Administrator, Chief of the Public Information Office, and Spokesperson of the Court.
Marquez obtained both his AB in Economics and his Juris Doctor degree from the Ateneo de Manila University. He was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 1994.
How is the Chief Justice chosen?

Under Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, the Chief Justice, other members of the SC, and judges of the lower courts are appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the JBC for every vacancy.
The Constitution states that such appointments need no confirmation.
He shall hold office during good behavior until he reaches the age of 70 or becomes incapacitated to discharge the duties of their office.
Gesmundo is set to compulsorily retire on November 6 at the age of 70. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: DBM sees P10.7B savings if PNP, BJMP, BFP retirement age is raised
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Friday said the government may save approximately P10.74 billion should the compulsory retirement age of personnel of the Philippine National Police…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 9:20pm

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Friday said the government may save approximately P10.74 billion should the compulsory retirement age of personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP), Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP), and Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) be raised from 56 to 57.

DBM Chief Budget and Management Specialist Reynaldo Moreno revealed this during the hearing of the Senate Committee on Public Order and Dangerous Drugs on the bills seeking to extend the retirement age for the mentioned uniformed personnel by one year.
According to Moreno, the possible savings would include P7.34 billion for the PNP; P1.72 billion for the BJMP; and P1.68 billion for the BFP.
“Sa kabuuan po, P10.74 billion ‘yung estimated savings na aming na-kwenta,” he added.
(In total, the estimated savings we calculated amount to P10.74 billion.)
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III then clarified whether the projected savings would result from the deferred monthly retirement pension for the PNP, BJMP, BFP personnel.
“Mr. Chair, dahil nga po ‘yung bilang na nabanggit ko sa possible na extension na isang taon, ‘yun po ‘yung kapalit naman po…kasi mas made-delay ‘yung implementation,” Moreno answered.
(Mr. Chair, because of the possible extension of one year, this is what we get in return given the delay in their retirement.)
The DBM official noted that raising the retirement age for the uniformed personnel would also incur costs to the government for their additional pay and allowances.
Specifically, for fiscal year 2027, he said it would take approximately P1.18 billion for 1,210 PNP positions; P386 million for 271 BFP positions; and P258 million for 546 BJMP positions.

“Ito pong maaaring impact ay ma-o-offset ng posibleng savings sa PGF (Pension and Gratuity Fund) dahil nga ma-e-extend. Pero mahalagang mai-konsidera din po na ‘yung proposed na extension ng service, in the long run, may epekto sa retirement requirements,” Moreno said.

(This potential impact could be offset by possible savings in the PGF, given the extension. However, it is also important to consider that the proposed extension of service will have an effect on retirement requirements in the long run.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Europe's killer heat this summer claims record 50,000 lives, study suggests
articles.summary: Blistering record heat in Europe this summer helped kill more than 50,000 people, with nearly two-thirds of that death toll blamed on human-caused climate change, a new study found.

image.caption: Paramedics take a patient to the emergency department of the Paris-Saclay Hospital, outside Paris, during a heat wave this past June. (Christophe Ena/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Blistering record heat in Europe this summer helped kill more than 50,000 people, with nearly two-thirds of that death toll blamed on human-caused climate change, a new study found.

Researchers modelled heat-related deaths for different age groups in 854 European cities during repeated heat waves in June, July and August and found that 50,391 people died from warmer temperatures, and of those, 32,619 died because of the extra heat caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas, according to a study in an upcoming issue of Nature Health.

That's 71 per cent higher than the previous deadliest summer, which was 29,480 in 2022, according to the same researchers, who produced a study earlier this month tracking yearly summer heat-related deaths in those European cities. And this summer's death figures are underestimates because they don't count a deadly heat wave in May and they only look at deaths in those 854 cities, which hold about 40 per cent of Europe's population, study authors said.
Millions across Europe facing record temperatures from major heat wave

About one-third of the deaths were from June 17 to July 1, a particularly intense heat wave when temperatures were 5.3 C above normal, said study co-author Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, a biostatistician at Imperial College London.

"Much of Western and Northern Europe, our infrastructure is just not designed to cope with the sort of temperatures that we are seeing now because of the effects of human-caused warming," said lead author Clair Barnes, a climate scientist at Imperial College London. She said some European cities this summer had temperatures 12 C warmer than normal.

Of those 50,000, more than 32,000 died from the added heat of human-caused climate change, the study also found. Italy, France, Spain and Germany had the highest death tolls, the study said. Of all the European capitals, Rome had the highest heat death total from 2000 to 2025, according to the team's study earlier this month.
An extra dose of heat from fossil fuel burning

This would've already been an abnormal natural hot spell on top of a huge amount of climate change, Barnes said. She said Europe is the fastest-warming continent — although the Arctic, which is not a continent, is warming even faster — and is 2.5 C hotter than pre-industrial times.

"Just the underlying warming from human activity, from mostly the burning of fossil fuels, it's increasing all of our temperatures by what sounds like quite a small amount," Barnes said. "For many people, it's certainly the case that that extra two-and-a-half degrees [Celsius] of warming is what's going to tip those temperatures from uncomfortable to dangerous and potentially deadly."
Raging fires in Europe force 300,000 from homes
More than half of the people who died in Europe's heat were age 85 or older, but the stifling temperatures also killed more than 800 people between the ages of 20 and 44, Konstantinoudis said.
How the death numbers are calculated

The team used an established and accepted scientific method to figure out how many of the 50,000 heat deaths were from natural high summer heat and how many were due to what heat-trapping gases have done to the climate. They ran computer simulations of a world without climate change and compared it with the deaths that happened this summer. The difference is what was caused by global warming.
The percentage of heat deaths attributable to global warming has grown from about 45 per cent in the early 2000s to 65 per cent now, Barnes said.

"Summers are getting hotter, and the analytical tools for attributing deaths to heat are getting more accurate," said Dr. Howard Frumkin, former director of the National Center for Environmental Health in the U.S., who wasn't part of the study. "Together, these two trends yield increasingly high and increasingly accurate counts of heat-related deaths."
El Niño-fuelled heat could kill half a million people by February: study

The scientific team also had to use statistical modelling to come up with the base count of 50,000 heat deaths because those deaths are underreported and often not listed in death certificates, despite being a major factor, Konstantinoudis said. Several outside experts agreed with him, calling the methods state-of-the-art.

The researchers ran a complex mathematical equation that has been used in several previously peer-reviewed studies, Barnes said, which factors in specific age and temperatures for each of the 854 cities based on a localized optimal temperature that coincides with the fewest deaths. When it's warmer or colder, the equation calculates excess deaths above lowest-death conditions.

Researchers then checked their calculations against real-time estimates from government agencies. Mostly — but not always — they matched fairly well, Konstantinoudis said. The team's methods for May and June British heat waves calculated 2,700 excess deaths and the United Kingdom health statistics agency said it was 2,800, he said.
Cooling and adapting are needed, but they're not enough

"We need to prepare for the heat we cannot now avoid, with urgent investments in heat early-warning systems, equitable access to low-carbon cooling, and neighborhood buddy systems that check on and support people most at risk — while rapidly reducing the fossil fuel use driving the crisis," said Canadian emergency room physician Dr. Courtney Howard, president-elect of the Canadian Medical Association, who wasn't part of the research.
How extreme heat affects your body
Adapting is only part of the answer, said Dr. Jonathan Patz of the University of Wisconsin-Madison, who wasn't part of the research but also praised it.

"We can't just be mopping up the mess on the floor without thinking about turning the faucet off," said Patz, a professor of health and the environment. "So we need prevention at different levels. We need better cooling and protecting vulnerable populations from inevitable increased frequency and extreme heat waves. But we also need to go to the root of the problem and absolutely address the burning of fossil fuels."

articles.title: Finding a way, and still becoming
articles.summary: There is a familiar way of describing solo mothers: strong, resilient, self-sacrificing. But while these words are often meant as compliments, even these positive labels can sometimes become a kind…

blocks.text: There is a familiar way of describing solo mothers: strong, resilient, self-sacrificing. But while these words are often meant as compliments, even these positive labels can sometimes become a kind of box, reducing a woman’s story only to what she has endured rather than who she is, what she wants, and who she is still becoming. It is this space between identity and possibility that globally acclaimed Brazilian photographer Angélica Dass explores in “100 Portraits of Becoming,” TECNO’s two-year global storytelling initiative that brings together 100 real people and their evolving personal stories across Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Brazil, and the Philippines.

Dass has spent much of her career questioning the assumptions people make based on appearance, identity and skin color. It is this long-standing interest in representation that makes Dass a natural collaborator for ‘100 Portraits of Becoming.’

“100 Portraits of Becoming is an amazing opportunity, because I get to meet and have conversations with so many people all over the globe. It’s a project about meetings. When you think about the word becoming you think of the moment of transformation. Each time I learn about a new story, it transforms the way that I see this person, people who are similar, and I can see their culture, too. So, becoming is the transformation that we experience when we meet each other. We are becoming all the time, we are changing, we are being transformed,” Dass expressed.
Her-story in the making

For the campaign’s Philippines chapter, Dass turned her lens toward Filipino solo mothers and the people who form part of their everyday world. What emerged was not simply a montage of stories about hardship, but a more nuanced look at how these women navigate changing circumstances, making choices, adapting, asking for help, and finding ways to keep moving forward.

Dass considers this an important distinction because at the heart of these stories is a question that feels particularly relevant in the Philippines: beyond what she has gone through, who is she, and how is she still becoming?

For her, a woman may be a solo mother, but she can also be a professional, daughter, friend, student, athlete, content creator or a community builder. Motherhood may be central to her life, but it does not necessarily erase the other dimensions of her identity.

blocks.caption: Internationally recognized photographer Angelica Dass captures a solo mom using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G.

blocks.text: The process of becoming is also about children who carry their mothers’ lessons forward, and about grandparents, relatives and friends who quietly become part of the ‘village’. It is about people who learn, adapt, ask for help and find a way. This is where the Filipino concept of diskarte (resourcefulness) enters the conversation.

Diskarte, in this context, is about finding a way. “What I heard in these stories was about finding a way, adapting, using limited resources, asking for help, making choices and making something workable,” Dass shared. “Diskarte is also deeply connected with my own Brazilian roots. The word may be Filipino, but the experience is universal because everywhere life is hard and we have to find a way to make it lighter”.
The Village and Mutual Care

Being a solo mother does not necessarily mean she has to do things alone. The way Dass sees it, they are surrounded by a community filled with people they can trust. And this principle defines Twinkle Dimayuga Zamora’s story.

Rather than trying to become a superwoman and carry all the burdens alone, Twinkle reached out to friends and learned to ask for help. In fact, she helped build MAMA, a community supporting solo mothers through parenting and grief support, self-care and legal guidance. “I learned to ask for a village. Now I’m building one for others,” Zamora proudly said. Her experience offers perhaps the clearest reminder that asking for help can also be diskarte.

blocks.caption: Twinkle Dimayuga Zamora photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: Support systems also form an essential part of these portraits. Such is the case of Mark Joseph Robis, who cared for his cousin while the child’s single mother worked abroad. Their arrangement became part of a wider family relationship built on reciprocity. Years earlier, she had helped care for him and supported his education. Now, that care has come full circle. “In our family, care always finds its way home,” he said, challenging the assumption that distance equates to absence.

blocks.caption: Mark Joseph Robis photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: Zamora and Robis’ stories are similarly reflected in content creator Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio’s. Her grandmother had raised a family on her own, and when her mother later became a solo mother and worked abroad, the grandmother stepped in to help care for the family.

blocks.caption: Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: “It’s not just function, it’s community,” Dass emphasized.
Uncompromised Ambition

A mother’s strength can also serve as a blueprint for personal fulfillment. A case in point, breadwinner Ely Haig refuses to let her identity be redefined solely on her role as a solo mother. Instead, she balances family responsibilities with her passion as a padel player because for her, motherhood was never about compromising your ambitions, it’s about expanding her identity and capacity as a person. “Motherhood added to who I am. It never had to replace who I was,” she said.

blocks.caption: Ely Haig photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: This same spirit of ambition is also seen in the journey of Eunice Angeles, a fourth-year nursing student raised by a Qatar-based solo mother. “People saw what was missing. My mother showed me how to find a way, and now I find my own,” she beamed.

blocks.caption: Eunice Angeles photographed by Angelica Dass using TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: That adaptability spans generations in the story of content creator Jessica Rose “Nanay Jecka” Tinio. Her grandmother had raised a family on her own, and when her mother later became a solo mother and worked abroad, the grandmother stepped in to help care for the family.

The stories in 100 Portraits of Becoming complement that idea by showing both advocacy and context. The women find ways forward, but their ability to adapt does not mean every burden should be theirs to solve individually. A mother’s diskarte may solve an immediate problem, but it can also shape how a child understands possibility tomorrow.

“We don’t romanticize their struggles at all. In front of the camera, I see beauty, power; I see people who love themselves and this is what I want to show in my images. There is such amount of human suffering, stereotyping, and what we want to really show is the celebration of who they are. This is something that I am really happy to do. Everybody in front of my camera are proud, happy, shining, confident and comfortable,” Dass said.
When technology becomes a tool to break labels

Society quickly categories people based on first impressions, and these impressions can easily turn into lasting stereotypes. To dismantle them, we need a different approach—an approach that captures the full depth of a person’s story. This is where technology steps in to not simplify the reality, but to reveal it.

In 100 Portraits of Becoming, the camera is therefore not simply documenting what someone looks like. It becomes a way of asking the viewer to pause before categorizing, to look again, and see the person before and beyond the label.

The fascinating second layer of this project is that the portraits were created using TECNO’s CAMON Slim 5G. For a photographer of Dass’s stature, choosing a smartphone over the traditional professional camera could easily become the story. But she sees it differently. “The CAMON Slim 5G is a tool,” she shared. “TECNO gave me a tool to do what I do best, and that’s taking pictures, connecting with human beings, doing portraits.” Technology, in her own words, does not replace the photographer’s vision; instead, it enables it.

blocks.caption: Photographer Angelica Dass using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G

blocks.text: It is important to note that CAMON Slim 5G’s Universal Tone technology is designed to represent a wider spectrum of human skin tones more accurately. “We also brought our cameras and other gadgets, but I found that it is easier to take pictures with a phone, and the colors are amazing! For someone like me—a woman with an African descent, someone that belongs south of the planet—being able to try this technology is something that can help us,” she affirmed.

For this project, CAMON Slim 5G was more than just a device, it embodied the campaign’s message. As Dass pointed out, technology is only ever a tool, and it’s used to showcase human connection. TECNO extended this idea by choosing working women, particularly single working mothers, as the emotional lens of 100 Portraits of Becoming.

These women represent the brand’s philosophy, ‘Make it Lighter,’ because of the diskarte they display that keeps families afloat—from balancing work, caregiving, managing finances, and deciding what’s best for the family.

The CAMON Slim 5G, with its slim design and Universal Tone camera, reflects that same principle. It lightens their load and captures them not only as mothers, but as women with their own dreams and stories and as women becoming.
The bigger picture

Perhaps that is where TECNO’s ‘Make it Lighter’ brand philosophy finds its most natural place in the story. Making life lighter does not mean pretending life is easy; a smartphone cannot solve the realities of solo parenthood, and it can never replace family, community or government support. For Dass and other visual storytellers, technology can help make creative expression more immediate and accessible.

blocks.caption: Photographer Angelica Dass captures a moment with a campaign participant using the TECNO CAMON Slim 5G.

blocks.text: At its core, TECNO is a technology brand built around possibility. TECNO’s technology simply enters that story as one more tool in the hands of people who are already finding ways to move forward.

“When we think about ‘becoming’ as transformation, we should also think about ways we can become who we want to be. So, if I can share something that I learned from this project, it is this: ‘becoming’ is also trying to find ways to be you,” Dass concluded.

The Philippines chapter of 100 Portraits of Becoming resonates beyond the stories of solo mothers themselves. It asks audiences to reconsider the labels they place on other people as well as the labels they place on themselves.
One hundred portraits. One hundred stories. One hundred ways of seeing humanity, not as categories, not with labels, but as real people in the process of becoming.
To know more about TECNO and the ‘100 Portraits of Becoming’, visit the company’s official site: www.tecno-mobile.com.

articles.title: Japan-Russia ties erode as journalist sits in Moscow jail
articles.summary: Japan is demanding access to a journalist who was arrested by Russian security services. Moscow claims Tokyo is using journalists as spies.

image.caption: Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on spying claims.

Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept.

The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia-Japan relations.

Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pre-trial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release.
Officials of the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been refused access to Imai. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy.

Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," Russia's TASS news agency reported. He has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use Japanese journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability."
Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies'

Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies.
"One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said.

"I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added.
Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands

Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, said that Russia may see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for its nationals detained overseas.
However, Nagy doubts Japan will give in to pressure.

"They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he told DW.
"It would set a dangerous precedent," he added.
The arrest comes after a member of a Russia-linked hacking group "Qilin" was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center.

The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released.

Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.

blocks.caption: Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court.Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strained Japan-Russia ties
Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin.

Nagy said Imai's seizure is designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East.

"Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said.

"This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he told DW. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo."
Decades-long row over disputed islands

Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Moscow, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine.
Anno said Moscow's timing on turning up the heat on Tokyo is puzzling.
"Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he told DW.
At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II.

Known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, there have been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return them to Japanese sovereignty.

That campaign has faltered in the last couple of years, however, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide non-lethal assistance to Kyiv.

In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands, only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands and talks are under way on the possibility of economic cooperation.

items: The DILG and PNP have given Senator Bato dela Rosa a one-week deadline to surrender, offering a P50-million reward for information leading to his capture.

MANILA, Philippines – The Department for the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Philippine National Police (PNP) set a deadline of one week for International Criminal Court (ICC) suspect Senator Bato dela Rosa to surrender.

“Senator Bato mistook my gesture of negotiation as a sign of weakness. Now the gloves have to come off. It is time to bring justice to his victims,” DILG Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla said in a press conference on Friday, October 23.

In the same briefing, Remulla also announced that his department is offering a P50-million reward for those who can help capture Dela Rosa. The interior chief also described Dela Rosa as “armed and dangerous.
“We have given him all the courtesy that could be afforded a senator of the Republic of the Philippines, and he has shown nothing but cowardice by going into and remaining in hiding,” Remulla added.
The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I, in November last year, issued a warrant against Dela Rosa due to his role in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war.

He was Duterte’s first PNP chief who implemented the anti-drug campaign which human rights organizations said took the lives of nearly 30,000 people. The ICC named him a co-perpetrator in the case. It added that those involved “controlled a structure of power” which enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out drug war killings.

In November, the warrant was still sealed. It was only made public on May 11, after Dela Rosa, following months of absence in the upper house, showed up at the Senate to back Alan Peter Cayetano’s election as Senate president. For three days, Dela Rosa hid inside the Senate building until a shooting chaos — allegedly triggered by his mistah Senate sergeant-at-arms Mao Aplasca — ensued on the night of May 13.
Hours later, Dela Rosa escaped from the Senate at around 2:30 am with his ally Senator Robin Padilla.
Padilla is now facing an obstruction of justice complaint due to the incident, while Aplasca has been dismissed by the Office of the Ombudsman.

On Friday, Remulla said there’s already a task force, headed by PNP deputy chief Police Lieutenant General Wilson Joseph Lopez, directed to locate and arrest the senator. The DILG said they are validating reports of Dela Rosa’s sightings in Western Mindanao, Eastern Visayas, Bicol, Metro Manila, and Southern Luzon.

“The PNP is always ready for that whether peaceful or armed confrontation… whether with search warrant or arrest warrant. We have the necessary force, personnel, and training for that,” said Nartatez.

The Department of Justice announced on May 21 that the PNP and National Bureau of Investigation had been ordered to arrest the senator – but this happened weeks after Dela Rosa’s escape. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trump’s top border official defends Big Bend border wall plan despite mounting opposition
articles.summary:
CBP commissioner Rodney Scott says $46bn Texas project is justified amid court-ordered pause on wall’s construction

The Trump administration’s top border official defended plans to

blocks.text: The Trump administration’s top border official defended plans to build a wall and other infrastructure in the Big Bend of Texas despite mounting opposition against the project and a court-ordered pause on construction, saying his goal of fortifying the country’s borders was “non-negotiable”.

Rodney Scott, the commissioner of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), said the $46bn wall project was justified despite a bipartisan coalition of landowners, local businesses and environmentalists who view it as a waste of taxpayer money that could be destructive to a region with historically low migrant crossings, in an exclusive interview with the Associated Press.

“Our number one goal right out the gate is we have to know who and what is coming into the United States,” Scott said on Thursday. If the Big Bend region were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he said, “I am 100% convinced it will be completely overrun and destroyed.”

The fight over the spectacular Big Bend area, close to the US-Mexico line, where the Rio Grande flows along a massive curve on its way to the Gulf of Mexico, has become a major test for how far the Republican administration is willing to go to shut off the border.
Scott, a former border patrol agent, was tapped by Trump to complete the border barrier.

His agency is responsible for executing a plan funded last summer by Republicans in Congress to line the roughly 2,000-mile (3,200km) border with Mexico with a mixture of steel fences 30ft (9 metre) high, vehicle barriers, new roads and surveillance technology to prevent irregular immigration – and smuggling of drugs and humans.

The Trump administration says it is building about 12 miles (19km) a week. Scott, who gets daily progress updates, said it will be complete by the end of Trump’s second term. The primary border wall – some areas also get a secondary layer – will be done by the end of December 2027.
“We’re actually ahead of schedule,” Scott said.

The wall plan has run into stiff – and bipartisan – resistance in some places, especially Big Bend. The Trump administration suffered a big setback earlier this month when a judge ordered a pause on border wall construction in the region, citing what could be a likelihood that plaintiffs “will suffer serious, irreparable harm without an injunction”. The administration has asked the supreme court to lift the order.
The ruling included any construction in Big Bend national park, an area that has seen a loud bipartisan outcry, including from some Republican lawmakers.

After bulldozers were spotted in the park tearing up ground in August, Scott ordered a pause on all construction-related activity there while he went to talk to people in the region. He said the agency is making other outreach to locals to discuss how to build projects so they don’t mar the park.

“We’re talking through and figuring out what is the right solution for that area,” he said. But he added that “protecting the country” with a barrier is “non-negotiable”. Scott added that the huge steel fences will not go up in the national park because of ongoing lawsuits.

articles.title: Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
articles.summary: Once the world's largest producer of mink pelts, the nation's industry has declined in recent years.

blocks.text: Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.

Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.
Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.
"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.
The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.
However, the current coalition government, elected in June 2026, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.
Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.
However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years.

The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed.
At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling.
There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark.

No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher.
The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago.
But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur.

articles.title: Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny
articles.summary: Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria crossed paths at Uganda's main airport as conflicting accounts cloud the source of one infection.

image.caption: Both patients are known to have traveled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3Image: Sumy Sadurni/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.
Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.

Uganda insists it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.

Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.

The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers, or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes?
The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.
Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an imported Ebola case in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.
"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.
The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.
Pate said the patient was stable and that health officials had identified 44 contacts, including healthcare workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.
But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.

Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.
Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account
Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.
"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.
But on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.
"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.
The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.

blocks.caption: Ebola cases have now been detected in four African countries: DR Congo, ​Uganda, Kenya ‌and NigeriaImage: Afolabi Sotunde/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.

The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.
Uganda maintains it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.
Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation

In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.

Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.
But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.
According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.
"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth told the newspaper.
The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.
Being an untraced contact does not mean he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.
Can border screening stop Ebola?
Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.
Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
Ebola symptoms typically develop between 2 and 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.
Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.

The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.
Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry, while Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.
Anxiety grows in Nigeria

In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.

Others fear Nigeria's healthcare system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.
Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and that contact tracing is continuing.
What remains unanswered?
Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.

But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3, and where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?

The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.
Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.

For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.
The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.
