articles.title: Ukraine troops report ongoing problems with Starlink satellite network
articles.summary: Communications system still faces speed restrictions despite Trump claim that Musk had resumed full service

blocks.text: Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.

The slowdown, which has affected the key communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Starlink founder Musk publicly criticised Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.
“I don’t comment one way or the other,” Trump said on Thursday when asked about reports that he had personally called Musk to demand the restrictions be lifted.
“The bottom line: he put it back.”
But Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.

“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.

The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering both offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.

The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, have plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.

Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
after newsletter promotion

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.

Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war.
“The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.

The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Parks Canada plan to cut 500 jobs draws criticism from union
articles.summary: Parks Canada is restructuring its workforce following a $145-million budget cut over the next three years. The union representing the public servants said the impending layoffs are "disappointing."

image.caption: Nearly 3,000 Parks Canada staff are being notified this week that their jobs are at risk. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Parks Canada is restructuring its workforce following a $145-million budget cut over the next three years. The union representing the public servants said the impending layoffs are "disappointing."
Reductions come in response to federal funding cut of $145M over next 3 years
Parks Canada expects to eliminate the equivalent of 500 full-time jobs across the country as part of a “workforce adjustment,” the federal agency confirmed to CBC News on Thursday.
Nearly 3,000 Parks Canada staff are being notified this week that their jobs are at risk, according to a memo sent to employees and posted online on Tuesday.

"We have used, and are using, every means we have to minimize the number of team members who may need to involuntarily leave the agency," Andrew Campbell, interim president and CEO for Parks Canada, said to employees.
He said a large number of staff were notified so that more employees will have the opportunity to leave the agency by choice.
The staffing reductions will be carried out in the coming months, but the exact timeline is unclear.

Krysty Thomas, regional executive vice-president for the Public Service Alliance of Canada’s (PSAC) Prairie region, called the impending cuts “disappointing,” especially coming on the heels of the free Canada Strong Pass program.

items: 'When it’s full, it’s full': Canada Strong Pass raises overtourism issues in Banff

blocks.text: "As the federal government encourages more Canadians to visit, they must ensure that the parks have the staffing and resources to serve them safely,” said Thomas.
“To say that now your work isn't vital to the sustainability of these parks is extremely disappointing, frustrating, and there's a lot of uncertainty for these members.”
‘Attrition alone’ not enough

The workforce restructuring comes after the federal government’s comprehensive expenditure review, which requires Parks Canada to absorb nearly $145 million in budget reductions over the next three years.
Some Parks Canada programs will be scaled back or discontinued, and the number of positions required to deliver certain programs and services will be reduced.
“Given the scale of the required savings, I have been clear that attrition alone will not be enough to meet our targets,” Campbell said to employees in June.

items: Can nature benefit Canada's economy? New report says parks contribute billions in taxes, wages

blocks.text: At that time, Thomas said she didn’t expect that 2,917 workers — or nearly two-thirds of the Parks Canada workforce — would get an “affected” letter.
An “affected” letter doesn’t necessarily mean a layoff. It could signal that a position may no longer be required due to a lack of work, is getting fully discontinued, changed or will be relocated.
The “affected” staff members could get shuffled around based on vacant positions, or receive an “opting” letter, meaning they will be laid off.
Those who are laid off have rights under the collective agreement between Parks Canada and PSAC, such as the ability to exchange jobs with a non-affected employee who is willing to leave.
Uncertainty compounded by wildfire recovery

Thomas said the feeling of uncertainty is compounded for the roughly 375 Parks Canada employees who are still working to help Jasper recover from a devastating wildfire in 2024. The fire destroyed a third of the townsite and 20 per cent of Parks Canada assets in the park.
"These workers have already experienced tremendous hardship following wildfires in both Jasper and Waterton," Thomas said, also referencing the 2017 Kenow Wildfire in Waterton Lakes National Park.
"They're continuing to help build our community and now they're worried about the security of their own jobs."

items: Jasper to get $520M in additional reconstruction funding from federal government

blocks.text: In an email to CBC News, a Parks Canada spokesperson said that “over the coming weeks, decisions will be made on all positions being assessed," and more information relating to how this will impact the Jasper field unit will be made available as soon as possible.

"Responsible choices are being made so that programs and services can be delivered smarter, faster and more effectively for all Canadians," the spokesperson said, adding that Parks Canada’s commitment to conservation, visitor safety and memorable experiences remains unchanged.
Campbell emphasized that staff are not alone during the federal agency's period of uncertainty, and support is available for employees who need it.
"At the end of our transformation, Parks Canada will continue as the strong, future-oriented organization that we all love to work for, for many years to come."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Maggie Kirk is a reporter for CBC News in Hinton, Alta.

Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, said Friday she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's former home. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.
Statement comes after new report child porn images were found at father's house

Meghan, also known as the Duchess of Sussex, issued the statement after the Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that her half-brother found the images while clearing out the home of their father, Thomas Markle Sr., in the Philippines.
"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan said in a statement.
She also addressed the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service's Royal and Specialist Protection unit, which later shared its contents with her.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated. I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."
Brother reported father to police

Thomas Markle Sr., a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father. While some reports suggested she had shunned him in favour of her new royal status, Meghan said her decision to distance herself was intended to protect her children.

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children," she said in her statement.

Thomas Markle Sr. was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.

The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr. recently found "hundreds, if not thousands" of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father's former home in the Philippine city of Cebu when he was clearing out the property.

"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told the Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."

articles.title: ‘An orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal’: the musical activists targeted in Paris
articles.summary:
New World Orchestra’s musicians are shocked at French police targeting peaceful gathering with teargas

As riot police encircled Place de la République last week, lobbing teargas canisters to…

blocks.text: As riot police encircled Place de la République last week, lobbing teargas canisters to disperse demonstrators, the conductor Étienne Jarrier and his orchestra played on. They kept playing even after everyone else had disappeared and teargas was being fired into the central Paris square.

It was only when Jarrier noticed his musicians were being directly targeted that he ordered them to stop. “There were teargas canisters landing in the double bass and music stand cases, and starting fires the musicians had to stamp out,” he told the Guardian.

The Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (the ONM, or New World Orchestra) is used to accompanying protests. Co-founded by Jarrier in 2022, the Paris-based ensemble is made up of hundreds of young professional and amateur musicians, all volunteers and all committed to blend classical music and activism, particularly social and climate justice.

The orchestra describes itself as “anti-racist, anti-capitalist, feminist, environmentalist and committed to de-growth”, with the dual aim of linking artistic performance with activism and increasing awareness of classical music among the young rather than its traditional “white bourgeois and elderly” following.

In 2022, ONM played at the foot of a melting Alpine glacier; two years later it was outside the headquarters of the far-right Rassemblement National (RN), performing a parody of an anthem popular with Marshal Pétain’s Vichy regime that collaborated with the Nazis. Last year, it formed a welcoming committee outside a television station for the Eurosceptic RN leader Marine Le Pen, and played the EU anthem, Beethoven’s Ode to Joy.

“We’re very happy to play at demonstrations,” Jarrier, 25, said. “There are lots of anthems for social struggles in France, like the Marseillaise or the International or activist music of the last centuries, but it’s important to play music that appeals to new generations.”

For the recent protests, its repertoire has included The Hanging Tree from The Hunger Games, and the theme from Marvel’s The Avengers film. “Music from a superhero movie on a day of social struggle seemed appropriate” said the conductor.
Jarrier, whose late father was a photographer and whose mother is an archeologist, studied classical music and the clarinet until the age of 17, but is a self-taught conductor.

Photographs of last Saturday’s protests show Jarrier, baton raised, conducting the ONM against the backdrop of the 10-metre high bronze monument representing Marianne, symbol of the French republic, and a dense white cloud of teargas.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

French security forces, including the CRS riot police, were unimpressed. The squadrons of police, often nicknamed Robocops, have been widely criticised for their aggressive policing of recent demonstrations, particularly their liberal use of stun grenades (that emit a deafening explosion), flash-balls, baton charges and teargas against protesters. Yet they seemed impotent to stop those looting shops and destroying public buildings.

On Saturday, Jarrier had invited musicians to join the orchestra at Place de la République, the starting point for the official demonstration by high-school students protesting a failing and unjust education system, and by unions angry with the government’s failure to address wider grievances.

“It was a day of what we call a convergence of struggles,” Jarrier said. “The orchestra is engaged politically in the fight, so our presence was necessary on such a day. We appealed to any musicians with an instrument who wanted to play to come to Place de la République before the official protest march starting at 1pm.
“We planned to make music when it set off,” he added.

blocks.caption: The New World Orchestra amid smoke and teargas drifts at the Place de la République in Paris last Saturday. Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News

blocks.text: As between 400 and 500 musicians gathered in the square, orchestra members alerted the CRS that they would be present and performing, Jarrier said. “We asked them to let us know if they plan to charge or gas the square, and they said they would warn us,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“While we were rehearsing, a very happy crowd of people of all ages gathered around us. Then the teargas canisters started being thrown around the orchestra. Not directly at us at that point. After a while there was almost nobody there except us.

“Clearly the aim was to clear a peaceful crowd from the place, which is quite serious and something we’ve not seen before. But even when the square was empty all around us, the CRS continued to gas the orchestra. After 20 minutes we had no choice but to stop playing.”
Jarrier said the musicians were “stunned” and “truly shocked”.
“It was quite scary,” he said. “We’d reassured the musicians before the protest saying: ‘Don’t worry – they’re not going to use teargas or charge us when we’re peaceful.’”
As the musicians packed away instruments, the orchestra’s security volunteers formed a human chain between the musicians and police.

blocks.caption: The New World Orchestra rehearses at Place de la République last Saturday. Photograph: Babeth Aloy/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: “We are very angry about what happened,” Jarrier said. “It’s an extremely serious shift in maintaining order; the [government] is not listening to demands and is responding not with politics but police.

“It’s trying to divert attention from a legitimate movement that demands better public services, better lives. By making this about violent police repression they divert attention from the real concerns. We are not the martyrs, but the image of an orchestra being gassed should be an alarm signal,” he said.
The French Ministry of Defence and the Paris police prefecture were asked to comment on the use of teargas at Place de la République, but did not respond.

articles.title: Torreon law firm questions P50M reward for arrest of Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: The Law Firm of Torreon and Partners has questioned the basis of the P50-million reward the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has offered for the arrest of Sen. Ronald "Bato"…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 7:52pm

The Law Firm of Torreon and Partners has questioned the basis of the P50-million reward the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has offered for the arrest of Sen. Ronald "Bato" Dela Rosa.

Dela Rosa, who has been in hiding since May after the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant against him, has been deemed armed and dangerous, according to Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla.

“The only document the government has is a warrant from the International Criminal Court. That is a foreign tribunal under a treaty the Philippines withdrew from effective March 17, 2019. No Philippine judge has examined that warrant, adopted it, or issued one of his own,” the firm said on Facebook.
“A reward system built on Philippine warrants cannot be used for a person who has no Philippine warrant,” it added.

The law firm of Dela Rosa's counsel, Atty. Israel Torreon, said that the DILG would have to disclose several details when it offers a reward, including the offense, the issuing court, the criminal case number, the DILG memorandum circular number, and the reward amount.
Citing the Philippine National Police (PNP) Memorandum Circular No. 2011-001, the law firm said that the police must have an original or authenticated copy of the warrant.
The law firm also took issue with Dela Rosa’s labeling as “armed and dangerous”.
“No court has found that Senator Dela Rosa is armed and dangerous. The label came from a press briefing,” it said.
The law firm also said that since the P50 million came from the DILG’s intelligence funds, it needed to abide by Commission on Audit (COA) rules.

A joint circular from COA and various government agencies said that the operation needed to be approved by the head of the agency, supported by documents showing the activity’s success, and directly related to the agency’s confidential activities.

“These funds were appropriated for Philippine law enforcement, peace and order, and national security operations under Philippine law. They are not a blank check for enforcing a foreign court’s process that no Philippine judge has passed upon,” the firm stated.
It urged the government to identify a Philippine court that issued the warrant, the criminal case number, the DILG memorandum circular, and the legal basis for paying the reward. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Serbia: Hope, tension and apprehension as voters prepare to elect new parliament
articles.summary: After two years of protests, Serbia faces a pivotal election on Sunday, with a student-led challenge to Aleksandar Vucic's lengthy rule. Allegations of electoral irregularities and fears of a…

image.caption: Three days before a pivotal parliamentary election in Serbia, supporters of the Student List poured into central Belgrade for a final campaign rallyImage: Marko Djurica/REUTERS

blocks.text: A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years.
The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election.

Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination.

"We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd.
"People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List.
Students emerge as agents of change

After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power.

blocks.caption: Three is the number of the Student List on the ballot paperImage: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign.

"These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote."
The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure.
In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics.
SNS presents itself as a guarantor of continuity
Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally.

blocks.caption: 'They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements,' Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters on ThursdayImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos.
The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests.

"They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements."
Rising tension
The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies.

blocks.caption: It's not just students who support the Student List. The red hand became a symbol of the student protest movement in November 2024Image: Uros Arsic/REUTERS

blocks.text: By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners.

CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters.
Allegations of links to criminal networks
In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks.

Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government.
But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome.
He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports.
Concerns about irregularities
There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process.
The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election
CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters.

Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative.

Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party.

DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party.
What could come after the election?
Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety.

For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night.
The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result.

blocks.caption: Supporters cheered Aleksandar Vucic and the ruling SNS party at a rally this weekImage: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW

blocks.text: "But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally.
The EU's reaction could be crucial
Whatever happens, the European Union's response could be crucial.

"I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW.

An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012.
Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo, a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box.
But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed.

articles.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears US will renew strikes on Iran
articles.summary: Brent crude rises to $114.72 a barrel after Tehran threatens retaliatory attacks on Gulf oil and tech facilities

blocks.text: Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to $114.72 a barrel – its highest level since May.
The increase came after Tehran said it would strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli attack was launched against Iran.

“Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month,” said Richard Hunter at the broker Interactive Investor.
Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to $126 a barrel by the end of April.

Tensions in the region have been rising this week; Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategists at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.

“At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

articles.title: Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England
articles.summary:
Dozens of schools in Cornwall also affected by conditions as another storm heads for Scotland, Northern Ireland and the north of England

Thousands of homes are without power and schools have…

blocks.text: Thousands of homes are without power and schools have been closed as the first named storm of the year hits UK shores.

Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s Airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. Just before 11am, more than 16,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid.
Dozens of schools across Cornwall were forced to open late, while others did not open at all.
Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, warned: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”

A government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked if the government was playing catch-up with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham speaking at a wildfires summit in Aintree, Liverpool, on Friday. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

blocks.text: He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

“It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”
National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 12,000 properties affected by Storm Austen by 8am on Friday.
A Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.
after newsletter promotion

It has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.
The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and warned of danger to life from flying debris.
It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and rail and flight cancellations.
The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.

articles.title: The mega-Maga contender in deep-red Florida who doesn’t want to talk about Trump
articles.summary:
Byron Donalds removed mentions of the president from his website and has barely uttered his name – will his ploy prove successful in a tight governor’s race?

It took Byron Donalds,…

blocks.text: It took Byron Donalds, addressing a wildly supportive crowd at a rally in Florida’s bluest county, some time to list those he blamed for any “affordability” issues they might be experiencing.

Joe Biden, and the radical policies of the Democrats, were at fault, the Republican nominee for Florida governor insisted in his stump speech at Broward county’s Green Glades West ranch, even though neither has wielded power in Washington for almost two years.
Donalds also pointed a finger at other traditional betes noires of the modern Republican movement, New York’s democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and the despised Dr Anthony Fauci.

Another to receive a lengthy verbal lashing was David Jolly, his opponent in a closely watched race that will help gauge the strength of a Democratic resurgence in a state that has veered reliably red in recent years.

Yet one name – Donald Trump – remained conspicuously unspoken, as did any mention of the war in Iran, soaring gas prices, unaffordable healthcare premiums, or any number of issues that have caused the president’s approval rating to drop to new lows.
How to handle Trump has become something of a conundrum for Donalds, an ultra-Maga, three-term Republican congressman, as he navigates a race that remains much closer than he would like it to be.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Byron Donalds wave placards as he speaks to the crowd in Dallas. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Such is the president’s unpopularity that the Donalds campaign made the decision last month to purge almost every mention of Trump from his campaign website, including the removal of “enact the Trump agenda” as his top priority as governor.

That, and his notable reluctance to invoke his name, or policies, on the campaign trail, appeared to be working, until Trump announced that he would be coming to Fort Myers on Friday, a little more than a week from election day, on the latest stop of the president’s late red-state tour in support of vulnerable candidates.

Some prominent Republicans seeking election have chosen to be elsewhere when Trump comes to town. Perhaps in an effort not to be seen too closely aligned, the Texas governor, Greg Abbott, discovered an unavoidable commitment as Trump visited San Antonio this month.
But not Donalds.

“Of course I’m going to be there. What kind of question is that?” he snapped at a reporter after last Friday’s joint rally with the Republican senator Ashley Moody, who is also on the 3 November ballot.

Another journalist asked Donalds if his silence on Trump was a deliberate uncoupling from some of the president’s more unpopular policies, such as his immigration crackdown that is polling poorly with Florida’s large Latino and Hispanic voting blocs.

“This is what I’m talking about. You guys are so caught up in, ‘Do you agree with this, do you agree with that?’” he said, not answering the question. “I was giving a speech about my campaign for governor because I’m running for governor.”

blocks.caption: Donalds speaks to voters and members of the media in Lakeland, Florida, earlier this month. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: The distancing is a calculated gamble that may prove inconsequential anyway, given that registered Republican Florida voters outnumber Democrats by more than 1.5 million.

But his snippy responses suggest he is aware that Trump is probably uppermost in voters’ minds as they decide whether to allow him to succeed Ron DeSantis, whose endorsement has replaced Trump’s on Florida TV ads, and extend the Republican grip on the governor’s mansion that dates to January 1999.

Donalds’s speech last Friday, which was warmly received by the mostly white, middle-aged and above audience at the private ranch lodge resembling an upmarket Cracker Barrel restaurant on the edge of the Everglades, contained plenty of what they wanted to hear, and nothing that they didn’t.
He did not touch the wars in Iran or Ukraine, or gas prices. Any extra financial burden on Florida’s families, he said, could be laid at the door of “the craziness from the previous administration”.
Political analyst Larry Sabato said the distancing was a ploy that will be quickly forgotten if Donalds wins.

“Donalds is super-Maga. This is just a campaign tactic being used by quite a few Republicans all across the country,” said Sabato, founder and director of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics and author of the election analysis website Sabato’s Crystal Ball.
“Look, Donalds has no choice but to make the most out of Trump, but not be devoured by him. And you know it’s not easy to do. You’re walking a very fine line there.”

Democratic leaders point to Donalds’s ultra-conservative, pro-Maga positions during almost six years in Congress. They include refusing to certify Biden’s 2020 election win, arguing that undocumented immigrants are not entitled to due process, denying climate change is human-made, championing abortion restrictions, and opposing transgender women and girls in sport.
Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic party, told a press conference Thursday, one day before Trump’s Fort Myers, visit that Donalds is not fooling voters.

“Even when Byron Donalds tried to distance himself from Trump by scrubbing the president from his website, he went running back into Daddy’s arms within hours, but there is no hiding from this presidency,” she said.

“Tomorrow, Donalds and the rest of the Florida Republicans will once again reveal their true loyalties. The people of our state are tired of spineless politicians who kiss the ring and fall in line instead of standing up.”

blocks.caption: Donalds at a campaign event in Fort Lauderdale. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

blocks.text: But several attenders at the rally at the ranch, hosted by the environmentalist and businessman “Alligator” Ron Bergeron, a close ally of DeSantis, said they were unbothered by Donalds’s avoidance of any Trump talk.
“We’re all on the same page with our president supporting what is right,” said Luis Breton, a Republican voter and US citizen originally from the Soviet Union.

Stella Patrick said she saw Donalds and Moody as fighting for Florida’s interests, while Trump was busy “defending the nation”. The Fort Lauderdale retiree said: “Byron Donalds doesn’t need Trump’s blessing to win, and I’m happy he spoke about what he’s going to do for us in Florida. That’s what matters to me.”

To win and become Florida’s first Black governor, Donalds cannot afford to lose huge chunks of the alliance that helped Trump win the state at three successive presidential elections, including Black voters and Hispanics.

According to polls, Hispanic voters appear to be wavering about sticking with the Republican cause, favoring Donalds 48%-43% in an NBC6/Telemundo 51 survey published last week. Support from Black voters looks to have slipped away, the same poll giving Jolly a 76-10 advantage.
Meanwhile, Democrats nationally see a tightening race, and on Tuesday pledged an extra million dollars to bolster Jolly in late campaigning.
Sabato’s Crystal Ball, and Fox News, list the Donalds-Jolly contest as “leans Republican”.

Sabato said the days when Florida could be considered a purple state are long gone. “It’s not even close,” he said. “Trump won it easily, and so you can’t underestimate the Republican vote there, or overestimate the Democratic vote.”

articles.title: France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris
articles.summary: French police have arrested a suspect after gunshots were fired in a town in the suburbs of Paris on Friday. Police are investigating a possible racist motivation.

image.caption: Police are investigating the shooting on suspicion of a possible racial motivationImage: Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP

blocks.text: One person was killed and four others were injured when gunshots were fired from a vehicle in a town outside Paris on Friday, local authorities have confirmed.

The shooting occurred in Trappes, about 20 kilometers (13 miles) west of the French capital, close to Versailles, and a suspect was arrested in the neighboring town of Coignieres and has been taken into police custody.
Mayor: 'Miracle' that more were not killed
"An individual fired shots from his vehicle at multiple people along his route," the mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, wrote on social media.
He later told French broadcaster BFM TV that one of the locations at which shots were fired was a playground.
"It is a miracle that there were not more victims," he said.
Rabeh said the person killed was of African origin, while one of those critically wounded was of North African origin.

blocks.caption: The shooter allegedly opened fire from a vehicle, shooting indiscriminatelyImage: AFP

blocks.text: Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon."
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the incident "very serious" and said that "all available resources of the security forces and judicial authorities have been fully mobilized."
He added that France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (Pnat) is monitoring the situation.

The Pnat itself said it had opened an investigation into "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed on the basis of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion."
France shooting: what else do we know?

The potential motive for the shooting was not immediately clear, but it came as France braces for yet another day of protests against the high cost of living on Saturday, with major museums in Paris and other major cities closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence.

"We are not talking about ​a nice protest," Interior Minister Nunez told reporters, announcing the deployment of 70,000 security personnel. "We are ​ready ⁠tomorrow to be extremely firm ⁠and ​not tolerate anything."
France: Why students are taking to the streets
France has also seen a spate of Islamist terrorist attacks in recent years and, although the number of incidents has fallen, authorities have warned that risks remain.

The town of Trappes has experienced its own share of tension, with a local teacher reporting receiving threats after saying that the state did not do enough to protect Samuel Paty, a teacher in another Paris suburb who was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.
There was no immediate suggestion that Friday's shooting was linked either to the current protests or Islamist terrorism.

articles.title: A shared sense of purpose: 5 career lessons from a Pru Life UK leader
articles.summary: What principles helped Haidee Plopenio, Head of Business Continuity Management, power through her journey with the company?

blocks.text: Photography by Lem Atienza; makeup by Dorothy Mamalio; hair by Marjorie Caballos
What principles helped Haidee Plopenio, Head of Business Continuity Management, power through her journey with the company?

items: Haidee Plopenio, Head of Business Continuity Management at Pru Life UK, emphasizes the importance of preparation and collaboration in her role, which focuses on ensuring the company can serve its stakeholders during disruptions.

Plopenio's diverse career path has equipped her with skills in various disciplines, allowing her to understand the broader concept of protection, which she defines as being ready to support families during uncertain times.

As Pru Life UK celebrates its 30th anniversary, Plopenio expresses her hope for the company to continue innovating and investing in its people, reinforcing the idea that protection is fundamentally about caring for individuals and communities.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by Pru Life UK and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.
“My career did not follow a straight line.”
This sounds like inspiring advice from the get-go – and even more so when you discover that this came from Haidee Plopenio, Head of Business Continuity Management at Pru Life UK.
This year, she marks her 29th year with the top insurance company, which is celebrating its 30th year anniversary.

blocks.caption: Photography by Lem Atienza; makeup by Dorothy Mamalio; hair by Marjorie Caballos

blocks.text: As the head of Business Continuity Management, Plopenio says her role shouldn’t be seen as intimidating as it sounds. “My title may sound formal, but my work is really about people, preparation, and collaboration. I work with different teams to help ensure that Pru Life UK can continue serving our customers, employees, and stakeholders, even during disruptions,” she said in an interview with Rappler.

Before she landed her current role, Plopenio juggled many hats in different disciplines: technology (which taught her structure), business analysis (understanding needs), project management (collaboration and delivery risk), risk management (foresight), and eventually business continuity and resilience, which tied all these things together.

In our exclusive chat, Plopenio walks us through her journey with Pru Life UK, where we pick up career advice that can fuel anyone – even from unrelated fields. She mentioned that over time, she was given opportunities to grow across different functions, and each role helped her prepare for the work she does today.
In Plopenio’s job, delayed gratification is in motion.

“What I find most fulfilling is knowing that the work we do, although often behind the scenes, helps protect what matters most: Our customers, employees, and the trust that they place in Pru Life UK,” Plopenio said. “In business continuity, you may not always see the impact immediately, but when something happens, preparedness becomes very real.”
But preparedness goes beyond her job description. For her, protection – which is central to Pru Life UK’s service for its customers – is synonymous with preparedness.

“Protection means being ready and being present when people need you most. Protection is not only about products or processes. Earlier in my career, I may have thought of protection mainly in terms of insurance [or] insurance coverage,” she explained.

blocks.caption: Screenshot

blocks.text: “But over time, especially through my work in business continuity and resilience, I have come to see protection more broadly. It means helping families prepare for uncertainty. It means ensuring customers can continue to rely on us during difficult moments.”
In dealing with company curveballs, Plopenio stressed the importance of bringing all hands on deck.

“I also value the collaborative culture in Pru Life UK. In crisis management and business continuity, I have seen teams from different departments come together quickly during challenging situations,” she recalled. “That shared sense of purpose and teamwork is one of the reasons I have stayed.”

“I believe Pru Life UK has helped address a very Filipino need – the desire to protect and provide for one’s family. So many Filipino families worry about illness, loss of income, education, emergencies, and even natural calamities. So these are realities we also consider in business continuity because disruptions can affect people’s ability to access important services,” she said.
“The company has also helped make insurance more understandable and accessible through its people. We have financial advisors who guide customers based on their needs, life stage, and goals.”

Let’s face it: Although more Filipinos are now aware of insurance and its significance, not a lot would treat it as an immediate necessity. Oftentimes, it gets put aside as a “next time” expense, rather than something integral to one’s everyday life.
“The more we connect insurance to real-life concerns, family, health, education, emergencies, and peace of mind, the more people see it not as an expense but as an act of care.”
Now that Pru Life UK has crossed its 30th year, Plopenio wishes that in the next 30 years, the company remains a trusted partner for Filipino families.

“I hope the company continues to innovate, strengthen resilience, and make protection more accessible to more Filipinos. I also hope it continues to invest in its people because my own journey shows how much an organization can shape and grow its people when it provides trust, opportunity, and purpose.”
In fact, in our conversation, “people” is the word that showed up the most.

“My journey with Pru Life UK has taught me that protection is not just about policies or plans; it is about people. It is about preparing today so that families, customers, employees, and communities can face tomorrow with more confidence.”
“The first and foremost consideration in everything we do is our care for our people,” she said, highlighting the need to empower people to grow.

And with how Plopenio is warmly surrounded by different Pru Life UK employees who cheered her on – from the start until the end of our shoot and interview – I know this isn’t just lip service. You really get what you give. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care
articles.summary: Last month Paige Adamson was stopped at a U.S.-Canada border crossing and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election. She died at home on Sunday after a fall,…

image.caption: Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing in Tsawwassen and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

Last month Paige Adamson was stopped at a U.S.-Canada border crossing and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election. She died at home on Sunday after a fall, telling friends she was scared of being detained if she sought medical care.
Neighbour says Paige Adamson refused to call paramedics despite being unable to stand unaided
A 61-year-old Canadian woman living in the isolated U.S. town of Point Roberts, Wash., has died after refusing to seek medical care out of fears she would be detained or deported.

Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing, south of Tsawwassen, and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election.
The U.S. permanent resident was scheduled to appear at a deportation hearing before a federal immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.
Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman said Adamson called her on Thursday night asking to borrow a pair of crutches from local nonprofit Circle Of Care.
"I took them over and found her literally debilitated on the sofa, in very, very bad pain," Norman said.
"She told me that she had slipped and fallen on her right side … she was relying on the help of a few friends to come and help her get up and take her to the bathroom."

items: Canadian citizen detained at U.S. border crossing, questioned for hours about voting

blocks.text: Norman, who was also a friend and neighbour of Adamson, said she urged the distressed woman to call paramedics or visit the local Point Roberts health-care clinic.
"And she said, 'No, no, I'm afraid if I go, I won't be able to come back. They'll keep me or they'll deport me.'"
Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman says she urged Paige Adamson to call paramedics or visit the local health-care clinic. (CBC News)
Point Roberts is a U.S. pene-exclave at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country.

U.S. immigration lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson had mentioned not feeling well and needing to see a doctor. Residents of Point Roberts have to cross into Canada in order to get to other parts of Washington state or the U.S. and there was a risk she would be detained by ICE upon return to the U.S.
Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years and crossed the Canadian border countless times. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
"She was quite frankly scared about trying to drive up to Canada and come back in," Saunders said.
"There are no doctors where she lives. For all practical purposes, she was in detention," he said.
"I mentioned to her that I'd heard of people in the past maybe taking a boat or taking an airplane. But financially, I don't think she could afford it. She didn't have a lot of money."
Norman said she checked in on Adamson over the weekend, but her friend's condition had not improved.
"The next message that I got was on Monday, telling me to show up at her address," she said.
"She had died sometime in the hours previous."

items: Canadian detained at U.S. border, questioned for hours about voting as permanent resident

blocks.text: In a statement, Whatcom County Sheriff public information officer Deb Slater said the death "appeared to be of natural causes."
Louise Trapp, operations manager with the medical examiner, said Adamson's body was in her office's care pending examination by a forensic pathologist.
'Absolute worst case outcome'
Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years.

According to Saunders, her status meant she was legally entitled to leave and enter the country while awaiting deportation proceedings, but border officials had the right to detain her if they saw fit.
"Officers have the right to take you into detention and send you on a one-way trip to the Northwest Detention Centre down in Tacoma," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders says Paige Adamson had been missing appointments with her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., due to fears of being detained or deported trying to cross the border. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)
"I asked her to speak to the Peace Arch port-of-entry. I believe she had called them but was given no guarantees on what would happen … I could understand her concerns."
As a U.S. resident, accessing health care in British Columbia was not an option. CBC News reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for comment but did not hear back before deadline.
Saunders said he couldn't believe it when he was advised of Adamson's death on Sunday.
"This is an absolute worst case outcome. Here's a lady with no prior immigration violations, no criminal convictions. She was about as squeaky clean as you could get," he said.
Adamson is survived by two sons, both residents of B.C.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ruby Cornish is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver. She spent more than a decade reporting, producing and presenting with Australia's public broadcaster before relocating to Canada in 2026.

articles.title: Developer wants to build 500 modular homes on roof of struggling Sask. mall
articles.summary: The Prince Albert project reflects a national trend of denser, centrally located housing since the federal government increased incentives a few years ago, an expert says.

image.caption: A conceptual rendering of Alrifai Real Estates' housing proposal for Gateway Mall in Prince Albert, Sask. (Submitted by Alrifai Real Estates)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
The Prince Albert project reflects a national trend of denser, centrally located housing since the federal government increased incentives a few years ago, an expert says.
Plan is 'not crazy, but it's pushing the limits,' expert says of Prince Albert project
Louai Alrifai says the future of a struggling mall in central Saskatchewan comes down to a math equation: "700 cars and light trucks weigh around 3,000,000 pounds. Our modules weigh much less."
Alrifai's firm bought the Gateway Mall in Prince Albert, Sask., earlier this year and has announced plans to build 500 modular housing units on its roof, replacing a parking lot.
It's a reflection of a national trend toward building denser housing within city boundaries, according to one expert.
Though there are cases of builders incorporating new homes into existing malls, CBC News could not identify another case of modular housing units going on top of one.
Alrifai says his company focuses on properties others don't want. (Submitted by Louai Alrifai)
"Due to the size of the land, it makes much more sense to go on the roof," said Alrifai, who is president and CEO of Alrifai Real Estates.
He said the one-bedroom homes would each be about 329 square feet and geared toward students, young professionals and health-care workers.
He expects them to be ready in 2027, with a monthly rent of $1,000, including utilities.

Alrifai's company bought the mall building earlier this year. He said he plans to spend $40 million on the housing development and an additional $10 million on the interior of the mall, fixing a leakage issue and encouraging new stores and study spaces.
"I think people in Prince Albert are great, hardworking people and they deserve to improve their downtown," he said.
The company intends to build more parking spaces to replace what's on the roof. Greg Dionne, former mayor of Prince Albert, is an advisor for the firm.
A conceptual rendering of what a unit might look like. The company says each will cover 329 square feet and will rent for $1,000 a month. (Supplied by Alrifai Real Estates)
Alrifai said they're preparing to submit formal plans to the city and have received a positive reception from city staff and officials.
Michael Nelson, acting director of community development for the city, said Prince Albert needs more housing.
"We do have a shortfall on some housing units that we do want to help achieve and we're always open to new ideas and new developments."
Nelson said a series of assessments and reviews will determine if Alrifai's plan is feasible.

items: Could re-imagining malls help solve the GTA housing crunch? Some developers are betting on it

blocks.text: "I think anything's possible, it's just all the proper reviews and approvals have to be in place."
Nelson said the company can apply for financial incentives. Alrifai said they're optimistic about receiving support, but the project is about more than money.
"I didn't buy Gateway Mall to collect rent only. I bought it to reposition the whole thing, to actually turn it into a true hub for the downtown of Prince Albert," he said.
Expert sees national trend of denser housing
Scott Bell, a professor of geography and planning at the University of Saskatchewan, said he's never seen anything quite like this proposed project.

"It does seem novel. I have seen small house developments, I've seen redevelopment within city limits of different types. I've not seen one like this where it's using an existing structure and then placing housing units on top of that structure," he said.
Scott Bell is a professor of geography and planning at the University of Saskatchewan. (Submitted by Scott Bell)
Bell said there's been a rise in construction of dense housing within city limits over the past few years, since the federal government increased incentives to encourage it.
He cited the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties funding for cities to how much centrally located and dense housing is built.

"These look like tiny container homes, so melding that type of construction and house type with redevelopment is maybe pushing the next step for urban growth…. not crazy, but it's pushing the limits," Bell said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Maeve Ellis is a reporter and associate producer with CBC News based in Saskatoon. You can reach her at maeve.ellis@cbc.ca or maeveellis_ on X. She would love to hear from anyone with Sask-related story ideas.

articles.title: Court denies Revilla's motion to exclude judge from malversation case
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan has denied, due to lack of merit, the appeal of former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr. to exclude Sandiganbayan Third Division chairperson and Associate Justice Karl Miranda from…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 6:55pm

The Sandiganbayan has denied, due to lack of merit, the appeal of former Senator Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr. to exclude Sandiganbayan Third Division chairperson and Associate Justice Karl Miranda from presiding over the P92.8 million malversation case over a non-existent flood control project in Bulacan.

In an October 22 Resolution, the anti-graft court sustained its earlier decision denying Revilla's motion seeking the inhibition of Miranda by citing that Revilla merely repeated his earlier arguments which were already addressed by the Sandiganbayan in its September 24, 2026 Resolution.

“Revilla had not provided any new or additional act, conduct, or circumstance that could be considered as clear and convincing evidence of Justice Miranda’s bias and prejudice that would warrant his recusal from hearing the instant case,” a statement from the anti-graft court said.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division said that in determining the appearance of impartiality, the circumstances are measured based on the metric of a reasonable, fair-minded, and informed person, not on Revilla’s perception as an accused.

“Based on the perspective of a reasonable observer, the circumstances enumerated by Revilla would not create an impression that Justice Miranda is impartial. Even if these circumstances are examined in their totality, a reasonable observer would find that there is absolutely no connection between Justice Miranda’s remarks on Good Conduct and Time Allowance Law before all accused and his relationship with Atty. Buenaventura B. Miranda, counsel of former Undersecretary of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Roberto R. Bernardo,” the anti-graft court said.

“Moreover, the court ruled that a reasonable observer would not simply ascribe Justice Miranda’s vote to deny Revilla’s petition for bail to the former’s relationship with Atty. Miranda but instead examine whether such vote was supported by a thorough review of the evidence presented to the court,” the Sandiganbayan added.
It was Miranda who is the lone Sandiganbayan Third Division justice who voted against the granting of Revilla's petition for bail. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father
articles.summary:
Meghan also reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police

The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving…

blocks.text: The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.

Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.

It is understood that authorities in the UK had previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.

Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and has never met his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.

Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

articles.title: Philippine peso sinks to 31st record low at P63.615
articles.summary: The decline came a day after the BSP raised its benchmark rate to 5.5%.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 6:50pm
Philippine peso bills in P1,000 denominations
bugking88 from Getty Images via Canva Pro
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine peso sank to a fresh record low of P63.615 to $1 on Friday, October 23, marking the 31st time this year that it closed at an all-time low.
The peso weakened by 9.5 centavos from Thursday's P63.52 finish, which had set the previous record.
Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said Thursday that the central bank was not raising interest rates to support a particular exchange rate.
The central bank, however, may step into the foreign-exchange market to curb sharp swings that could fuel inflation.

"We do intervene a little bit in the foreign exchange market, but that's mainly to avoid swings in the exchange rate that tend to be inflationary. We have estimates of how much the peso has to move before it becomes inflationary, and that's when we tend to intervene," Remolona said.
His remarks followed the Monetary Board's decision to raise the BSP's benchmark interest rate by 50 basis points to 5.5%, its fourth consecutive increase.
The BSP described the larger move as a response to broadening price pressures and further risks to the inflation outlook, rather than an attempt to defend the peso.

A weaker currency can make dollar-priced imports, including fuel, more expensive in peso terms and add to inflation. That gives the central bank reason to limit disorderly exchange-rate swings even as it allows the market to determine the peso's level.

articles.title: Carney defends doing business with countries that don’t share Canada’s values
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government’s pursuit of trade with countries accused of human rights abuses, arguing few nations meet Canada’s standards. Wrapping up a visit to Turkey, Carney…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, left, and Turkish President Recep Erdogan shake hands during a news conference at the presidential palace in Ankara, Turkey, on Thursday, when both countries signed a new trade and defence partnership. (Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Presidential Press Office/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government’s pursuit of trade with countries accused of human rights abuses, arguing few nations meet Canada’s standards. Wrapping up a visit to Turkey, Carney insisted engagement does not equal approval, but declined to say whether he personally challenged President Erdogan over his government’s crackdown.
As Ottawa deepens ties with Turkey, PM argues engagement does not mean endorsement
Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government's approach to balancing human rights and trade on Friday, saying very few countries in the world can meet Canada's standards.

He made the remarks near the end of his trip to Turkey, where he signed a strategic partnership with the government of President Recep Erdogan, which has faced sustained criticism from human rights groups.

The complaints intensified this month when the Turkish government executed several high-profile operations to systematically silence opposition voices, suppress independent journalism, and restrict marginalized groups.
In the past Carney has said Canada is pursuing values-based realism in its approach, recognizing that not every partner will share all Canadian values.
"Engagement in those partnerships does not mean approval," Carney said Friday.
"There are very few countries in this world that have the standards of Canada."
A statement from the Prime Minister's Office said Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand raised the issue of human rights with her counterpart during meetings on Thursday.
Carney was asked by journalists on Friday whether he personally raised concerns with Erdogan during their separate meeting. The prime minister refused to be pinned down.
Carney hails new trade, defence pact with 'exceptional partner' Turkey

"My approach on these issues is I have direct conversations with leaders," Carney said. "I find those conversations are more effective when they're direct and open and not then reported out in detail, but we have raised these issues."
Concern about the authoritarian reflexes of the Turkish government have partly overshadowed Carney's initiative to deepen trade ties.

The prime minister is looking to make Canada less dependent on the United States market and to diversify its trading markets. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific, but it has also included other states with questionable human rights records, including recently Saudi Arabia.
'Disappointed' by U.S. claims
Carney is holding a series of meetings with business leaders in Istanbul after the political talks in Ankara on Thursday.
One of the deals being pursued involves the possible sale of Canadian nuclear technology to Turkey as the Middle Eastern nation attempts to reach its climate goals.

Carney told reporters said, following the signing of the strategic partnership, there were ‌now "good chances" for Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis to be picked as a partner to build the two power plants ⁠Turkey is planning.
Also Friday, Carney pushed back more forcefully against allegations of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections.
The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a fact sheet on Thursday, officially accusing Canadian leaders of election meddling ahead of the Nov. 3 vote.

items: Carney announces trade and defence partnership with Turkey
Canadian diplomats advised to avoid appearing with midterm candidates

blocks.text: "There is no merit to these claims, so I'll call it out that way," Carney said. "I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions."
The prime minister went on to say Canada has a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States and lots of interaction with American companies, citizens and individuals.
"As a country Canada is very, very careful to not be seen to interfere in the democratic process," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
