articles.title: Malawi opposition demands answers over president's prolonged stay abroad
articles.summary: This is President Peter Mutharika's fifth visit to South Africa this year.

blocks.text: Mutharika returned to power in October last year after defeating then-president Lazarus Chakwera.
He previously governed Malawi between 2014 and 2020.
His latest absence comes amid growing public scrutiny of his frequent visits to South Africa.

On Thursday, MCP campaign director Moses Kunkuyu told journalists in the capital, Lilongwe, that the opposition was not questioning the president's right to travel for personal reasons but wanted Vice-President Jane Ansah to address the nation over the country's mounting challenges.
He said that Malawians deserved to know who was managing the country's affairs.
"The issue is not that the president has traveled," he said. "The issue is that people are suffering and want reassurance that somebody is in charge."

He called on the government to explain how it intended to address persistent fuel shortages, frequent electricity blackouts, shortage of essential medicines in public hospitals and difficulties accessing foreign currency.

The information minister responded by telling local media that "a state president is always in charge at any time, anywhere," insisting that the president remained firmly in control of government affairs.
Asked about the purpose of the visit, the minister said: "A private trip is private."
He accused the opposition of attempting to exploit problems he said had developed under its previous administration.
"That is why Malawians voted us into government, not them. May I request them to seal their mouths as we address the problems they miserably created and failed to solve," he added.
On Thursday, Mutharika delegated the trade minister to lead Malawi's delegation to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) summit in Zimbabwe.
Earlier this month, officials dismissed reports on social media that Mutharika had travelled from South Africa to India for medical treatment.
Chief Secretary to the Government Justin Saidi said the president remained in South Africa and urged the public not to spread unverified information.
Mutharika has previously dismissed speculation about his health, describing such claims as "silly and laughable" and insisting that he was well.
Malawi faces a severe shortage of foreign currency, which has disrupted fuel imports and contributed to rising transport costs.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations, while unreliable electricity supplies and shortages of medicines have added to public frustration.

articles.title: PCG: No permission needed for BRP Sierra Madre resupply missions
articles.summary: The Philippines does not need permission from anyone for the conduct of its resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said on Friday.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 6:29pm
The Philippines does not need permission from anyone for the conduct of its resupply missions to the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said on Friday.

PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea (WPS) Commodore Jay Tarriela refuted claims from the Chinese Coast Guard (CCG), saying that on October 21, the Philippines was able to deliver supplies to the BRP Sierra Madre "with approval from the Chinese side."

"The Philippines did not ask for, and does not need, anyone's 'approval' to resupply our own troops aboard BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal. The October 21 mission was a sovereign act of the Philippine government inside our own exclusive economic zone," Tarriela said in a Facebook post.

"Ayungin Shoal lies about 105 nautical miles from Palawan and more than 500 nautical miles from the nearest coast of China. No country asks permission from a neighbor that far away to feed its own soldiers in its own waters," Tarriela said.
On Thursday, the Chinese Embassy in Manila posted on Facebook a statement from CCG spokesperson Jiang Lue, which claimed that they supervised the resupply mission.

"The Philippines delivered living necessities to its ship illegally 'grounded' at China's Ren'ai Jiao. The China Coast Guard inquired and verified the Philippine vessel conducting the delivery, and monitored the whole process," the statement read.
Tarriela also dismissed the name, "Ren'ai Jiao," saying it only exists in Beijing's maps.

"The 2016 Arbitral Award, final and binding on China, ruled that Ayungin Shoal is a low-tide elevation forming part of the Philippine continental shelf and EEZ (exclusive economic zone), where China has no entitlement whatsoever," Tarriela said.

China's state-owned Global Times news agency had also posted a video that supposedly documented that Filipino vessels sought permission from the Chinese side to board the vessel. The video showed what appeared to be a Chinese official on China Coast Guard Ship 5306 supposedly speaking to the Filipino crew on the Lapu-Lapu 1.
GMA News Online has reached out to Tarriela for a comment on the Global Times' report.

Diplomatic tensions between Beijing and Manila flared anew after Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan said China would easily win if it used force in the West Philippine Sea. This prompted many Filipino officials to ask President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to seek Jing's recall or to declare him persona non grata. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Puppy love: Finnish 24-hour newborn pup livestream is TV smash hit
articles.summary:
Show features live chat sessions with breeders, a podcast and updates on dogs’ progress from birth to weigh-ins

A 24-hour Finnish TV show dedicated entirely to the live progress of a dog and…

blocks.text: A 24-hour Finnish TV show dedicated entirely to the live progress of a dog and her six newborn puppies is drawing millions of viewers.

As well as a 24-hour webcam, Pentulive (Puppy Live) includes live evening chat sessions with the dogs’ breeder, a podcast and an instant notification service that updates followers on the puppies’ progress – from their birth to weigh-ins and first nail trims – for eight weeks.
This is the sixth season of the hit show by the broadcaster Yle and the latest contribution to the growing Nordic cultural phenomenon of “slow TV”.

The trend started in Norway in 2009 with Bergensbanen, a seven-hour train journey broadcast on NRK, and was followed by SVT’s Den stora älgvandringen (The Great Moose Migration) in Sweden, which features unnarrated glimpses of moose from the north of the country making their annual journey to summer grazing grounds.

blocks.caption: The seven Lagotto Romagnolo puppies with their mother, Hilkka. Photograph: Julia Kiiskinen/Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company/AP

blocks.text: Pentulive has long attracted interest from outside Finland, but this year it is also being broadcast in Sweden (under the name Valparna live). Yle recently announced that it had also sold the format to a broadcaster in the Netherlands.
Ville Alijoki, the editorial manager of Yle’s factual journalism, said: “There’s a certain magic to it, something that people miss when this world is sometimes quite dark.”

On Saturday, the Lagotto Romagnolo puppies – four male and two female – will mark their two-week birthday by being officially named after a vote by viewers. Among the nominations were Martha, Timo, Ronja and Dante.
In mid-December the puppies will leave their mother, Hilkka, and be adopted by new families.

blocks.caption: Moose in Junsele, Sweden, during preparations for the The Great Moose Migration – another slow TV hit. Photograph: SVT/AP

blocks.text: In the first two weeks of their lives, this year’s puppies have attracted millions of views online and on social media. Fans say the puppies offer a relaxing break from work and comfort from stress, loneliness and illness.
after newsletter promotion

Pirjo Koskinen, a science journalist who came up with the Pentulive concept with the aim of educating viewers on the latest dog research and the importance of the first few weeks of a dog’s life, said the show provided “relief from the terrible things happening in the world”.
She said: “Wars, bombing, climate change, habitat loss etc make us anxious and you can escape for at least a moment by watching the canine family.”
Watching the mother and breeder take care of the puppies is like watching “a loop of love and caring”.

“It’s real and we are in the basics of life: the miracle of birth, growth and development,” she added. “It’s so heartwarming to see eyes opening and first clumsy steps and it’s happening right now. That brings us joy, but also many funny moments during eight weeks.”

articles.title: The urban Filipino is tired, cash-strapped, and sick of the ‘resilience’ excuse
articles.summary: Nearly half of urban Filipinos surveyed in a study reject the romanticized narrative of resilience, as crises beyond their control leave them with little choice but to endure

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – For years, every calamity and crisis has been followed by a familiar consolation. Filipinos are resilient. Whatever happens, they find a way, pick themselves up, and keep going.
“Bagyo ka lang; Pinoy kami.” (You’re just a storm; we’re Filipinos.)

But many Filipinos are now rejecting that romanticized view. Nearly half (48%) of urban Filipinos surveyed by research firm Organic Intelligence said they rejected the romanticized narrative of “Filipino resilience,” according to its Pinoy, Kaya Pa Ba? study released in October.
The sentiment was strongest among younger respondents aged 18 to 24, of whom 64% rejected the narrative. In Mindanao, the figure reached 59%, compared with 38% in Metro Manila.
That said, at what point does enshrining the resilience of Filipinos for enduring hardship become an excuse for allowing that hardship to continue?

“We are not rejecting resilience per se. What we are rejecting is the necessity of it amid all of these crises. Why is that the default coping?” said Jason Ligot, Organic Intelligence group account director for development communication and communication design, in a press briefing on Friday, October 23.
“We should be holding government and institutions to account. And then second, why is the onus always on me?” he added.
Curiously, resilience was higher among groups facing greater hardship.

Mindanao respondents scored 86 out of 100 on the Resilience Index, compared with 80 in Luzon outside Metro Manila. Those aged 45 to 54 scored 87, against 77 among younger adults. Researchers said lower-income respondents also tended to score higher.
So how do these high scores square with the growing rejection of the resilience narrative?
Ligot suggested that those facing the greatest hardships may be drawing more heavily on their psychological reserves because they have little choice.

Although 69% of Filipinos maintained an optimistic financial outlook, 44% lacked enough savings to survive three months without work. Another 45% said inflation had drained them to the point of losing their drive to get ahead.

The Philippines may have officially reached upper-middle-income status in July, but that does not mean ordinary families have the financial security to weather another crisis. At the Zero Poverty PH 2030 forum on October 16, World Bank economist Sharon Faye Piza warned that many households remain vulnerable to economic shocks that could push them back into poverty, calling for better-paying jobs and stronger social protection.

blocks.caption: World Bank: 4Ps a ‘far more effective’ program for reducing poverty

blocks.text: The study also found that Filipinos are also borrowing just to get by.
The survey found that 46% had taken out a loan in the preceding one to two months, with 42% of all respondents borrowing for essentials, including food and transportation.

Official banking data similarly show a broader expansion in consumer credit. Outstanding consumer loans reached P2.84 trillion in August, up 17% from a year earlier, according to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP). Credit card receivables alone climbed 23.8%.

blocks.caption: The urban Filipino is tired, cash-strapped, and sick of the ‘resilience’ excuse

blocks.text: More worryingly, there are signs of growing repayment difficulties. Non-performing consumer loans grew nearly 20% from a year earlier, and the share of bad debt climbed to 5.67% of all consumer loans, according to BSP data.
So what can be done?

Of course, there are big problems to fix. The study calls for holding the government accountable, addressing the economic pressures on households, and building more free public spaces where Filipinos can relax for free. But these changes will take time.

But businesses can act more immediately to help struggling consumers and earn their loyalty along the way. Asked what would make them feel a brand was genuinely on their side, 27% of respondents chose a price freeze, the most popular response. Smaller or tingi sizes followed at 16%, free shipping at 14%, and promotional bundles at 12%.

“It has to be tangible,” said Sheila Mangila, Organic Intelligence group account director for marketing intelligence. “It’s about material conditions that will really help them survive the everyday.” – Rappler.com
The study surveyed 800 Filipinos in urban areas aged 18 to 65 through an online panel in May 2026. Its findings may not fully capture perspectives of rural or digitally disconnected Filipinos.

articles.title: Marcos vows to build more solar pump irrigation systems amid El Niño threat
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday committed to expanding solar-powered irrigation systems in the country in a bid to mitigate the impacts of the Super El Niño.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 6:14pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday committed to expanding solar-powered irrigation systems in the country in a bid to mitigate the impacts of the Super El Niño.
The President said this as he led the inauguration of the Tugbong Solar Pump Irrigation Project (SPIP) in Kananga, Leyte.

“Iniikot ko at tinitiyak ko na maayos ang ating mga patubig natin dahil parating na at napapag-usapan na parating ‘yung El Niño. Pero itong darating daw na El Niño ay mas mabigat kaysa sa dating mga El Niño. Sa ngayon, mayroon na tayo, nararamdaman na natin at umiinit na at sabi nila ay patuloy pa ‘to hanggang next year,” Marcos said.

(I am making the rounds to ensure that our irrigation systems are in good condition as the El Niño is coming. This El Niño is expected to be more severe than previous ones. We are already experiencing it now as the weather is getting hotter, and it is expected to persist until next year.)

“Kaya tinitiyak natin na ang ating mga irrigation systems ay nandyan na patuloy pa rin. Panay pa rin ang ating ginagawa na irrigation system para sa ating mga magsasaka at sa ating mga iba't ibang taniman,” he added.
(That is why we are ensuring that our irrigation systems remain operational. We are continuously working on irrigation systems to help our farmers.)
The Tugbong SPIP, one of two solar-powered irrigation projects inaugurated in Leyte, will provide irrigation to 115 hectares of rice fields in Barangays Tugbong and Sto. Niño in Kananga.
Meanwhile, the Guintigui-an Solar Pump Irrigation Project in Ormoc City, will serve 70 hectares of farmland and benefit over 80 farmers.
Through these solar-powered irrigation projects, Marcos said farmers would be able to save money on diesel costs.
“Sa paggamit natin ng solar power, alam niyo naman po, nakita naman po ninyo…gumagawa tayo ng kuryente na galing sa araw kaya’t libre,” the President explained.
(By using solar power, as you are well aware and have clearly seen, we generate free electricity from the sun.)

“Pagka ‘yung ganyang katumbas ng kuryente na lumalabas diyan sa solar…sa krudo na nanggagaling ang patakbo ng ating mga bomba ay siguro gagastos kayo ng mga P20,000 bawat season para makapagpatubig ng inyong mga lupain,” he added.
(If you were to generate the same amount of electricity by using diesel fuel to power your pumps, you would likely spend around P20,000 per season to irrigate your lands.)
Marcos said the Department of Agriculture is also distributing smaller solar-powered water pumps to farmers to further reduce irrigation costs.
He noted that around 3,000 solar pump irrigation systems have been established all over the country to improve agricultural productivity and provide farmers with a sustainable water source.
“Umaabot na tayo sa 70% ng irrigable lands ay irrigated na,” Marcos said.
(About 70% of our irrigable lands are now irrigated.)
“At pinapaspas natin para tiyakin na dahil alam ng mga magsasaka ‘yan na talaga naman ang pinakaimportante sa lahat pagka nagsasaka ay ang patubig. Kaya ito’y ginawa nating prayoridad,” he added.
(And we are planning to build more because we know that when it comes to farming, irrigation is the most important thing of all. That is why we have made this a priority.) — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.summary: Questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers, were raised earlier this month.

blocks.text: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
Image source, Getty Images
Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich - his lawyers have said he denies concealing his fortune
ByJames Oliver and Rory TinmanBBC Panorama

Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.

Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax

blocks.text: Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax

The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.

The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential, external investigation.

A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune
12 October
Watch now on BBC iPlayer

Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

items: Senators warn that recalling the House-approved 2027 national budget could lead to delays and a reenacted budget.
The Makabayan bloc is pushing for the recall to correct potentially unconstitutional provisions, but Senate leaders argue that this is not the solution.
Senate President Gatchalian believes the Senate can address concerns in the consolidated budget bill without needing a recall.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Recalling the House-approved version of the 7.2-trillion proposed 2027 national budget, as pushed by some lawmakers, may result in a reenacted budget, senators said on Friday, October 23.

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito warned of potential delays in the passage of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) after the Makabayan bloc proposed recalling House Bill No. 10858 to correct provisions they believe could be declared unconstitutional.
“There are proposals to recall the HGAB. In my opinion, there is a great chance the proposed 2027 national budget may not be approved if that would happen,” Ejercito said in a chance interview.

“The Senate is running on a very tight schedule due to the impeachment, regular plenary sessions, and budget hearings. Right now, we are targeting to pass our version of the budget bill by second week of November,” he added

The Supreme Court (SC) declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAA), or national budget laws, unconstitutional. Citing the court’s rulings, the Makabayan bloc called on the House to “clean its own mess,” pointing to provisions in the proposed 2027 budget involving the release of unprogrammed appropriations, cuts to foreign-assisted projects to accommodate congressional insertions, and prohibited lump-sum allocations.

ACT Teachers Representative Antonio Tinio told ANC’s Headstart: “If this were not corrected, [it] would risk many portions of the budget for 2027 as well. We don’t want yet another budget that will be declared unconstitutional.”
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, chairperson of the Senate committee on accounts, echoed Ejercito’s position, saying recalling the budget was “not the solution.”

“They can submit their proposals to the House or to the Senate finance committee for consideration. After all, the Senate version of the budget bill will be subject to the bicam so they should attest and address their concerns there,” Lacson said.
“Recalling the budget to the House is not the solution because that would result to a worse scenario — a reenacted budget,” he added.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian also said there was no need to recall the proposed budget, adding that the Senate could address the questioned provisions in the consolidated version of the budget bill.
“Looking at the Supreme Court decision on the 2026 budget, there are only a few provisions that will be affected. I don’t see the need to make major correction in the 2027 budget,” Gatchalian said.

Under the 1987 Constitution, if Congress fails to pass the GAB for the incoming fiscal year, the GAA for the preceding fiscal year is deemed reenacted and remains in effect until a new appropriations law is passed. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 4 million travelers expected as airports brace for Undas rush
articles.summary: Airports are preparing for the Undas rush with additional immigration, general and security personnel from Oct. 30 to Nov. 3.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 6:14pm
Air travelers wait for their luggage at an arrivals bay carousel at Terminal 3 of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport on Oct. 19, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Immigration and the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines are set to deploy additional personnel from October 30 to November 3 as airports brace for the Undas passenger surge.
CAAP expects passenger volume this year to reach 4 million, up from 3.7 million in 2025.

Immigration spokesperson Anisha Hadji Hassan said rapid response teams will be on standby at each terminal in case more immigration officers are needed or eGates at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport experience downtime.

"For the maximum availability of our officers, we are currently implementing a leave ban. From Oct. 30 to Nov. 3, we are limiting the approval of vacation leaves so that if additional personnel are needed, we will have officers available for deployment," Hassan said in Filipino on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon radio.

CAAP Public Information Officer Bea Bernardo said more general and security personnel will also be deployed as heightened security measures are implemented, including stricter baggage checks and help desks.
CAAP is also coordinating with other agencies to improve airport operations, she added.
"Under the DOTr's Oplan Biyaheng Ayos, all its attached agencies are working together to speed up processes and ensure the safety of passengers," Bernardo said in Filipino.
Travel reminders
Passengers, meanwhile, are reminded to prepare ahead and monitor advisories from agencies operating at airports.
"Passengers should know about advisories in advance so their travels can be hassle-free," Hassan said.
The advisories are posted on the agencies' websites. Immigration wait times are available on the BI website and Facebook page.
Hassan also advised passengers to arrive at the airport early and prepare their documents in advance, including eTravel passes, which are available 72 hours before departure and arrival.
For frequent travelers, Hassan recommended using eGates so immigration officers can "focus on passengers who are potentially vulnerable or threats."

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-born Wesley So recovered from a hard fall in the last round to clinch the 2026 US Chess Championship on Thursday, October 22 (Friday, October 23, Philippine time).

Shrugging off a harrowing last round loss, the 33-year-old pride of Bacoor, Cavite, beat top seed Fabiano Caruana in the rapid playoffs, 1.5-0.5, to bag the $56,000 (P3.55 million) champion’s purse at the Saint Louis Chess Club in St. Louis, Missouri.

With the crown for his taking, So faltered against cellar-dweller Sam Sevian in the 11th round, allowing Caruana to catch him at 7.0 points following a victory over Awonder Liang in the 12-man, all super-Grandmaster tournament.
After a see-saw draw in the first tiebreaker, So pounced on a dubious pawn sacrifice by Caruana to win the second and secure his fourth US national title, having prevailed in 2017, 2020, and 2021.
Enjoying a strong season, So — a three-time Philippine champion before transferring to the US Chess Federation in 2014 — also ruled the Americas Cup in March and the Sinquefield Cup in August.

So bested Sam Shankland in the first round, drew with Jeffery Xiong, Liang, Levon Aronian, Grigory Oparin, Abhimanyu Mishra in succession; trounced Ray Robson and Andy Woodward; and drew with Caruana and Hans Niemann in the ninth and 10th rounds.
In the post-interview, So admitted he barely slept after that defeat to Sevian, napping only two to three hours, but willed himself to victory as Caruana wasn’t in his best form.
Caruana had ruled the annual event since 2022, but So ended his reign.
WIM (Woman International Master) Rachel Li snared the US women’s crown, where 13-year-old Fide Master Megan Paragua, born of Filipino parents in New York, shared fourth place.
Li scored 8.5 points, IM Alice Lee 8.0 points, GM Irina Krush 7.5 points, and WGM Thalia Cervantes and Paragua, niece of US-based Filipino GM Mark Paragua, 6.0 points. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Winnipeg couple files complaint over birth registration laws after surrogacy legal hurdles
articles.summary: It took five weeks and cost Winnipeg dads Darrel Nadeau and Mackenzie Dyck about $6,000 to get formally recognized as parents after a surrogate mother gave birth to their son, Théo.

image.caption: Mackenzie Dyck, left, and Darrel Nadeau with their son, Théo, last month. (Submitted by Darrel Nadeau)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New
It took five weeks and cost Winnipeg dads Darrel Nadeau and Mackenzie Dyck about $6,000 to get formally recognized as parents after a surrogate mother gave birth to their son, Théo.
Manitoba premier apologizes to 2-father family for lengthy, expensive process
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 23, 2026 6:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago

After going through the process, they filed a complaint with the Manitoba Human Rights Commission and wrote a letter to the province because Nadeau said it discriminates against gay couples, people with fertility issues and those who can't give birth.

"For us, it was important to make a change, a lasting change for future families that go through this process," Nadeau, who's currently on parental leave, said in an interview Thursday at the Canadian Museum for Human Rights, where he works.
Surrogacy involves someone carrying and giving birth to a child for another person or couple.

Manitoba has a law that deals with surrogacy, but Nadeau said it unnecessarily and unfairly makes couples jump through lengthy, costly and complex legal hurdles both before and after birth to get their names on important documents, including a birth certificate.
"We faced discrimination as a two-dad family," Nadeau said, while holding Théo in his arms.
He said aspects of the law are "outdated."

The current law, which was amended in 2021, requires the intended parent or parents to enter into an agreement with the surrogate. Once the child is born, the surrogate consents to give up the child soon after, according to the province's website.

Nadeau and Théo at the Canadian Museum for Human Rights, where the new father works, on Thursday. He says it feels natural to lead a push for change because of his workplace. (Catherine Moreau/Radio-Canada)
"The woman who gives birth, in our case a surrogate, automatically gets listed as mother on birth registration documents," Nadeau said.
Getting the province to remove the surrogate and recognize both Nadeau and Dyck as Théo's parents meant jumping through more legal hurdles after their son was born.
"Before the pregnancy, there's a full legal agreement. And so other provinces, they use that to kind of pre-approve the change in parents at birth," Nadeau said.
"We had to go through that legal process just to medically be able to go for surrogacy."
He said that agreement is not taken into account after birth.
"You have to start a process completely from scratch because the law just doesn't have the flexibility to recognize a surrogacy agreement."
Nadeau suspects the law has been left this way because of a smaller number of people using surrogacy compared with other provinces.
"That doesn't mean that we should just sweep it under the rug and hope that they don't complain," he said.
Premier apologizes
Nadeau and Dyck's experience caught the attention of Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew.
In the letter to Kinew's office and Justice Minister Matt Wiebe sent last month, Nadeau called on the province to update its legal framework for families who use surrogacy.
He got a response back dated Oct. 6 suggesting his concerns were being taken seriously.
At an unrelated news conference in Brandon on Thursday, Kinew said he was "taken aback" by the couple's experience, calling it an "oversight" and promising to "fix it."
"I just want to apologize on behalf of the province of Manitoba," he said.
"It was my understanding that this issue had been resolved years and years and years ago."
While no exact timeline was given, Kinew suggested changes will be coming quickly.
"It's supposed to be the happiest moment of your life," the premier said.
"It's not supposed to be the start of an endless litigious process of cutting through red tape and paying fees and stuff like that."
Ontario's legislation changed in 2017 to "a more streamlined process," said Erin Lepine, a partner at Ottawa-based Richardson Hall who specializes in family and fertility law.

"Seven days after birth, the intended parents can apply for their birth certificate recognizing them as the parents and the surrogate not as a parent, without having to go through a court process," she said.
Lepine said it's an administrative process as long as four legislative requirements are met.

items: Manitoba parents who had child through surrogacy fighting for mat leave benefits
The path to parenthood: A made-in-Manitoba surrogacy story

blocks.text: A surrogacy agreement must be signed before conception, the parties in the agreement must get independent legal advice, there can be no more than four intended parents in the agreement and the child must have been conceived by assisted reproduction.
"Back before these changes were made in 2017, we did have to do the same thing as what I understand they're doing in Manitoba," Lepine said.
She said the longer, more expensive process had practical implications on intended parents beyond being more time-consuming and expensive.
"They were waiting a significant amount of time before they could apply for their government benefits and things you need for your child when they're born," Lepine said.
Nadeau welcomes the premier's willingness to update Manitoba's process but won't celebrate until he sees concrete changes.
"If nobody asks for change, it's not going to happen," the human rights museum employee said.
"For me, it feels natural to lead a process to make change on human rights. And so, that's our primary motivation."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Josh Crabb has been a reporter at CBC Manitoba since January 2023. He started reporting in 2005 at CKX-TV in Brandon, Man. After spending three years working in television in Red Deer, Alta., Josh returned to Manitoba in 2010 and has been covering stories across the province and in Winnipeg ever since.

articles.title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
articles.summary: The attack comes at a time of heightened tensions in the West Bank and four days before Israel's general election.

blocks.text: Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.
Unverified footage shared on social media shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.

The attack comes at a time of high tensions in the West Bank, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.

The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but unexpectedly ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security, said he had instructed the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media.
Netanyahu added that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning.

articles.title: MRT-3 privatization eyed by mid-2027 under P103.6-billion deal
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez says the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

blocks.text: TRAIN. Commuters crowd the MRT at the Araneta Cubao Station during the first day of the work week to avail of the month-long free train ride implemented by the government, on March 28, 2022.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
Transportation Secretary Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez says the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

MANILA, Philippines – The Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) may be privatized by mid-2027, with the Department of Transportation (DOTr) set to bid out the train line under a P103.6-billion public-private partnership project this year.
The decision to privatize the train line comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s order to prioritize the modernization of MRT-3.
DOTr Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez said the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

“Through public-private partnership, we bring in the expertise and investment this line needs. Ang kailangan natin dito ‘yung may matagal nang experience sa pagpapatakbo ng riles para sa kapakinabangan ng mga komyuter. At lilinawin ko po, mananatili pa rin sa DOTr ang pagtatakda ng pamasahe,” Lopez said in a statement released on Friday, October 23.
(What we need here is an entity with extensive experience in operating railways for the benefit of commuters. And let me make this clear, the DOTr will still be responsible for setting fares.)

Under the arrangement, a private company will be responsible for operating, maintaining, and upgrading the railway under a concession agreement. The project includes replacing trains and upgrading the signaling system to improve the line’s capacity, reliability, and efficiency.

Payments to the private operator, or concessionaire, will be linked to its delivery of services and compliance with performance standards covering train availability, reliability, cleanliness, and maintenance. The agreement is intended to hold the operator accountable for the quality of service it provides to commuters.
The DOTr said about 100 local and international companies have already expressed interest in the MRT-3 project. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Paolo Duterte files libel, cyber libel complaints vs NBI chief, Gracioso, GMA execs
articles.summary: The complaints name NBI chief Melvin Matibag, Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and several GMA Network personalities.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 5:31pm
Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City 1st District) visits his son, Davao City Acting Vice Mayor Rodrigo "Rigo" Duterte II, during a Sangguniang Panlungsod session on July 22, 2025.
Office of the Vice Mayor / Released

MANILA, Philippines — Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City, 1st District) filed libel and cyber libel complaints on Friday, October 23, against National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag, dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and several GMA Network journalists over a report that aired Gracioso’s claim that he delivered cash to the lawmaker.

The complaint filed before the Office of the City Prosecutor in Davao City names GMA Network chairman Felipe Gozon, president and chief executive Gilberto Duavit Jr., 24 Oras anchors Mel Tiangco, Vicky Morales and Emil Sumangil, and Darlene Cay, Marvin Parado and Joel San Luis, along with unnamed “John and Jane Does.”

Duterte’s lawyer, Peter Paul Danao, confirmed to Philstar.com that the complaint pertains to the September 25 episode of GMA's flagship broadcast 24 Oras, which aired pre-recorded interviews with Gracioso and Matibag.
In an initial statement, GMA Network said it had yet to receive a copy of the complaint.
Matibag said in an ambush interview that it was Duterte’s prerogative to file the complaint.

GMA had been the first to report on the affidavit of Gracioso, a former security aide to former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco. In it, Gracioso claimed that he delivered suitcases of cash to Vice President Sara Duterte, her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, and her brother on Velasco’s instructions.
He claimed to have delivered more than P2 billion to the vice president, P1 billion to the elder Duterte, and P100 million to Paolo Duterte.
The vice president and her brother have denied the allegations.
Matibag had earlier said Gracioso’s claims were "99 percent" truthful based on polygraph tests conducted by the bureau, though the NBI’s investigation into the allegations remains open.

Libel is punishable under the Revised Penal Code. Meanwhile, cyber libel, which covers defamation committed through a computer system, falls under the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 and carries a penalty one degree higher.
Press freedom groups have long raised concerns about the use of cyberlibel against Filipino journalists, especially during the presidency of the elder Duterte.
In that period, then-Rappler executive editor Maria Ressa was convicted of the offense in a case rights groups denounced as a "miscarriage of justice" and a form of harassment.
The government's own rights body, the Commission on Human Rights, has flagged how libel provisions in the Revised Penal Code and the cybercrime law have been repeatedly weaponized to silence critics.
— Cristina Chi with reports by Ian Laqui

articles.title: Sri Lanka: Death of iconic elephant raises habitat concerns
articles.summary: The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human-elephant conflict in rural communities. The island country sees a high number of deadly encounters.

image.caption: The 11-foot bull elephant 'Kavantissa' died after being shot in the leg earlier in OctoberImage: newswire.lk

blocks.text: The recent death of an iconic male elephant in Sri Lanka has raised concerns over ongoing contact between humans and the giant animals who are quickly seeing their habitats reduced.

The elephant known as "Kavantissa" had been considered to be the tallest living male elephant in the Sri Lanka. Thought to be anywhere from 45 years old and measuring roughly 3.3 meters tall (11 feet), he roamed Sri Lanka's northwest near the village of Galgamuwa, and was widely admired for his majestic stature.

In late September, villagers noticed the 5.5 ton-tusker (5,500 kg) was limping, and a closer look reveled a gunshot wound on his right leg. Despite the intervention of veterinary surgeons, the elephant died on October 16.

Sri Lanka records the highest number of elephant deaths annually and the second highest number of human deaths globally from violent interactions between elephants and humans, which usually happen when crop raiding elephants encroach on farmlands.
According to official statistics, since 2019, 370 elephants and 125 humans have died on average in human-elephant conflict incidents.
The situation affects the natural habitats of elephants and the livelihoods of rural communities.
Home to about 10% of the global Asian elephant population and occupying about 2% of their total natural range, Sri Lanka has the highest density of Asian elephants in the world.

The Sri Lankan elephant is an endangered subspecies in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, and protected under Sri Lankan law, with punishment by fines and jail terms for wildlife-related offences.

blocks.caption: Some villages use electric fences to keep elephants away from crops and peopleImage: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: A shrinking habitat for elephants
During the past few decades, forest cover in Sri Lanka has shrunk along with rapid population growth.
Statistics show the rural population of Sri Lanka increased from 8.25 million in 1960 to 17.8 million in 2020.
Agriculture remains the primary source of income for these rural communities. As a result, the land is cleared for agricultural activities.

According to Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) statistics, in 2024 an estimated 7,451 wild elephants were recorded in Sri Lanka. About 70% of these wild elephants live outside protected areas.
Research shows elephants have a massive daily dietary requirement of about 150 kilograms (330 lbs.) of green matter, which drives them into farmland.

"Driven primarily by habitat loss, agricultural expansion, fragmentation of elephant corridors, and increasing competition for land and resources, human-elephant conflict continues to cause hundreds of elephant deaths and more than 100 human fatalities annually," said Ravi Corea, President of Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society, a Sri Lankan non-profit conservation organization.
The conservationist told DW that rural communities are severely affected, and the agricultural losses caused by elephants can threaten a family's primary source of food and income.

"This distinguishes human-elephant conflict from many human-wildlife conflicts in economically developed countries, where wildlife encounters, although sometimes serious, generally do not threaten household subsistence to the same extent," he said.
Indian villages deter wild elephants with lemon trees
Elephants and humans clash
"Despite the efforts by the government to mitigate HEC, the numbers are rising demonstrating the continuing severity of the crisis," Corea added.
Elephants are shot, poisoned, or killed by improvised explosives hidden in food and train collisions, experts say.
In view of the escalation of human-elephant conflict, the Sri Lankan government in 2020 drafted a national action plan to mitigate the problem.

"The 2020 Action Plan provides a valuable foundation for reducing human–elephant conflict, but its recommendations must be strengthened through a comprehensive national conservation strategy with enforceable habitat protection at its core," Corea said.

"The ultimate measure of success must be not merely a reduction in human–elephant conflict, but the permanent protection of ecologically connected habitats, the survival of viable wild elephant populations and the ability of people and elephants to coexist sustainably for generations to come," he added.
Community-level initiatives protect people and elephants

Meanwhile, community-based programs by non-government organizations have proven effective and sustainable. These initiatives are complemented by elephant monitoring, scientific research, habitat assessments, community education, and the development of locally appropriate deterrents, Corea said

"Our flagship initiative Project Orange Elephant in Sri Lanka's Wasgamuwa region promotes the cultivation of citrus which elephants do not like to eat as a trophic deterrence. This reduces crop raiding while generating alternative income for farmers," Corea added, pointing to things like electric fencing protecting settlements and agricultural lands while encouraging local responsibility.

blocks.caption: Elephants do not like the taste of citrus fruits Image: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: Another issue is confrontations on elephant corridors, that in some cases have discouraged children from walking to school.
Elephant corridors are designated strips of land that connect larger forest and habitat patches, allowing elephants to move safely between them for food, water, breeding, and seasonal migration.

To address this, the "EleFriendly" bus service in Wasgamuwa, provides safe transportation for schoolchildren through elephant corridors and has reduced dangerous human-elephant encounters along its original route by over 90%.

blocks.caption: A bus takes students to school in order to avoid elephant paths Image: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: "An ethically just solution must protect human lives, livelihoods, and elephant populations simultaneously, said Kamal Shashendra, a Sri Lanka-based environmental ethics researcher.

He told DW that this required scientifically informed land-use planning, protection of elephant corridors, appropriate community-based fencing, effective early-warning systems, and fair compensation for affected families.

articles.title: Ombudsman hits 'impunity of corruption' as gov't execs extort from legit businesses
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Friday called out corrupt government officials who extort from business owners by delaying permit issuance, among others, for their own gain.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 5:24pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Friday called out corrupt government officials who extort from business owners by delaying permit issuance, among others, for their own gain.
Remulla made the statement during this meeting with the members of Cebu's lechon industry.

"Ang nangyayari ngayon is 'impunity of corruption.' Ang abuso from barangay captain, kagawad, tanod hanggang itaas. Grabe ang kikil. Pinahirapan nila ang negosyante. Hingi nang hingi. Iniipit. It comes to the point, kasosyo na sila ng mga negosyante. May porsyento na sila sa ginagawa niyo," Remulla said.

(What is happening is impunity of corruption. There's abuse of power starting with the barangay captain, council members, barangay watchmen, and up. The extortion is severe. They extort from businessmen and keep on asking for money. It comes to a point wherein these extortionists become business partners of the businessmen. They have a percentage of the profit.)

"Ang cost of doing business tumataas dahil maraming nang-iipit. At 'yan ang gusto natin baguhin. Maraming pressure sa amin. Protektahan 'to, huwag papatulan 'to. Huwag ikukulong 'yan, huwag idemanda 'yan. Hindi po. Kailangan gawin namin. Gagawin namin talaga," Remulla added.

(The cost of doing business is so high because there are lots of extortionists. And that is what we want to change. We face a lot of pressure. Protect this and that, don't send them to jail, don't file cases against certain people. No. We need to do our job and we will do our job.)
Ombudsman Remulla then said the government should enable legitimate business operations, instead of standing in their way.

"It shouldn't happen. Government should be there to assist business because you are the economy. The business sector's role is crucial in driving economic growth, generating employment and improving the purchasing power of Filipinos," Remulla said.

Remulla then cited the opening of the Investors' Window in the Ombudsman, which is a mechanism wherein business owners and investors may bring forward concerns involving government officials and transactions that impede their operations such as extortion, abuse of authority, unreasonable delays and other forms of misconduct in government.

"Kung ang Anti-Red Tape Authority report sa amin, 'yung permit hindi binibigay, susulatan natin 'yan. Sa susunod 'yan, 'pag hindi pa rin ginawa 'yan, suspend kaagad 'yan. Suspendihin natin kaagad 'yung concerned official. I can assure you that. Binigay sa amin ang power ng batas para gawin 'yan," Remulla said.
(If the permit to operate business is being withheld, then we will write them. If they still won't comply, we'll hand them suspension order. We have the power to do that.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning
articles.summary: Recent polls suggest the president is facing challenging headwinds in the state ahead of the midterms.

blocks.text: It was just before dawn in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas and the congregation were arriving for the Friday service at the tiny La Lomita Catholic Chapel.
The whitewashed building, which has been here since the days of the American Civil War, rises from the surrounding scrub and sits about 200 yards from the Rio Grande river itself.
As cars pulled up to the chapel, the sound of Father Roy Snipes' barking dogs signalled his arrival. He has been the priest here for almost half a century - and is known locally as the Cowboy Priest.
"I'm not sure why I picked that up, but it's nice," he said of the nickname.

In truth, it is pretty obvious why. Snipes wears a Stetson in place of the more traditional priest's hat. And moments later, the chapel was filled by the sound of a Roy Rogers song - the singer and actor known as the King of the Cowboys.

During the first Trump administration, Snipes resisted plans to seize the chapel's land to build the US president's border wall. Eight years on, at the early Friday service, he focused his short sermon on the actions of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
"There's no good excuse to detain, incarcerate and deport poor, good folks who are our neighbours," Snipes told the congregation of about 30, mainly Hispanic worshippers.
Texas accounted for roughly one-third of all ICE arrests nationwide in July 2026 - a larger share than any other state - according to government figures obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

"They said we're gonna seek out, capture, detain and deport the worst of the worst," Snipes said in his sermon. "Well, we're here on the border and the cartel is the worst-of-the-worst. So we thought, well, that's a good thing.
"But it turned out, you can hear almost every day, some poor guy going to work and they stop him and detain him and start a big fight."
After the service, two members of the congregation stopped to chat. "We're educators, and we have a lot of students that are having to go back because their parents are getting deported," one said.
"The cruelty that we're seeing - I think that's turning the tide, at least I hope so," their friend added.
Turning the tide politically is what Democrats are hoping they can do in Texas in the midterm elections on 3 November. But that will not be easy.

This stretch of the Rio Grande was once one of the busiest crossing points on the US-Mexico border. Under former President Joe Biden, hundreds of thousands of migrants came through here, with more than two and a half million apprehensions recorded in a single year.
Trump promised to stop these illegal crossings during his 2024 election campaign, and in large parts he has delivered.

Border crossings are now at their lowest level in decades. And it was that promise which in part drove Trump's astonishingly high level of support in the state, taking around 55% of Hispanic votes in Texas alone - a record for a Republican presidential candidate.

Javier Villalobos is the Republican Mayor of McAllen, one of the biggest cities in the Rio Grande Valley. He expects Republicans will find it tough this time around, but credits the Trump administration with stemming the border problem.

"I remember I put out a video… thanking the administration for immediately securing the border. That was great," he said. "And I think generally most people are okay with the deportation of criminals, violent people, or people that really are not productive at all."
But if you start deporting people that are productive and law-abiding, that is where the problem is, he added.
Guerrero is a reminder that, for many who live and work close to the US-Mexico border, security and immigration enforcement are two distinct issues.
A voter here may be supportive of securing the border and stopping illegal crossings, but oppose the actions of ICE and how the administration is enforcing its crackdown on undocumented migration.
Guerrero voted for Trump three times in a row - but is planning to vote Democrat in November, in part due to his unease with that crackdown.

"There's a man that I know that… last year, had 35 workers that were working for him every day," he said. "Right now, he just told me two days ago that he would be lucky if he would get four to six guys to show up to work."

Even though Guerrero plans to vote Democrat, he describes himself as neither Democrat nor Republican. And that, according to Mike Madrid, a leading Republican consultant and expert on Hispanic voters, is key to understanding the largest ethnic demographic voting group in the country.
"Latinos are more likely than any other racial or ethnic group to identify as independents rather than Republicans or Democrats," he said.

items: GUIDE: What are the US midterms?
EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms
IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope

blocks.text: It was in part the belief that Hispanic voters were shifting permanently towards the Republican Party that led Trump to press states such as Texas to redraw their congressional maps early, before the once-a-decade census.

The strategy was intended to capitalise on what Republicans saw as a realignment in Hispanic voting behaviour, particularly in border districts that had been Democratic strongholds for more than a century.
Texas's 15th congressional district was among those that were redrawn, and has become one of the clearest tests of whether electoral maps can guarantee political outcomes.

The seat was redrawn after the 2020 census and was won by a Republican in 2022. It was redrawn again in 2025, creating a notional 18-point majority for Republicans in these midterms. Even so, current polling suggests a Democratic lead of five or six points.
Bobby Pulido is the Democratic candidate hoping to win the district. As a popular Tejano singer and winner of two Latin Grammys, he is already a household name in the Rio Grande Valley.

At an event just weeks before the vote, he delivered a stock political speech followed by a musical performance. "A lot of people are disillusioned with both parties," he told the BBC shortly before he took the stage. "And I hear them."
To win in this part of Texas, you need to be a conservative. Pulido has distanced himself from the national Democratic Party brand and focused deliberately and consistently on economic issues.

"This isn't New York, this isn't LA," he said. "When you lead with issues like social justice, climate change and other topics, that's not what people want to hear first. They want to hear about the economy."
That message is consistent with what many current polls are suggesting - the economy, and the cost of living specifically, rank top on the list of most voters' priorities.

At a local avocado festival, a fruit that is a staple among Hispanic communities in the valley, a couple, Dave Baldwin and Veronica Salazar, began discussing rising prices as soon as they were asked about the upcoming elections.
When asked who they blame for spiking costs, the answer was swift. "The president," they said.
"He is in control of our destiny with all that, and right now he's not doing a very good job," added Baldwin.
Among many Republican campaigners here, there is a feeling that they are are on the back foot just weeks before the vote.
Alexis Uscanga, a student volunteer tasked with knocking on doors and checking on likely Republican voters in the district, was realistic about what he is trying to achieve.
"The midterms are just purely a game of turnout," he said. "It's not trying so much to convince individuals to vote one way or the other, it's about trying to get our people mostly to show up."

Tano Tijerina, the Republican candidate in the neighbouring, Democratic-held 28th district, credited Trump with "breaking through barriers" but acknowledged the "national political headwinds are real".

The Hispanic shift towards President Trump in 2024 was one of the most striking political facts of the past decade. While this expanding demographic may not have much love for either party, in a two-party system voters are mostly forced to make a choice.
And if polling is correct - and there is no guarantee of that - even a modest swing back to Democrats in November could reshape races not just across this state but far beyond.
In Texas, it could even be enough to put a US Senate seat in play - and Democrats haven't won one of those in the state in more than 30 years.

articles.title: Digital 2027 report: Global use of GenAI tools rises, web browser activity declines
articles.summary: 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up use AI tools each month, but only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up pay for subscriptions to an AI tool each month, the…

blocks.text: 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up use AI tools each month, but only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up pay for subscriptions to an AI tool each month, the study finds
MANILA, Philippines – Media intelligence company Meltwater and creative agency We Are Social released the Digital 2027 report this October, providing data on worldwide digital trends.

The more than 900-page report seeks to provide worldwide statistics on the various aspects of digital daily life, from the adoption of artificial intelligence tools like generative AI, to the use of web browsers and mobile phones. It is aided by a series of individual deep dives by author Simon Kemp into specific aspects of the main report.
In the local country headlines report, the Philippines is said to have a total population of 118 million people, a figure that increased by 936,000 from last year.

The report also showed 149 million cellular phone connections in the country, or 126% compared to the total population of the Philippines. The figure likely infers people having more than one phone on hand.

Meanwhile, 95.9 million individuals — or 81.3% of the population — were using the internet, while the report mentioned there were 94.7 million social media user identities in the country, which represent a decline of about 1.1 million user identities.

The report also mentioned 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up used AI tools each month. However, only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up paid for subscriptions to an AI tool each month.

Within the Philippine context, 71.17% of active AI users aged 16 and up use AI tools to find information, 37.6% of active AI users aged 16 and up use AI tools to seek advice on problems, 32.8% of active AI users aged 16 and up used AI tools for personalized recommendations.
Further, 27.5% of Philippine internet users aged 16 and up believe AI benefits society overall.
According to the report, 38.9% of the global population of 8.32 billion people — or around 3.24 billion — currently use generative AI tools each month.

This shows a growth of about 1.2 billion new users, though the report emphasizes a caveat of potential duplication —that a user may have more than one account for a generative AI service to decouple personal and work uses.

Meanwhile, social media user identities now number 5.81 billion or 69.9% of the world’s population, though a similar caveat applies here as some duplication due to decoupling personal and work social media identities may occur.

Citing two separate reports from GSMA Intelligence and Ericsson, there are now 5.86 billion unique mobile phone users worldwide as of the report’s release this month. Further information from Ericsson showed the 7.68 billion smartphones in use today account for nearly 90% of all active mobile phone handsets, and nearly 86% of total cellular mobile connections, with the caveat that some folks may have more than one smartphone.
The report said that across the world’s top 10,000 web domains, the total monthly web traffic declined by more than 10% since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
Combined traffic across the top 10,000 web domains fell by almost 50 billion visits per month between Q4 2022 and Q2 2026.

Further, there has been an 11.2% decline in the total time spent visiting the top 10,000 global domains over a two-year period, This fall is equivalent to more than 6.6 billion hours per month in that time frame.
Aside from the potential effects of AI use, the report suggests people are more readily using native mobile apps rather than using their browsers to get what they want from the internet.

That said, web users did load an average of just under 3 trillion pages per month across the world’s top 10,000 domains in the second quarter of 2026. The figure is up more than 2% compared to the same time period in 2024.
The full Digital 2027 report can be downloaded from this site. Meanwhile, Simon Kemp’s reports on some of the pertinent statistics are available here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Pig holiday extended as hog traders protest against rising pork imports
articles.summary: Hog traders staged a protest at the Department of Agriculture (DA) to decry the large number of pork imports hurting the industry.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 5:18pm
Hog traders staged a protest at the Department of Agriculture (DA) to decry the large number of pork imports hurting the industry.

In a DZBB report from Allan Gatus on Friday, hog traders are hoping that officials will listen to their plea and impose higher tariffs on pork imports. They are also seeking the cancelation of pork import permits.
The protesters are also asking the government to find a solution to end the rampant smuggling of foreign meat products, which was killing the industry.
According to the report, the protest remained peaceful until it ended in the morning, with DA officials going out to speak to the protesters and provide reassurance that the hog traders were heard.
Hog traders held a three-day “pig holiday” to protest foreign pork imports, which began on Thursday.
In a separate report, Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines chairperson and AGAP Party-list Representative Nicanor Briones said that the pig holiday will now last four days instead of three.
This means that participating hog traders will suspend the sale of pork until Sunday, October 25. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Greece joins countries putting age-limits on social media, banning access for kids under 15
articles.summary: Greece has passed legislation banning social media access for children under 15. New rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027, and are designed to protect children's mental health.

image.caption: Greece's lawmakers say 'uncontrolled internet use leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health' and claim the new law will give them back their childhood Image: Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: A bill to "ban the use of online social media services by minors" was passed by a majority vote of the Greek parliament Thursday and will go into effect on January 1, 2027.
The New Democracy party was the only bloc in parliament to support the measure; while opposition parties SYRIZA, Greek Solution, KKE, Niki and Freedom Course voted against it, and PASOK abstained.

Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou called the step, "necessary, effective, proportionate and EU-law-compliant," according to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, adding that social media platforms would have until the first of the year to, "determine whether the accounts they host and the services they provide are intended for adults or not."

Pointing to similar age limits on alcohol and tobacco sales to minors, Papastergiou said lawmakers had no time to wait for Brussels to pass "the perfect European law," saying, "let's send the message that the problem of uncontrolled internet use — which leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health — cannot continue."
Why does Greece want to introduce social media age limits?
The move to put legal age limits on social media use began last year in Australia, with numerous countries around the world swiftly following suit.

Greece is one of seven EU countries seeking to introduce standards for age-verification on social media, which proponents argue will curb the "endless scrolling" that deprives kids of sleep, destroys their attention span and ability to concentrate and keeps them from playing outdoors and spending time with their friends.
Papastergiou defended the use of an app known as "Kid's Wallet" as a means to that end, saying that it had been established according to codes and technical specifications set by the EU.

The minister was emphatic that the app, "does not provide any personal data whatsoever about children or users, other than whether they are over or under 15 years of age — not even their date of birth."

"We owe our children their childhood," said Papastergiou. "That is what we are doing today. We have a duty to protect them. Given the current challenges, the social media bill delivers what society has been waiting for."
EU-wide social media ban for kids?

articles.title: Ontario private school scrutinized over class video surveillance, making kids watch themselves ‘misbehaving’
articles.summary: A former student of a London private school and parents are concerned that children were under constant video surveillance in the classroom and asked to critique the footage with their peers. The…

image.caption: Lincoln Sandle, 11, is shown with his dad, Greg Sandle. Lincoln, a former student at Infinity School in London, Ont., says his teachers made the class watch back and critique footage of students captured on the school's surveillance cameras. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)

blocks.text: A former student of a London, Ont., private school and parents are concerned that children were under constant video surveillance in the classroom and asked to critique the footage with their peers.
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) says it’s investigating the matter after receiving a complaint.
Lincoln Sandle, 11, attended Infinity School from August 2023 until January 2026, when he was in Grades 3 through 5.
He said a common classroom activity involved watching back videos of himself and classmates that were captured by multiple surveillance cameras throughout the school.
“The whole class was in one room, and we had a projector and we watched us with audio,” Lincoln said. “[We watched] how we were misbehaving and who needed the most help.
“People watching me is weird. I just don’t like people invading my privacy.”
Family describes how surveillance cameras were used in son's classroom
Lincoln’s parents both gave CBC News permission to interview and photograph him for this story.
Infinity School focuses on hands-on and self-directed learning, according to its website.

It’s an affiliate of Acton Academy, a U.S.-based network of schools that emphasize Socratic discussions and project-based “quests,” its website explains. Each school is independently owned by “parent entrepreneurs,” who must follow a “shared learning design and high standards of excellence,” it says.
A map on the website shows nearly 300 Acton schools around the world, including nine in Canada.

Infinity School rents space in a church in London’s Wortley Village for its multi-grade classrooms and other facilities. Lincoln estimates there were up to 10 cameras around the school, including in classrooms, hallways, the gym and library.
Infinity School in London rents out a church building in the Wortley Village neighbourhood for its classes. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
“You couldn’t really talk about anything private with your friends,” Lincoln said. “It just cages us up.”
In a joint email statement to CBC News, the head of the Acton Academy Network, Jake Thompson, and Infinity School principal Eric Brown said cameras are meant to be a tool within the schools.

“At Acton, we trust young people with the responsibility for their own learning, and an important part of that learning is leadership,” Thompson said in a separate email. “Cameras give learners the ability to document, review and reflect on their leadership and learning experiences.”
Neither Thompson nor Brown responded to CBC's request for interviews.
Questions of consent
Lincoln’s father, Greg Sandle, said he didn’t know Infinity School had cameras when he first enrolled his two children, but started noticing them when he visited the school.

“I thought they were just for security … I didn’t believe that the cameras would be used for anything other than what I thought they were intended for, which was just safety of kids in the school,” Sandle said.
Greg Sandle says his family was not aware of how cameras were being used at Infinity School in London until he withdrew his children from classes there. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
He said he learned otherwise when the school's principal referred to camera footage in a December 2025 correspondence.
Some other parents told CBC News they also were also unaware of the cameras located inside the school until earlier this year, when conversations started within parent circles.
Thompson and Brown didn’t respond to CBC's questions about when and how parents were informed about the cameras, but said they are "openly discussed and visible to families."
What does the law say?
Public and private schools follow different privacy regulations laid out by different levels of government.
Ontario public schools are subject to the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, which is set out by Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario.

items: Russian website broadcast live pictures of Cape Breton schoolchildren
Supreme Court finds teacher who used camera pen guilty of voyeurism

blocks.text: A spokesperson from the office said school boards must determine whether they have “lawful authority” to collect personal information, including surveillance footage. Consent is not required, though public notice is needed as part of the school’s “transparency obligations,” the spokesperson said.

The OPC oversees the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), which applies to organizations that collect, use and disclose personal information for commercial activities.
The Infinity School logo is shown inside the doorway to the private school at 120 Bruce St. in London. (Kendra Seguin/ CBC News)
PIPEDA may apply to private schools "if they engage in activities that are commercial in nature."
Infinity School is listed on the Ontario Business Registry as a corporation.

"PIPEDA provides that, unless certain exceptions apply, the knowledge and consent of the individual is required for the collection, use, or disclosure of their personal information," spokesperson Vito Pilieci said.
Pilieci declined to share the nature of the complaint about Infinity School, but said it is reaching out to the school to collect more information and determine next steps.
Who else can access student footage?
Sarah Starrs, another parent, said she remembers learning about cameras during an interview with the school before enrolling her then seven-year-old son in September 2024.

She recalled finding out that cameras would be used in the older students’ classrooms as a learning tool, but didn’t think it would be in her son’s mixed-age classroom for children as young as four years old.

Sarah Starrs sent her son to Infinity School in London from September 2024 to May 2026. She says she has questions about why there were cameras in his classroom and who had access to the footage. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
While searching through the school’s parent portal in February, Starrs said, she noticed a privacy policy document for the first time that outlined camera usage and livestreaming capabilities.
“I felt surprised and confused,” she said.

According to a July 2026 privacy policy on Infinity School’s website, Acton Academy requires all schools within its network to have cameras, which include livestream capabilities “for schoolwide inspection purposes only.”
However, parents say it’s unclear who has access to livestream footage and where they are located, given that Acton is based in the U.S.

items: Administrators won't remove camera pointed at school bathrooms
'There is no trust': Parents of children with autism call for cameras in classrooms

blocks.text: CBC News requested this information from Thompson and Brown multiple times, but didn’t receive a direct answer.
"We regularly revisit our policies and are currently reviewing not just camera use, but our broader approach to privacy, to ensure we are best serving families across our campuses," they said.

Starrs said she continues to have questions about who has access to the livestream footage, which includes both images and audio of the children. She pulled her son out of Infinity School in May for unrelated reasons, but said the lack of transparency around cameras contributed to her decision to leave.
Impacts of surveilling children
Lincoln said the cameras at Infinity School made him feel stressed about going to class.
“I always tried to be the favourite person because then I wouldn’t have bad stuff happen to me, like people watching me."

Lincoln's parents withdrew both their children from the school in January following a series of unrelated challenges, said his father. That’s when Lincoln first told his family about the in-class footage reviews.
Lincoln says he's happier now that he's left Infinity School and started at a new school in London. (Kendra Seguin/CBC News)
“It was heartbreaking [to hear] because we wanted to do the best we could for the kids, and it makes us feel like it was the worst decision of our lives to put him in that situation,” Sandle said.
Alissa Centivany, co-director of the Starling Centre for Just Technologies & Just Societies and a professor at Western University, said she has concerns about camera surveillance in classrooms.

"Schools have a responsibility to student safety and well-being," Centivany said. "I think what we're seeing with the use of cameras in schools is that it's actually having the opposite effect, and it's diminishing schools' ability to carry out their legitimate and legal responsibilities."

She said surveillance cameras should be used only when it is authorized by law and if it's deemed necessary. For example, in a school setting, Centivany said, cameras could be justified when there is "illegal activity happening on school grounds or where there's been fights outside the school."

"How they were used as a way for school administrators and teachers to draw attention to classroom behaviour and use it as a teaching experience, to me, seems to not meet that second condition of being necessary.”
Lincoln started at a new school in September. He said there are no cameras on the premises.
“It makes me feel more open and able to share what I want with my friends,” he said.
