Wadephul warns shipping disruptions could lead to famine
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that continuing disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea could potentially lead to famine in the global south.

"We're all feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping lanes, whether at the gas station or in the supermarket," he said ahead of a meeting with fellow foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday. "But elsewhere, there is a threat of famine when fertilizers don't arrive in the places where they are essential for basic production."

Wadephul was referring not only to the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi threats to the Bab al-Mandab strait, but also to Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea as part of Moscow's ongoing war against Ukraine, one of the world's leading producers of wheat.

"This effects the poorest people in the world whose basic provisions are especially dependent on wheat, as well as our partners such as Turkey, the biggest wheat processing country in the world," he said.
"Together, we want to send a signal: we will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias [in Yemen] holding global trade hostage," Wadephul continued.

"The indiscriminatory attacks on free shipping and on neighboring countries must stop. For people across the region who are suffering from hunger, who no longer feel safe in their own homes, the continuing insecurity is not acceptable."

articles.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
articles.summary: One person has died after being swept away by waves in Taiwan's Liuqiu island, authorities say.

blocks.text: Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.

Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.

Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .

After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,

However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.

This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.

The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

articles.title: Rubio turns to small Indian town as US faces high oil prices
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio pushed a business and energy agenda over diplomacy on his second trip to India this year.

blocks.text: The western Indian port town of Jamnagar is not a usual stop for foreign leaders, yet it featured prominently in US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's recent visit.
So, why did Rubio visit the town? And, more importantly, why did he skip the Indian capital, Delhi?
The answer to both questions may have less to do with India and more to do with Donald Trump administration's domestic compulsions – or, more precisely, its domestic oil needs.

Rubio arrived in the financial capital Mumbai on Tuesday, where he met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and some of the country's top business leaders. He officially ended his trip in Jamnagar - in the western state of Gujarat - home to the giant oil refinery owned by one of Asia's richest men, Mukesh Ambani.
It was his second trip to the country this year and experts say what is significant this time is the timing of the visit as well as his choice of destinations.
The Trump administration is under pressure to keep fuel prices in check ahead of November's US midterm elections, while rising tensions in the Middle East threaten global energy supplies.

With little new refining capacity expected in the immediate future in the US, India's ability to process large volumes of crude oil offers Washington a potential way to ease pressure on the fuel markets.
And that puts Reliance's Jamnagar refinery at the centre of the equation.

The visit, however, comes at a tricky moment in India-US relations. Trump has imposed tariffs on Indian goods, there are sanctions against Delhi for buying Russian energy (though currently paused) and there is a trade deal between the two countries that has remained elusive for around 20 months now.
Announcing the visit, the US State Department had earlier said that it would focus on energy cooperation, commercial investment and economic ties.
The official itinerary also did not include Delhi, which raised some questions, especially from Indian opposition politicians. But analysts say the choice was strategic.

"Delhi is where the trust gap is largest. Officials there are unhappy with a number of decisions and policies from Trump's administration," Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the BBC.
But former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautions against reading too much into him skipping the capital.
"This was primarily an energy-focused visit," she says. "And after all, Rubio did meet the foreign minister in Mumbai."

The meeting between the two foreign ministers at the Taj Hotel covered trade, investment, energy security and defence cooperation, according to official statements. India's foreign ministry also said both sides welcomed progress in trade negotiations and reaffirmed their commitment to concluding a deal, which has long been in the works.
But once the diplomatic meetings were over, Rubio headed to Jamnagar, where the crown jewel of the Ambani business empire is located. This came to define the trip.
Shankar says the refinery visit "showed how much importance the US is attaching to getting more refined fuel into the market before the November midterms".
Reliance's Jamnagar complex can process about 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, roughly 1.5% of global refining capacity, according to the company website.
It is also a major exporter of diesel and other petroleum products, giving it a crucial role in global fuel markets.
During a tightly controlled visit on Wednesday, with limited media access, Rubio toured the facility and met members of the Ambani family, including Mukesh Ambani.

The company later released a statement, saying, "the visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy". It, however, did not specifically address any commitments to buy crude oil or supply refined products.
Just a day earlier, while speaking to the press, Rubio had called India a "refining superpower" and said the US wanted Reliance to process more Venezuelan oil.
"They have the capability to refine heavy crude. They've done so in the past, and I think as more and more Venezuelan oil comes online, that's something they could do," he told reporters.
Rubio added that oil from Venezuela "can certainly provide relief" in the short term and can possibly help ease supply pressures amid tensions in the Middle East.

Reliance was once among the largest buyers of Venezuelan crude before US sanctions disrupted trade. After Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US intervention earlier this year and Washington eased sanctions on the country's energy sector, Reliance re-emerged as a major importer.
Experts also say the visit might ease some tensions in the Delhi-Washington relationship over India's purchase of Russian oil.
India became one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil since Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2022.
Between December 2022 and July 2026, it accounted for 37% of Russia's crude oil exports, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
And Reliance was among the Indian companies that processed Russian crude.

In August 2025, US President Donald Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods over its Russian oil purchases, taking total tariffs on many Indian goods to 50%. The US, however, withdrew the additional penalty in February 2026 but India's import of Russian oil has continued to be an irritant in Washington-Delhi ties.
India has always said that securing affordable and reliable energy for its 1.4 billion people was its priority.
Then earlier this month, the US itself temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel.

In that context, experts say Rubio's Jamnagar visit is aligned to three goals that the US appears to be pursuing: reducing India's dependence on Russian crude, encouraging greater imports of Venezuelan and American oil, and advancing a trade deal in which energy cooperation could become a key area of agreement.
There is also another possible business angle behind this push.

Kugelman says Rubio had two reasons to meet the Ambani family. First, to secure greater refining of Venezuelan oil and second to seek assurances that Reliance remained interested in backing a proposed Texas refinery.
In March, Trump announced a proposed refinery at the Port of Brownsville in Texas on his Truth Social platform. He said that it would be the first major new refinery in the US in 50 years.
Reliance has not publicly commented on it and there are no details on the project or when the work is expected to begin.
"The Texas facility may not be as immediately important to US interests as the arrangement tied to Venezuelan oil, but I still think it's part of the story," he says.
However, analysts point out that closer cooperation with Reliance and progress on energy security do not necessarily mean a trade deal is imminent.

"I don't think anyone really expected a trade deal to be announced at this point, but this trip seems to have helped get the relationship back on track, to the extent that it can, given the significant points of tension that remain," Kugelman said.

Rajani Sinha, the chief economist at credit rating agency CareEdge, told the BBC that greater cooperation could allay energy security concerns in both countries, help push the stalled trade negotiations forward and "boost trade and sentiment" in India.
Meera Shankar says that India is possibly "waiting for the US to formalise its tariff positions so that we know whether Delhi has a preferential trade deal".
She adds that, although ties between the two countries have been strained in recent times, their bilateral trade continues to grow.

India's merchandise exports to the US was $50.81bn between April and September, up 11.1% from the previous year, according to India's ministry of commerce. Its imports rose to $32.33bn from $25.66bn in the same period. India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to $18.48bn from $20.07bn a year earlier.
"The economic relationship remains strong, but a long period of uncertainty could eventually affect it," Shankar said.
So, for now, the visit may have possibly helped get the relationship back on track, but whether that translates into a trade agreement or a lasting shift in energy ties remains to be seen.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 4:30pm
MANILA, Philippines — Announcing a P50-million bounty for the senator's arrest, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said he is done giving Sen. Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa special treatment.

"We have given him all the courtesy that could be afforded as a senator of the Republic of the Philippines, but he has shown nothing but cowardice by going into and remaining in hiding," Remulla said in a statement on Friday.
He also declared that "gloves are coming off" in efforts to capture him.

Remulla said November would mark one year since the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Dela Rosa over his alleged criminal responsibility for killings linked to the Duterte administration's war on drugs.
The DILG chief said Dela Rosa had mistaken his attempts at negotiation for weakness.
"It's time for the gloves to come off. It's time to bring just justice to his victims," Remulla said.
He also declared Dela Rosa "armed and dangerous" and announced the formation of a task force headed by Gen. Wilson Lopez, whose sole objective is to locate and arrest the senator.
Remulla said Lopez would provide further updates in the coming days. — Martin Ramos

articles.title: Israel orders home demolitions after soldiers killed in West Bank
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel is shutting down the occupied West Bank after having prevented a "major attack."

image.caption: The reported attack happened near the West Bank city of HebronImage: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Israeli Prime Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a massive operation in the West Bank, saying his country would "act to destroy this place" after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the West Bank city of Hebron on Friday morning.
Netanyahu said that Israeli forces would enter the attackers' neighborhood and displace its residents.

"We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed," Netanyahu said, according to his office.

The Israeli military said it killed the two attackers, and three Israeli soldiers had been lightly wounded in the attack that took place at a temporary military checkpoint at the entrance to Hebron on Friday.
The deadly shooting in Hebron comes four days before Israeli elections on October 27, the first to take place since the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.
The deadly shooting in West Bank: What to know
The Israeli far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for a military campaign in the West Bank, "exactly like in Gaza," in response to Friday's incident.

"There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign in Judea and Samaria to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon," Smotrich said, using the Israeli term for the West Bank.
He said he called for the demolition of buildings near the site of Friday's shooting.
"Following the attack, I have ordered the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site," he said.
"The order will be carried out within the next hour and will take place throughout the afternoon hours."
Smotrich, himself a settler in the West Bank, is widely known for championing ultranationalist and inflammatory policies.
He has previously made similar calls for "war" in the West Bank.
Netanyahu ordered closure of West Bank after Friday's shooting incident
Netanyahu said in an earlier statement on X that he had instructed the military to "impose a cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full closure of the entire West Bank starting today."
There was not much known about the Israeli operation in the West Bank at that time.
Israel has steadily tightened its grip in the occupied West Bank, having built dozens of outposts, considered illegal under international law, in the territory over the years.
Settler violence has been on the rise in the West Bank, which Israel occupied during the 1967 Six-Day War, with dozens of Palestinians having been killed since the start of the year.
Israeli elections take place next week: What to know
The incident comes at a critical time for Israel.

The Israeli election on October 27 is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, who has been criticized by opponents for failing to prevent the Hamas attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023.
Polls indicate that the elections will be a close race between the pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs.
Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger?
Despite international attention on Gaza and the West Bank, there is little difference between the two blocs regarding Israel's treatment of Palestinians.
Just days ago, masked Israeli settlers attacked a group of European diplomats and journalists in the West Bank as they accompanied Palestinians for the start of the annual olive harvest.

The IDF condemned the acts of violence and opened a rare investigation into the settlers. Both Israel's occupation and the settlements, which are dotted throughout the territory, are illegal under international law.

articles.title: Starlink access for Ukraine limited after Trump’s claims satellite service restored, officials say – Europe live
articles.summary:
The satellite service was still operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences

A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 22m agoDid Trump or Musk restrict Starshield access?
34m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight attacks:
Ukraine says Russia targeted energy sites in six different regions. Currently more than 500,000 people are without power.
Russia’s defence ministry confirmed strikes on Vilkovo port in Odesa, a railcar depot in Poltava and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.
Did Trump or Musk restrict Starshield access?

blocks.caption: Jonathan Yerushalmy

blocks.text: Jonathan Yerushalmy
A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink.

The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials.

The US president said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning. What has Trump said?

Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”
Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.

The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.

He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”.

What about Musk? Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.
Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.

Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.
Amid the war of words, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll begin in Ukraine.

Local authorities reported explosions overnight in Lutsk, a city not far from the Polish border, and in the central Poltava and southern Sumy regions. Russia this morning has also claimed strikes on ships in the Black Sea.
Both sides engaged in heavy strikes yesterday with Russia bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sending swarms of drones to Moscow.

Trump has declared that Starlink is once again running at full speed across Ukraine after the service was throttled last week -but Ukrainian and European officials say they haven’t seen that speed and functionality resume.

The satellite service was still only operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences and limiting mid-range strikes, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent after Trump’s comments. “Overall, nothing has changed anywhere,” the paper quoted the unnamed official saying.

Elsewhere we’re watching this continued wave of student-led protests across Europe. From Rome to Athens, Madrid and Paris, young people are venting their anger over the lack of resources in schools as well as wider housing and cost-of-living concerns. They’ve often been joined by their teachers in these ralies.

Fearing another weekend of street marches descending into violence and looting, French authorities have banned some protests over the coming days. President Emmanuel Macron, just returned from his mid-week tour to the Gulf states, is due to meet with student leaders around lunchtime in Paris.
It’s Frances Mao today in London, covering for Jakub, stay with me for all the developments.

articles.title: Government won’t put together ‘shopping list’ for public to stockpile for emergency – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Ministers have repeated several warnings in the last 18 months about the threat of hybrid attacks from overseas

Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal collectors to mark the start of the year’s campaign.
Burnham welcomed them to Number 10 North’s office in central Manchester, contrary to the usual convention of making a donation to the cause on the steps of Number 10 in Downing Street.

Good morning from London, where we’re less than a week from Andy Burnham and John Healey’s first budget, and the Government has been telling people to build up 72 hours of supplies in case of a disaster. We’ll be bringing you updates throughout the day. I’m Harry Taylor.

The Government has said that will not be putting together a “shopping list” for the public to buy in anticipation of a disaster, despite launching a campaign on Thursday which told people to stock up on supplies.
Treasury minister James Murray has been on the broadcast round this morning where has been asked about the announcement yesterday that people should assemble three days of supplies.
It’s come after repeated warnings in the last 18 months about cyber-attacks from overseas that could affect key systems.
It’s also timely as 32 Government services were taken offline yesterday after millions of attempts to exploit a weakness in numerous’ websites coding.
However Murray told Times Radio this morning: “This is not about the Government sending out a shopping list to everyone in the country.

“This is about putting the right information there on the government website, having an information campaign so that people are aware about it and then people taking the right choices for themselves about what they need to make sure they have supplies of at home.”
Meanwhile it’s five days until Healey’s budget, and Murray was asked on BBC Radio 4 whether he would be reducing red tape for business.
He said cutting “pointless bureaucracy” was “at the heart of what the Chancellor is going to be thinking about”.
Healey said the Treasury would aim to cut £800m of red tape for businesses at the budget, including reduced reporting requirements.

articles.title: Why Quebec's strategic reserve of maple syrup is running dry
articles.summary: Quebec maple syrup producers say the province's strategic reserve will be "completely depleted" by the end of February. What's going on?

image.caption: Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec, the group that represents nearly 13,500 maple syrup producers in the province, says the strategic reserve it oversees will be 'completely depleted' by the end of February. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: It's roughly the size of 53 Olympic swimming pools, but the world's only strategic reserve of maple syrup — spread out across three Quebec warehouses — is running dry.

Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ), the group that represents nearly 13,500 maple syrup producers in the province and oversees the reserve, said its stockpile will be "completely depleted" by the end of February.

According to PPAQ president Luc Goulet, that's largely because demand for Canadian maple syrup has soared around the world, including in the United States — the $1.2-billion industry's largest export market.
There has been a "sharp rise in exports," Goulet said in an interview with Radio-Canada's Midi-Info radio program this week.
"We have major challenges with the strategic reserve, which needs to be replenished. But we also have the challenge of developing our sector" to meet increased demand, he said.
So what exactly is going on, and should breakfast lovers be worried? Here's what we know.
Why more people are choosing Canadian maple syrup — instead of American
First, how does the reserve work?

Quebec's maple syrup producers set up the reserve in 2000 to try to stabilize supplies and prices, said Maurice Doyon, a professor at Laval University in Quebec City who specializes in agri-food economics.
The province produces 90 per cent of Canada's maple syrup and more than 70 per cent of the world’s supply.

items: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report

blocks.text: But the industry is heavily dependent on weather conditions: maple trees need regular springtime cycles of freezing and unfreezing to produce sap, which is transformed into syrup.
Is your maple syrup real or fake? It’s not that hard to tell
Before the reserve existed, Quebec producers would have to lower prices when supplies outpaced demand. Conversely, prices would go up when demand exceeded supply after bad harvests.
"The idea was to manage that a bit better," Doyon told CBC.
A quota system was also put in place in the early 2000s to regulate production levels.
Today, the reserve can hold as many roughly 60 million kilograms, or 218,000 barrels, of maple syrup. "When there's a bad harvest, [they] can dip into that reserve to supply the market," Doyon said.
So did Quebec have a bad harvest?
No. This time, the reserve is running dry because Quebec's authorized maple syrup processors — who buy, bottle, process and market the sticky stuff — appear to have bought out what was there.
The reserve held 39.4 million pounds (around 18 million kilograms) of maple syrup in February, the PPAQ said.

In an email to CBC News, the organization said while it expects the reserve to be depleted by the end of February "once all volumes under contract have been delivered to buyers," the overall supply remains similar to what it was a year ago.
"Inventories have simply shifted from the strategic reserve to buyers' warehouses. We estimate that buyers' inventories have increased by more than 35 million pounds [about 15.8 million kilograms]."
Cans of maple syrup sit at the Bistro La dent Sucre sugar shack in St. Eustache, Que., on April 6, 2021. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)
Why would processors buy from the reserve?

Doyon said processors don't have a strong incentive to dip into the reserve when it's full because they need to pay both for the syrup and to store what they don't immediately sell. But when the reserve is low, they are in competition with each other to secure their supply.
"It's initiated by the fact that the reserve is low," said Doyon, who likened buying up the reserve to taking out insurance.
"If disaster strikes — in other words, a bad harvest — they're going to be happy to have taken those precautions."
The Conseil de l'industrie de l'érable (CIE), which represents authorized processors in Quebec, said they "maintain inventories in their own warehouses to meet market needs throughout the year."
Asked how much maple syrup the processors have stored right now, the group told CBC it couldn't comment, citing confidential business practices.
"In a context where market growth is putting increased pressure on supply, our members must plan their needs flexibly to ensure business continuity and meet demand."
Why is there increased pressure on supply?
Both PPAQ and CIE say there has been a surge in global demand for maple syrup.
Canadian exports of maple products increased by 15.8 per cent in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to data provided by CIE. That followed a 9.3 per cent jump from 2023 to 2024.
Statistics Canada also said $844.2 million worth of Canadian maple products were exported last year — a 17.2 per cent increase from the previous year.
Inside the world’s only maple syrup reserve
What's fuelling demand internationally?

PPAQ's Goulet pointed to several factors, including uncertainty linked to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs, which have not hit the maple industry yet, as well as success in promoting Canadian maple syrup abroad.
Sixty-five per cent of all Canadian exports in 2025 went to the U.S., the CIE said. The next largest market was Germany at seven per cent, followed by the U.K. at five per cent.

items: International demand for Canadian maple syrup surges amid U.S. trade war
Why more people are choosing Canadian maple syrup — instead of American

blocks.text: Growing demand for "natural sweeteners" also has been credited with making maple syrup more popular, according to experts.
Will Quebec run out of maple syrup?
The PPAQ says it's not time to panic.

It said the processors' inventories coupled with an increase in the number of taps being installed across Quebec mean "there are no concerns about market supply in 2027, even if the upcoming crop is not particularly strong."
"That said, we are hoping for an exceptional season so that we can replenish the reserve."
Barrels of pasteurized maple syrup are stored at a strategic reserve warehouse in Plessisville, Que., on March 6. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
But will 'an exceptional season' be possible?
We can't say for sure. Doyon said there are ultimately only two ways to get more maple syrup: get more sap out of the trees that are already tapped or tap more trees.
But both those things could be easier said than done, said Guillaume Moreau, another professor at Laval University who specializes in maple syrup production.
Tapping more trees is a challenge because maple syrup producers are competing with other interests — notably the hardwood lumber industry — to gain access to forests on public lands in Quebec.
Climate change also has created new challenges for producers, who have seen harvest periods gradually shift earlier in the year due to fluctuating temperatures, Moreau said.
"We're having trouble to know ahead of time whether it will be a bad year."
And with the reserve now sitting empty and climate change fuelling uncertainty, "we're ultimately at the mercy of that uncertainty," he told CBC.

articles.title: A polarized Brazil heads to presidential vote Sunday with economy, corruption top of mind
articles.summary: Frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation driving voting choices as Brazil heads to presidential run-off on Sunday, Oct. 25.

image.caption: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left, is running for re-election against Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party. (REUTERS)

blocks.text: During a recent Bible study service in the Río de Janeiro neighbourhood of Vila Isabel, the congregation recited a prayer about God and being faithful.
Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, one of the congregants, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens.

"We have ... expectations that our country’s leadership would be concerned with meeting essential needs — such as health care and education —and that, at the very least, these areas would be properly cared for," she said.

Still undecided about who to vote for, Andrade said she was leaning toward Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45 year-old senator son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former Brazilian president convicted of plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Brazil's former president gets 27 years for plotting a coup in 2022 | Hanomansing Tonight
Andrade said Flávio Bolsonaro was a better candidate than his father.
"Bolsonaro … may waver between one extreme and the other at times, but I see a genuine interest on his part in finding balance," she said.
"I don't know if he'll succeed, but I'm not particularly concerned — his father engaged in corruption to the point of ending up in prison."
Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, centre, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens. (Douglas Engle/CBC)
Presidential race 'never this close,' journalist says

Flávio Bolsonaro — campaigning on tax cuts, a hard line on crime and family values — emerged from the first round of voting on Oct. 4 in Brazil's presidential election with about 2.2 million more votes than Lula, the 80-year-old incumbent.
Recent polls have shown the race between the two candidates tightening.
"It's really a toss of a coin," said Pedro Doria, editor of MEIO media group in Río de Janeiro.
Still, Doria said no presidential candidate who came in second after the first round of voting has ever won an election since 1989 — when the current electoral system was put in place.
"But it was never this close. Flávio's difference against Lula was 1.9 percentile points. This is basically nothing."

items: Lula and Bolsonaro head to run-off in Brazil's presidential election

blocks.text: Doria said that the Brazilian population is heavily polarized, and some voters are more motivated to vote against a candidate than in support of someone they believe in.
"A third of Lula's voters are not voting for Lula, they are voting against Bolsonaro," said Doria. "Half of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's voters are voting against Lula, not for Flávio."

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's Centre for International Relations Research, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro. (Courtesy of Marsílea Gombata)

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's Centre for International Relations Research, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro despite the actions of his father and the candidate's own record of controversy.

Bolsonaro has in the past been tied to paramilitary groups — he praised them in a two decade-old speech while a state deputy, and his office once employed the mother and wife of the founder of a paramilitary group linked to the killing of a human rights activist.

items: See the Amazon rainforest wildfires that have politicians pointing fingers amid Brazil presidential elections

blocks.text: Bolsonaro's father's coup-plotting conviction — which included allegations there were plans to assassinate Lula — and subsequent 27-year sentence has had limited impact on Flávio Bolsonaro's support, said Gombata.
"We can see that it doesn't matter to people."

While Lula, who previously served two presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, strengthened and reintroduced social programs in his last term to help the poor such as Bolsa Familia, which provides conditional direct cash transfers to families, a large swath of the population has felt left out, said Gombata.
The lower middle class, where many work a second job in the gig economy, has felt "betrayed" by Lula's promises of prosperity that, they believe, never materialized for them.
"They were hoping for a better life, for their children, but it didn't happen and today life is more difficult," said Gombata.
Bolsonaro's promises of tax cuts for fuel, electricity and transport, as well as reductions in government spending appeals to this segment of the population, she said.
Paulo Coelho, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, 64, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro. (Douglas Engle/CBC)

The 2014 Operation Carwash investigation, which ensnared several top officials in Lula's Workers Party and Lula himself — until the Supreme Court overturned his corruption-related conviction in 2021 — still casts a long shadow, Gombata said.
"We are still living those consequences … the theme of corruption is a big one."
Both candidates facing corruption probes
Bolsonaro has been side-swiped during the election campaign by his own corruption allegations.

It recently emerged that Bolsonaro requested and received millions of dollars for a documentary about Jair Bolosonaro from a key player in a major bank fraud case. Flávio is also under investigation in relation to the case.
However, Lula has faced his own troubles. His son is under a separate influence peddling and corruption probe ordered by the Supreme Court, Reuters reported.
Paulo Coelho, 64, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro.
"Everyone is worried about slowing economic activity in Brazil," he said.
"Flávio Bolsonaro has an economic plan and vision that I am more aligned with."
The Brazil election's U.S. factor

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries a Bolsonaro government will sever the social safety nets that have kept many people from misery.
"I have three children, ages 15, 11 and five, and I don’t want to jeopardize their future," she said.
"There is a real risk to our population given the stances they've taken on social issues."

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries that a Bolsonaro government will lead to a severing of social safety nets. (Douglas Engel/CBC)
Solange Marquez, vice-president of policy with the Canadian Council for the Americas, says Sunday's results could impact Brazil's relationship with the United States.

The close relationship between the Bolsonaro family — Flávio is one of three brothers — and the U.S. administration of Donald Trump could lead to an escalation of U.S. military involvement in South America through boots on the ground in Brazil in joint security operations against armed drug trafficking groups, said Marquez.
"I think [Flávio] Bolsonaro is eager to open the door to Donald Trump in exchange for a better economic, commercial relationship with Washington."
Trump threatens 50% tariff on Brazil over Bolsonaro trial
U.S. boots on Brazilian soil is something that worries retiree Carlos Vitor, 65, who voted twice for the elder Bolsonaro. This time, he says, he's voting for Lula.
"I’m afraid that the United States might invade Brazil because of the drug traffickers," he said.
Vitor said a Flávio win will magnify the deep divisions that currently exist within the country and possibly lead to violence.
"The left, they're going to fight. If Flávio wins, they're going to fight," he said.
"Will this place turn into a civil war? For sure."

articles.title: Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year
articles.summary: Searches of electronic devices such as phones and laptops of travellers entering the United States are up more than 32 per cent this year and are on track to set a new record, CBC News has learned.

image.caption: The U.S. agency responsible for land and air crossings is searching more personal devices. Its first fiscal year of the second Trump administration hit a record 55,424 searches, and its second fiscal year is on track to surpass that figure. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Searches of electronic devices such as phones and laptops of travellers entering the United States are up more than 32 per cent this year and are on track to set a new record, CBC News has learned.
After a record fiscal 2025, customs officers on track to search even more devices

Searches of electronic devices such as phones and laptops of travellers entering the United States are up more than 32 per cent this year and are on track to set a new record, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data obtained by CBC News.

The numbers show that during the first three quarters of its 2026 fiscal year, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, CBP officers searched 52,080 electronic devices. During the same period the previous year, CBP searched 39,251 devices.
In fact, CBP searched almost as many devices in the first three quarters of 2026 as it did during the entire 2025 fiscal year, when a record 55,424 devices were searched.

According to CBP, 47,517 were basic searches, which can be done by an officer without any reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing. Another 4,564 were advanced searches, which allow an officer who believes there is a reasonable suspicion of an activity that violates the law or a national security concern to analyze and/or copy the contents of an electronic device.

items: Canada updates travel advice to warn of U.S. border officers' power to search electronic devices

blocks.text: However, the customs agency won't reveal what percentage of the searches took place at the northern border with Canada or the southern border with Mexico. Nor would it provide a breakdown between searches at airports versus land borders or a breakdown by land border posts.

It also would not say how many travellers entered the U.S. during the first three quarters of 2026 or how many searches targeted U.S. citizens versus non-U.S. citizens — numbers it generally provides in its annual reports.

Jessica Turner, public affairs officer with CBP, said in 2025, the searches only affected a small fraction of the 419 million travellers who entered the U.S. and searches of electronic devices "remains exceedingly rare."

"CBP's border searches of electronic device numbers are consistent with increases since 2021, and year-over-year only 0.01 per cent of travellers have their devices searched," Turner wrote in an emailed response.
"These searches are conducted to detect digital contraband, terrorism-related content and information relevant to visitor admissibility, all of which play a critical role in national security."

However, Esha Bhandari, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Speech, Privacy and Technology Project, says the increase in searches of electronic devices by U.S. border officials requires more congressional oversight and accountability.

"It's hard to speculate on the reasons for the increase because the government doesn't explain it," she said. "But I think what we're seeing is a classic example of when the government has the power to do something, it will exercise that authority to the detriment of travellers' privacy."
Bhandari said the aggregate numbers provided by the U.S. government make it difficult to "really get a handle on what's going on."
However, she said the anecdotal evidence her group hears is "certainly troubling."

"They're often asked questions at the border about their political opinions or perhaps their writing or things related to their religious practice that might suggest that's the reason they've been singled out for a search," she said.

In January, CBP updated its guidelines governing searches of electronic devices at the border to spell out that it included devices like flash drives, SIM cards, GPS systems, unmanned aircraft systems, vehicle infotainment systems and smart watches. It also added smuggling narcotics, firearms or other goods and transnational theft of proprietary information and digital contraband to the list of crimes the searches are designed to detect.

But Bhandari says the new directives only changed "a few procedures at the margins." She believes the increase in searches may have more to do with advances in technology and the failure of federal courts to put limits on the government's authority to conduct them.

items: U.S. customs searched a record number of electronic devices last year
Canadians caught in crossfire as searches of devices rise at U.S. borders

blocks.text: Laura Dawson, executive director of the Future Borders Coalition, which focuses on cross-border issues, said the increase in searches is difficult to assess without knowing where they took place and the number of people who travelled to the U.S. during that period.
"These searches are taking place not just at land borders, but also at seaports, at airports and there's lots of people coming in and out. And we had World Cup this summer," she said.
"It could be a greater diversity of traveller coming in."
Dawson said she is also seeing more focus on border security and more co-operation between Canadian and U.S. border services in areas such as human smuggling and the Ryan Wedding case.

items: Ryan Wedding murder trial delayed to 2027 due to 'unusual and complex' case

blocks.text: "Having more scrutiny at the border is actually a positive in many ways," she said.

While Canadians may be alarmed by stories shared on social media of device searches at the border, Dawson points out that the practice is still rare. She said one in 9,000 border crossings result in a U.S. inspection and one in 14,000 crossings result in a search on the Canadian side of the border.

In recent years, Canadian officials have searched a much smaller percentage of devices at the border than their U.S. counterparts and the numbers have been dropping. Canada Border Services Agency officials say statistics on the number of electronic device searches carried out in 2026 are not yet available.

articles.title: How the Brewers and Rays got to baseball's biggest stage with small budgets and small ball
articles.summary: A new World Series champion will be crowned this year, as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy. Here's how they…

image.caption: The Milwaukee Brewers are getting ready to do battle with the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series. The best-of-seven Fall Classic begins Friday evening. (Ashley Landis/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

A new World Series champion will be crowned this year, as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy. Here's how they got there and what to expect.
Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, two of MLB's lowest-spending teams, have the chance to make history this season
A new World Series champion will be crowned as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy.
Neither franchise has won it all before, meaning it will be a history-making outcome no matter who wins the Fall Classic.

Ahead of the first game in the best-of-seven series on Friday, we're taking a look at how the Brew Crew and the D-Rays got here, the Canadian connections, their World Series records and what it means to see two teams with relatively small payrolls make it this far into the playoffs
Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates his team's Game 6 victory over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. (David J. Phillip/The Associated Press)
Comparatively puny payrolls
Milwaukee and Tampa are in the bottom-half of MLB's 30 franchises when it comes to payroll spending.

The Brewers had an Opening Day roster payroll of just over $124 million US — 19th in the majors according to The Associated Press. The Rays' payroll was just $88.7 million US, ranked 26th at that time.
Compare that to Toronto's Opening Day payroll of nearly $269 million US, the fifth-highest in baseball. And yet, the Jays missed the playoffs.
The deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers had a payroll of nearly $317 million US at the season's start. And while they made the playoffs, they got swept — by the Brewers.

items: Shorter regular season among drastic changes MLB proposes to players
Baseball labour talks have begun — here's what could be in store for the league and the Jays

blocks.text: None of this is helping the argument of the MLB owners, who are pushing for a salary cap to be established in the league, arguing that baseball's richest teams are too dominant. It's all part of negotiations taking place as baseball's current five-year deal expires in December.
The Associated Press says this year's World Series marks the first time since 1991 that two teams with payrolls in the bottom half of the majors will compete for the title.

Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers hits a home run in Game 3 of the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Bauers led his team with 26 homers during the regular season. (Kiyoshi Mio/Imagn Images/Reuters)
Homer drought
The Brewers were tied for the second-lowest, regular-season home-run total, with just 154 round-trippers. Only the Blue Jays hit fewer home runs (152).
Despite this power outage, Milwaukee put together a 103-59 season — the best in the game.
Tampa's lineup slugged 169 homers prior to the playoffs, which put them at 22nd in the majors. The Rays wrapped their regular season with a 98-64 record.
Toronto Blue Jays leave fans with little to cheer about
The power of 'small ball'

The strategy of small ball — getting runners on base and advancing them by stealing bases or putting the ball in play with sacrifice hits and bunts — was key for both Milwaukee and Tampa as they outplayed rivals in their respective leagues.
The Rays led the majors with 45 sacrifice bunts during the regular season. The Brewers had 37, the fifth-most overall.
The two teams also stole a ton of bases: The Rays swiped 164 bases prior to the playoffs, while Millwaukee claimed 162.

This year's World Series could be the first with a 104-mile-per-hour pitch, thanks to Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski. The 24-year-old threw a record 1,115 pitches of 100 miles per hour or higher in his first full major league season. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)
Triple-digit heat
The Brewers' ace starting pitcher, Jacob Misiorowski, is the most prolific, hard-throwing pitcher in the game.
He's thrown more than 1,100 pitches at speeds exceeding 100 miles per hour this season.

items: Surprising Rays-Brewers showdown to open Friday with Jacob Misiorowski's record heat

blocks.text: Misiorowski has already set the record for the fastest pitch thrown in a playoff game (104.8 miles per hour) — at least, since tracking started in 2008. Amazingly, that's not the hardest pitch he's ever thrown.
He's slated to start Game 1 for the Brewers on Friday night.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Freddy Peralta and catcher Liam Hicks celebrate after a strikeout in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians on Oct. 13. (Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)
Canadian catcher
Toronto-born ballplayer Liam Hicks joined the Rays at the trade deadline.
The 27-year-old catcher is in his second big-league season, joining Tampa in August, after first getting to the big leagues with the nearby Miami Marlins.

items: Liam Hicks spent teenage years in Toronto area before baseball career blossomed

blocks.text: So far this post-season, Hicks has six hits, one run, three walks and four RBIs across nine games he's played with the Rays.

Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash has served as the team's skipper for 12 seasons — including in 2020, when the Rays played in the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. (Kim Klement Neitzel/Imagn Images/Reuters)
The ex-Jays catcher
Rays manager Kevin Cash was a player before he was a manager and started out his major-league career in Toronto.
Cash appeared in 101 games for the Jays from 2002-2004. He later played for the Rays, the Boston Red Sox, the New York Yankees and the Houston Astros.
He's managed the Rays for 12 seasons, including in 2020 when Tampa lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
A long wait for Brewers fans
Milwaukee last made it to the World Series in 1982 — back when Ronald Reagan was in the White House, and years before any of the current Brewers players were born.
The Brewers lost in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Hall of Famer Robin Yount was part of the Milwaukee team that lost to St. Louis, and he recently said he'll "never get over it until the Brewers win one."
On Tampa's side, the Rays have been to the World Series twice, losing both times: First in 2008 and again in 2020.
Brewer Robin Yount plays in Game 4 of the 1982 World Series against the St. Louis Cardinals, which the Brewers went on to lose. (The Associated Press)
Where to watch
Canadian baseball fans can catch the World Series on Sportsnet.
Most games will air on the main Sportsnet channel — except for Games 2 and Game 7 (if necessary), which will run on Sportsnet One.
All games will also stream on Sportsnet+.
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North again
articles.summary: South Korea is attempting to mutually determine the land border with North Korea amid military incidents and escalating tensions.

image.caption: The DMZ is the four-kilometer-wide strip of land that has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday proposed military talks with North Korea in an attempt to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels.
The ministry said it had proposed talks last November to resolve differences over the line, and reduce the risk of accidental deaths, but Pyongyang had not responded.
Why is South Korea proposing talks with the north?

The latest proposal, announced by Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy Kim Hong-cheol, follows a landmine blast in the demiliterized zone (DMZ) in September that injured three South Korean soldiers.

North Korean troops have been building tactical roads, fences and been laying mines in the DMZ in the recent years. South Korea's Kim said the North's troops have repeatedly crossed the line in the process.
Seoul's military also concluded that North Korea had buried mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) which caused the recent blast. Pyongyang has rejected those findings.
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs
Avoiding future incidents on the Korean peninsula

Miliatry tensions between the two Koreas has been escalating. Just days ago, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong announced that Pyongyang had moved new troops into "firing position" along the border.
She later said the North would also place loudspeakers on standby along the border, a repeated move of aggression aimed at harassing South Korean soldiers and villages along the border.
Jin Yong-sung, chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, also ordered the military to "respond with firm resolve" should North Korea use Seoul's actions as a pretext for aggressive action.

It is difficult to predict "what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed," the South's Defense Ministry said on Friday, adding that they hoped for a positive response from their rival neighbor.
It also proposed the option of "three-way talks involving the United Nations Command would also be possible."

articles.title: Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return
articles.summary: Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

image.caption: The U15 World Cup has been met with some criticism, and not just because of Russia's participationImage: Patrick Reichardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the under-15 boys World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."
Rejection continuation of German caution, Moukoko an exception

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.
That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.
Youssoufa Moukoko: Bundesliga's youngest-ever player

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But it is a part of the game often poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."
Germany not alone in declining invitation to tournament

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February that: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.
"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."
FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

blocks.caption: Some believe Arsène Wenger (left) is the man to replace Gianni Infantino as the head of FIFAImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers."

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

articles.title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
articles.summary:
Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer…

blocks.text: The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.

From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.

Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.

blocks.caption: Sarojam Radhakrishan initiated the court action after being unable to pay for her cancer drugs. Photograph: Facebook

blocks.text: The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.

A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.

“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.

Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.

As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.

Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.

Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.

“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.

As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.

“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.

Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.

The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

articles.title: Claire Castro to retain post as all PCO execs file courtesy resignations
articles.summary: Acting Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano will not accept the courtesy resignation of Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, he said on Friday, October 23.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 2:44pm
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro on October 20, 2026
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Acting Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano will not accept the courtesy resignation of Palace Press Officer Claire Castro.

Cayetano confirmed this in an interview with reporters on Friday, October 23, where he also said all undersecretaries and assistant secretaries of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) were asked to file courtesy resignations.

Cayetano gave no timeline for acting on the other resignations. He told reporters that evaluating his team would be an ongoing process rather than a one-time reshuffle, with some decisions coming within days and others months later.

“Usec. Claire, I don’t want to say we’re a package deal, but Usec. Claire is a treasure in this government,” Cayetano said in mixed English and Filipino. “I haven’t seen someone articulate [that] well what this government is doing.”

Without giving further details, Cayetano said the PCO currently has an "innovation" that he wants Castro to be a part of. "In this age of digitalization, we want an analog office. I think the PCO also needs to focus on being on the ground," he said.
Cayetano was all praise for Castro's combative style of responding to issues and affirmed he would like both of them to continue working closely.
"In terms of being combative (sic) and protecting what this administration is doing, to explain [why we do what we do], I admire Usec. Claire," he added.

"For me, that's the strength of Usec. Claire. That's her personality. We will balance that out, that if there is a need to explain a policy, we will invite the relevant department or Cabinet secretary [during briefings]," Cayetano said.

Cayetano became the PCO’s head after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced during a press interview in Singapore on October 11 that he was replacing Dave Gomez, whose appointment had been bypassed by the Commission on Appointments.

He took his oath in Malacañang on October 13, becoming the sixth official to lead the PCO under the Marcos administration, after Trixie Cruz-Angeles, Cheloy Velicaria-Garafil, Cesar Chavez, Jay Ruiz and Gomez.
A former Taguig City mayor and television director, he had been general manager of state-run PTV-4, a PCO-attached corporation, since June.
This is the third leadership transition Castro has been a part of since she entered the PCO.
Asked whose resignations he would accept, Cayetano said: “That will be a process as long as I am here.”

articles.title: Taiwan braces as El Nino-supercharged Typhoon Champi approaches island
articles.summary: One person has died and thousands have been evacuated as Taiwan prepares for a possible direct hit. Though no longer a "super" typhoon, Champi is still packing winds of nearly 200 kmh and will bring…

image.caption: One person was killed after being swept away by waves reaching heights of up to 10 meters (33 feet) while thousands have been evacuated to higher groundImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: Taiwan is bracing for potential impact as Typhoon Champi bears down on the island after weakening slightly, with nearly all businesses, shops and schools closed.
Over 1,300 people have been forced to evacuate to higher ground, and hundreds of flights have been cancelled across the region according to the Ministry of Transportation.
At least one person has already been killed after being swept out to sea and dozens more have been injured.
What do we know about Typhoon Champi?

On Friday, locals were still busy installing sandbags and metal barriers in front of doors and windows to defend against flooding, while authorities positioned inflatable boats and amphibious vehicles around the island to aid in rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: Shops and houses have been boarded up in preparation for Champi's arrivalImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: In the capital Taipei, public transport was still operating, but at reduced capacity.
Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA) says Champi is currently about 220 kilometers (137 miles) east of the island's southern shore.

The storm is projected to move past Taiwan's northeastern shore before turning north to China and eventually moving east into southern Japan. But forecasters say that any deviation from its current course could mean a direct hit for Taiwan.
Why are there so many big storms in the Pacific this year?

The storm is expected to bring torrential rain, massive waves and sustained high winds to Taiwan throughout Friday and Saturday. Military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts throughout.

"As it approaches Taiwan's northeastern tip, the typhoon may slow down. If it slows down, its impact will last longer," CWA Administrator Lu Kuo-chen told reporters, adding, "People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow."
Forecasters say the storm's radius is currently about 320 kilometers, wide enough to blanket most of the island.

blocks.caption: Though no longer a 'super typhoon' Champi has maintained high winds and has a footprint big enough to cover all of TaiwanImage: CSU/CIRA/JMA/JAXA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Fueled by this year's exceptionally strong El Nino season — a cyclical weather phenomenon that sees water temperatures in the tropical Pacific rise, in turn turbocharging storms, or inversely droughts — Champi attained "super typhoon" status as it built strength during its approach, with winds clocking 298 kmh (185 mph).
Though it has weakened, the CWA says Champi is still packing wind gusts of about 190 kmh as it approaches from the southwest.

This year's El Nino phase, which the United Nations on Wednesday described as "heading off the charts," is expected to peak in December. It's impact however, could last years, with the UN urging nations in the Pacific to prepare for the worst.
What happens when El Nino meets climate change?
